cases.name: ho-h-checkpoint-response-rnaseq
cases.promptMarkdown: I'm a bioinformatics postdoc building a classifier that predicts response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1 or anti-CTLA-4) from pre-treatment tumour RNA-seq. I need cohorts of patients who actually received checkpoint inhibitors, with bulk expression data and a recorded clinical response (RECIST or clinical benefit), ideally several independent cohorts so I can validate across studies. Any cancer type is fine. Where can I get these, and which ones can I download right away versus having to apply for?

graders.name: 01-recall-imvigor210
graders.evidence:
## What I assumed you need

- **R1 (must):** patients received anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1 or anti-CTLA-4.
- **R2 (must):** pre-treatment bulk tumour RNA-seq.
- **R3 (must):** recorded RECIST or clinical-benefit response.
- I assumed any cancer type is fine and that you can wait for a controlled-access application.

**How much I checked:** I confirmed very little today. The registry tool covers Zenodo, OpenAIRE and DataCite, not GEO, EGA or dbGaP, and its hits were mostly noise. The GEO, PMC and ENA pages came back as bot challenges or JavaScript shells, and dbGaP redirected one link to its home page. The only access page I actually read was IMvigor210's. Everything else is from memory, so open each link in a browser before you plan around it.

## Shortlist

| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Riaz 2017, melanoma, nivolumab (GSE91061) | Open on GEO | Not stated | ~50 patients | Strong | From memory |
| 2 | Hugo 2016, melanoma, pembrolizumab (GSE78220) | Open on GEO | Not stated | ~28 patients | Strong | From memory |
| 3 | Gide 2019, melanoma, anti-PD-1 ± anti-CTLA-4 (PRJEB23709) | Probably open via ENA, plus paper supplement | Not stated | ~90 patients | Strong | From memory |
| 4 | Mariathasan 2018 (IMvigor210), urothelial, atezolizumab | Processed data: open R package. Raw data: EGA application | Not stated | ~300 patients | Strong | Page read today |
| 5 | Kim 2018, gastric, pembrolizumab (PRJEB25780) | Likely open (ENA) | Not stated | ~45 patients | Partial | From memory |
| 6 | Liu 2019 / Van Allen 2015, melanoma (dbGaP phs000452) | dbGaP application, weeks to months | dbGaP terms | ~120 patients | Partial | From memory |
| 7 | Braun 2020, renal, nivolumab (CheckMate 009/010/025) | dbGaP application (accession unconfirmed) | dbGaP terms | RNA-seq on a subset | Partial | From memory |
| 8 | Cho 2020 / Jung 2019, NSCLC (GSE126044) | Open on GEO | Not stated | Small | Unknown | From memory |

## Details

- **Open now, from memory (rows 1, 2, 8):** these are GEO series. Download the expression tables from GEO, and take the response labels from each paper's supplement. Riaz includes patients who had already progressed on ipilimumab. For Hugo, check which samples are pre-treatment. For row 8, I haven't checked the platform, treatment or response labels.
- **Gide and Kim (rows 3, 5):** the reads are in ENA. Check the data availability statements for what is processed and what is controlled. I could not load the ENA pages.
- **IMvigor210 (row 4):** this is the only one I confirmed. The page at http://research-pub.gene.com/IMvigor210CoreBiologies/ says:
  - Processed data come with the `IMvigor210CoreBiologies` R package.
  - "The human raw gene expression data will be availabe at the European Genome-phenome archive (EGA) under the accession number EGAS00001002556."
  - The EGA data are the controlled-access part. The package licence is not stated on the page.
  - The cohort is anti-PD-L1 only, and my first attempt to fetch the page failed with a connection error before a later read worked.
- **dbGaP cohorts (rows 6, 7):**
  - Access needs a Data Access Request approved by your institution's signing official, which usually takes weeks to months.
  - The Liu and Van Allen data are mostly exome, so confirm RNA-seq coverage.
  - The Braun accession (phs002277) is my recollection. Its link redirected to the dbGaP home page, so don't trust it yet.
  - Row 6 merges two studies under one accession, and I am not certain both are there.

## Known, not confirmed

- **Larger cohorts from memory:** I recall a Lee et al. cohort at EGA (EGAD00001005738, from a web search result) and a Miao 2018 renal dataset at dbGaP phs001519. I have not confirmed either one's contents.
- **More cohorts via curated resources:** ICBatlas (25 studies, 1,515 samples), the 2023 ICB benchmark (PMC10452274, 29 datasets) and IOhub (36 bulk datasets) list the accessions. None of them is verified, and I could not open any of the tables. Start there for more cohorts, and use ICBatlas Table S1 for accessions.
- **Cross-cohort caution:** an arXiv preprint (2604.05478) is titled "Transcriptomic Models for Immunotherapy Response Prediction Show Limited Cross-cohort Generalisability". I only saw the title and have not read it.

## Not recommended

- **TCGA:** the patients were mostly not treated with checkpoint inhibitors, so there are no response labels.

## What I could not find

- No GEO, EGA or dbGaP accession was confirmed through its own registry page.
- Licences are mostly unstated. GEO data are public, but reuse terms depend on the submitters.
- The tool found no papers using these cohorts for response prediction beyond the IMvigor210 paper.

## Next step

1. Pull the accession tables from ICBatlas and the 2023 benchmark. Together they should give you the 5–10 independent cohorts you want.
2. Start the dbGaP and EGA applications now, since they take the longest, and build on the open GEO cohorts in the meantime.

I checked on 2026-11-12. The interactive page is at `/private/tmp/e-jYACS9/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

graders.name: 01-recall-imvigor210
graders.evidence:
Several well-used cohorts are open downloads, and the largest trial cohorts need a controlled-access application. Access terms below are as of 2026-11-12. I checked most of them through web search and the COMPASS portal. I could not open GEO, PMC or the ENA browser from here, because they returned bot challenges, so I never saw those records directly.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** patients treated with anti-PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4, with a pre-treatment bulk tumour RNA-seq sample.
- **R2 (must):** a response label (RECIST responder vs non-responder, or clinical benefit).
- **R3 (must):** several independent cohorts, so you can train on some and validate on others.
- **R4 (nice):** a download you can start today. Any cancer type is fine.

## Shortlist
Sizes are responders/non-responders (R/NR) as listed on COMPASS, a portal that curates these cohorts. The "Checked" column says how I know the access condition.

| # | Cohort | Cancer / drug | n (R/NR) | Access | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hugo 2016, GSE78220 | Melanoma, anti-PD-1 | 26 (14/12) | **Open** (GEO) | COMPASS and a paper's data statement; GEO page not opened |
| 2 | Riaz 2017, GSE91061 / PRJNA356761 | Melanoma, nivolumab | 51 (10/41) | **Open** (GEO/SRA) | Same as above |
| 3 | Gide 2019, PRJEB23709 | Melanoma, anti-PD-1 ± CTLA-4 | 73 (40/33) | **Open** (ENA) | Same as above |
| 4 | Kim 2018, PRJEB25780 | Gastric, pembrolizumab | 45 (12/33) | **Open** (ENA) | Same as above |
| 5 | Rose 2021, GSE176307 | Bladder, ICI | 89 (16/73) | **Open** (GEO) | COMPASS only |
| 6 | Zhao 2019, PRJNA482620 | Glioblastoma, anti-PD-1 | 25 (11/14) | **Open** (SRA) | COMPASS only |
| 7 | Snyder 2017 | Bladder, atezolizumab | 21 (7/14) | **Open** (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.546110) | Conflict, see below |
| 8 | IMvigor210 | Bladder, atezolizumab | 298 (68/230) | **Open processed data**, controlled raw data | Confirmed by search |
| 9 | Liu 2019 and Van Allen 2015, dbGaP phs000452 | Melanoma, anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4 | ~107 and ~39 | **Controlled** (dbGaP) | Confirmed by search |
| 10 | Braun 2020 (CheckMate 025), Miao 2018 (CheckMate 009) | Kidney, nivolumab | ~17 for Miao; Braun larger | **Controlled** (EGA / dbGaP phs001493) | Accessions confirmed; Braun access terms not confirmed |
| 11 | Ravi 2023 (SU2C-MARK), dbGaP phs002822 | NSCLC, ICI | 102 LUAD and 25 LUSC | **Controlled** (dbGaP) | COMPASS only |
| 12 | IMmotion150, EGAS00001002928 | Kidney, atezolizumab ± bevacizumab | 165 (48/117) | **Controlled** (EGA) | COMPASS only |

## Details
**Open and ready now (rows 1–7).**
- These are raw reads or counts in GEO, SRA, ENA or Zenodo, with response labels in the paper supplements.
- **Riaz and Gide** include on-treatment biopsies as well as baseline ones. Filter to pre-treatment samples, or your "pre-treatment" classifier will leak.
- **Gide** mixes monotherapy and combination arms.
- **Hugo** is small, and I did not check how many of its samples are pre-treatment.
- **COMPASS** (immuno-compass.com/download) lists 23 cohorts with clinical TSVs. For the open cohorts, its mRNA links point to a `data_request.md` file. I could not tell whether that means a request step, so treat COMPASS expression data as unconfirmed.
- **Snyder conflict:** COMPASS attributes Zenodo 546110 to Snyder. A separate paper's data statement attributes that DOI to the IMvigor210 RNA-seq. Check the Zenodo record before you rely on it.

**IMvigor210 (row 8).**
- **Raw data:** controlled access at EGA, study EGAS00001002556. You request access through the EGA study page.
- **Processed data:** Genentech distributes the `IMvigor210CoreBiologies` R package, with counts and clinical data for 348 patients. Response is available for 298 of them. The package is at `research-pub.gene.com/IMvigor210CoreBiologies/`, and it is how most papers use this cohort. I have not confirmed its licence.
- **Other atezolizumab data:** IMvigor211 and OAK appear on EGA (EGAD00001007703, EGAD00001008391, EGAS50000000497), also controlled. I did not check what response data they carry.

**Controlled cohorts (rows 9–12).**
- **dbGaP:** you need an eNRA account, a data access request, and institutional signing-official approval. Expect weeks to months.
- **EGA:** you submit a request to the study's Data Access Committee, and it needs a signed agreement. Expect weeks to months, from memory.
- **Braun 2020:** a later paper reports that CheckMate 025 normalised RNA-seq is at EGAS00001004290, EGAS00001004291 and EGAS00001004292. I did not confirm who approves access.
- **Fallback for processed data:** check each paper's supplement for processed tables. Several of these studies publish normalised expression there. I haven't confirmed this for any of the controlled cohorts.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Compilation portals:** TIDE (tide.dfci.harvard.edu), CRI iAtlas, ICBatlas, Cancer-Immu and ICBcomb all curate ICI cohorts. The web search described them, but I did not open them or check their terms. They are worth trying because they can save you the harmonisation work. Whatever they redistribute cannot be more open than the original source.
- **Other cohorts:** COMPASS lists Freeman (MGH, melanoma, dbGaP phs002683) and Choueiri (kidney, via CRI iAtlas, n=16). I have not verified either.
- **Cohorts I know of but did not search for:** Auslander 2018 (melanoma, possibly GSE115821), and a few NSCLC cohorts. Their accessions are from memory, so confirm them before use.

## Not recommended, and why
- **TCGA** has no checkpoint-treatment or response labels.
- **Microarray or NanoString cohorts**, such as Prat 2017 and Cristescu 2018, are not bulk RNA-seq. They would complicate cross-platform validation.
- **Scripta/single-cell ICI datasets** (the Curated Cancer Cell Atlas, for example) are single-cell, not bulk.

## What I could not find
- I did not check each cohort's response definition (RECIST vs clinical benefit). It differs between papers, so harmonise it before pooling.
- The registry search in the skill's tool (Zenodo, DataCite, OpenAIRE) returned mostly noise, because these cohorts live in GEO, ENA, EGA and dbGaP, which that tool doesn't cover. This list is therefore built from the literature and web search, and it may be incomplete.
- I did not build the interactive shortlist page, because I ran out of reliable registry data to put in it.

## Next step
1. **Today:** download rows 1–6 (melanoma ×3, gastric, bladder, GBM) and filter to baseline samples. That gives you about 300 patients across three cancers.
2. **Start the dbGaP and EGA requests now** (rows 8–12), since they run in the background for weeks. IMvigor210 is the highest value, because the processed R package gives you ~300 patients with no wait.
3. **Pick a validation strategy:** train on melanoma and validate on bladder and gastric. Also consider leaving one cohort out at a time, since cohorts differ by cancer type and by whether the antibody targets PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4.

graders.name: 02-recall-riaz2017
graders.evidence:
Several well-used cohorts are open downloads, and the largest trial cohorts need a controlled-access application. Access terms below are as of 2026-11-12. I checked most of them through web search and the COMPASS portal. I could not open GEO, PMC or the ENA browser from here, because they returned bot challenges, so I never saw those records directly.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** patients treated with anti-PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4, with a pre-treatment bulk tumour RNA-seq sample.
- **R2 (must):** a response label (RECIST responder vs non-responder, or clinical benefit).
- **R3 (must):** several independent cohorts, so you can train on some and validate on others.
- **R4 (nice):** a download you can start today. Any cancer type is fine.

## Shortlist
Sizes are responders/non-responders (R/NR) as listed on COMPASS, a portal that curates these cohorts. The "Checked" column says how I know the access condition.

| # | Cohort | Cancer / drug | n (R/NR) | Access | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hugo 2016, GSE78220 | Melanoma, anti-PD-1 | 26 (14/12) | **Open** (GEO) | COMPASS and a paper's data statement; GEO page not opened |
| 2 | Riaz 2017, GSE91061 / PRJNA356761 | Melanoma, nivolumab | 51 (10/41) | **Open** (GEO/SRA) | Same as above |
| 3 | Gide 2019, PRJEB23709 | Melanoma, anti-PD-1 ± CTLA-4 | 73 (40/33) | **Open** (ENA) | Same as above |
| 4 | Kim 2018, PRJEB25780 | Gastric, pembrolizumab | 45 (12/33) | **Open** (ENA) | Same as above |
| 5 | Rose 2021, GSE176307 | Bladder, ICI | 89 (16/73) | **Open** (GEO) | COMPASS only |
| 6 | Zhao 2019, PRJNA482620 | Glioblastoma, anti-PD-1 | 25 (11/14) | **Open** (SRA) | COMPASS only |
| 7 | Snyder 2017 | Bladder, atezolizumab | 21 (7/14) | **Open** (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.546110) | Conflict, see below |
| 8 | IMvigor210 | Bladder, atezolizumab | 298 (68/230) | **Open processed data**, controlled raw data | Confirmed by search |
| 9 | Liu 2019 and Van Allen 2015, dbGaP phs000452 | Melanoma, anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4 | ~107 and ~39 | **Controlled** (dbGaP) | Confirmed by search |
| 10 | Braun 2020 (CheckMate 025), Miao 2018 (CheckMate 009) | Kidney, nivolumab | ~17 for Miao; Braun larger | **Controlled** (EGA / dbGaP phs001493) | Accessions confirmed; Braun access terms not confirmed |
| 11 | Ravi 2023 (SU2C-MARK), dbGaP phs002822 | NSCLC, ICI | 102 LUAD and 25 LUSC | **Controlled** (dbGaP) | COMPASS only |
| 12 | IMmotion150, EGAS00001002928 | Kidney, atezolizumab ± bevacizumab | 165 (48/117) | **Controlled** (EGA) | COMPASS only |

## Details
**Open and ready now (rows 1–7).**
- These are raw reads or counts in GEO, SRA, ENA or Zenodo, with response labels in the paper supplements.
- **Riaz and Gide** include on-treatment biopsies as well as baseline ones. Filter to pre-treatment samples, or your "pre-treatment" classifier will leak.
- **Gide** mixes monotherapy and combination arms.
- **Hugo** is small, and I did not check how many of its samples are pre-treatment.
- **COMPASS** (immuno-compass.com/download) lists 23 cohorts with clinical TSVs. For the open cohorts, its mRNA links point to a `data_request.md` file. I could not tell whether that means a request step, so treat COMPASS expression data as unconfirmed.
- **Snyder conflict:** COMPASS attributes Zenodo 546110 to Snyder. A separate paper's data statement attributes that DOI to the IMvigor210 RNA-seq. Check the Zenodo record before you rely on it.

**IMvigor210 (row 8).**
- **Raw data:** controlled access at EGA, study EGAS00001002556. You request access through the EGA study page.
- **Processed data:** Genentech distributes the `IMvigor210CoreBiologies` R package, with counts and clinical data for 348 patients. Response is available for 298 of them. The package is at `research-pub.gene.com/IMvigor210CoreBiologies/`, and it is how most papers use this cohort. I have not confirmed its licence.
- **Other atezolizumab data:** IMvigor211 and OAK appear on EGA (EGAD00001007703, EGAD00001008391, EGAS50000000497), also controlled. I did not check what response data they carry.

**Controlled cohorts (rows 9–12).**
- **dbGaP:** you need an eNRA account, a data access request, and institutional signing-official approval. Expect weeks to months.
- **EGA:** you submit a request to the study's Data Access Committee, and it needs a signed agreement. Expect weeks to months, from memory.
- **Braun 2020:** a later paper reports that CheckMate 025 normalised RNA-seq is at EGAS00001004290, EGAS00001004291 and EGAS00001004292. I did not confirm who approves access.
- **Fallback for processed data:** check each paper's supplement for processed tables. Several of these studies publish normalised expression there. I haven't confirmed this for any of the controlled cohorts.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Compilation portals:** TIDE (tide.dfci.harvard.edu), CRI iAtlas, ICBatlas, Cancer-Immu and ICBcomb all curate ICI cohorts. The web search described them, but I did not open them or check their terms. They are worth trying because they can save you the harmonisation work. Whatever they redistribute cannot be more open than the original source.
- **Other cohorts:** COMPASS lists Freeman (MGH, melanoma, dbGaP phs002683) and Choueiri (kidney, via CRI iAtlas, n=16). I have not verified either.
- **Cohorts I know of but did not search for:** Auslander 2018 (melanoma, possibly GSE115821), and a few NSCLC cohorts. Their accessions are from memory, so confirm them before use.

## Not recommended, and why
- **TCGA** has no checkpoint-treatment or response labels.
- **Microarray or NanoString cohorts**, such as Prat 2017 and Cristescu 2018, are not bulk RNA-seq. They would complicate cross-platform validation.
- **Scripta/single-cell ICI datasets** (the Curated Cancer Cell Atlas, for example) are single-cell, not bulk.

## What I could not find
- I did not check each cohort's response definition (RECIST vs clinical benefit). It differs between papers, so harmonise it before pooling.
- The registry search in the skill's tool (Zenodo, DataCite, OpenAIRE) returned mostly noise, because these cohorts live in GEO, ENA, EGA and dbGaP, which that tool doesn't cover. This list is therefore built from the literature and web search, and it may be incomplete.
- I did not build the interactive shortlist page, because I ran out of reliable registry data to put in it.

## Next step
1. **Today:** download rows 1–6 (melanoma ×3, gastric, bladder, GBM) and filter to baseline samples. That gives you about 300 patients across three cancers.
2. **Start the dbGaP and EGA requests now** (rows 8–12), since they run in the background for weeks. IMvigor210 is the highest value, because the processed R package gives you ~300 patients with no wait.
3. **Pick a validation strategy:** train on melanoma and validate on bladder and gastric. Also consider leaving one cohort out at a time, since cohorts differ by cancer type and by whether the antibody targets PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4.

graders.name: 01-recall-imvigor210
graders.evidence:
I found about five cohorts you can download today and several larger ones that need an application. I couldn't build the interactive shortlist page. The registry tool doesn't index GEO, EGA or dbGaP, so it produced none of the verification records the page needs.

Searches and cohort checks were run on 2026-11-12. GEO and PMC pages blocked my fetcher, which says nothing against the datasets. I confirmed the GEO series through NCBI's API instead. I did not check anything else on GEO, so response labels and per-patient details are marked "from memory" below.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** patients treated with anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1 or anti-CTLA-4.
- **R2 (must):** pre-treatment bulk tumour RNA-seq.
- **R3 (must):** a recorded RECIST or clinical-benefit label.
- **R4:** several independent cohorts, any cancer type.
- **R5:** I've separated what you can download now from what needs an application.

## Shortlist
| # | Cohort | Access | Licence | Size | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Gide 2019, melanoma, anti-PD-1 ± anti-CTLA-4 (ENA PRJEB23709) | Open download | No licence stated; public ENA record | ~90 patients (memory) | Public status today |
| 2 | Riaz 2017, melanoma, nivolumab (GSE91061) | Open download | GEO, no per-dataset licence | 109 samples | Series today; labels from memory |
| 3 | Hugo 2016, melanoma, anti-PD-1 (GSE78220) | Open download | GEO, no per-dataset licence | 28 pre-treatment samples | Series today; labels from memory |
| 4 | Auslander 2018, melanoma (GSE115821) | Open download | GEO, no per-dataset licence | 37 samples | Series today; drugs from memory |
| 5 | Kim/Jung, NSCLC, anti-PD-1 (GSE135222) | Open download | GEO, no per-dataset licence | 27 samples | Series today; drug and response from memory |
| 6 | Cho, NSCLC, anti-PD-1 (GSE126044) | Open download | GEO, no per-dataset licence | 16 samples | Series today |
| 7 | Kim 2018, gastric cancer, pembrolizumab (ENA PRJEB25780) | Open download | No licence stated | 61 patients | Public status today; RNA-seq coverage unconfirmed |
| 8 | IMvigor210, bladder cancer, atezolizumab | Processed data open; raw reads need an application | Processed data reported as CC-BY; raw reads under DAC terms | 348 pre-treatment RNA samples | Raw-data record today; package route from search results |
| 9 | Braun 2020, kidney cancer, CheckMate 009/010/025 | Processed data open; raw reads need an application | Not stated | ~300 patients (memory) | Search results only |
| 10 | Liu 2019 / Van Allen 2015, melanoma (dbGaP phs000452) | Application to dbGaP | Controlled access | ~150 melanomas in the study | Study page today |

## Details

**Download today**
- **Gide (#1):** the ENA project is public, with the last update in 2020, and compares anti-PD-1 alone with anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA-4. You get raw reads, so you'll need to run your own alignment and quantification. The response labels are in the paper's supplement.
- **Riaz (#2):** the 109 samples include on-treatment biopsies, so keep only the pre-treatment ones. Many patients had already progressed on ipilimumab (memory).
- **Hugo (#3):** a small cohort, useful as a validation set.
- **Auslander (#4), Kim/Jung (#5), Cho (#6):** small. For #5, the GEO page I could retrieve shows a methylation paper's RNA-seq series. Check which patients have response labels before you rely on it.
- **GEO licensing:** from memory, GEO data is free to reuse, but submitters can claim copyright, so cite each paper.
- **Kim gastric (#7):** the ENA project is public, but its description centres on tissue and ctDNA sequencing. Confirm that RNA-seq is included before counting it.

**Open processed data, raw reads by application**
- **IMvigor210 (#8):** Genentech distributes the processed counts and clinical response in the `IMvigor210CoreBiologies` R package. Two sources describe its licence as CC-BY, but they conflict on the version and the package points to a LICENSE file, so read that file. I could not open the Genentech page to confirm.
- **IMvigor210 raw reads:** the raw RNA is EGAD00001003977 on the European Genome-phenome Archive (EGA). You click "Request Access", and the IMvigor210 Data Access Committee (EGAC00001000945) decides. I couldn't find a timeline, so assume weeks to months.
- **Braun (#9):** search results report a supplementary Excel file in Nature Medicine with the processed RNA-seq and clinical data. They also report EGA accessions EGAS00001004290–92 for the raw data. I did not open either.

**Application required**
- **dbGaP phs000452 (#10):** the page includes RNA-seq and directs you to "Request access via Authorized Access" with a Data Use Certification. You'll need an institutional signing official, and approval typically takes weeks. The v3 page is marked as superseded, so request the current version.

## Known, not confirmed (from memory)
- **Aggregated resources:** TIDE (998 tumours from 12 ICB studies), TIGER (18 bulk transcriptome datasets), and ICBatlas (29 datasets, 5 cancer types) have already collected and harmonised many of these cohorts. Reviews describe them as freely accessible. I could not reach their download pages, so check their terms. These are the fastest route to a multi-cohort matrix.
- **Roche trials:** IMmotion150 and IMmotion151 (kidney cancer, atezolizumab) are on EGA with a Data Access Committee. This is from memory.
- **Other trials:** CheckMate 214 (EGAS00001005501) needs an application, per search results. The Zhao glioblastoma anti-PD-1 cohort is not confirmed.

## Not recommended
- **TCGA:** none of its patients received checkpoint inhibitors.
- **Registry hits from Zenodo and OpenAIRE:** these were mostly single-cell, mouse, CyTOF, or supplements with no bulk RNA-seq and response pairing.

graders.name: 01-recall-imvigor210
graders.evidence:
I'm answering from memory and haven't checked live, so confirm each accession and access status before you build on it. Access terms do change.

## Download now (open access)

| Cohort | Cancer / treatment | n (pre-treatment RNA-seq, approx.) | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| Riaz 2017 | Melanoma, nivolumab | ~50 | GEO GSE91061 (counts/FPKM), clinical in the paper's supplement |
| Hugo 2016 | Melanoma, pembrolizumab | ~25–28 | GEO GSE78220 (FPKM) |
| Gide 2019 | Melanoma, anti-PD-1 ± anti-CTLA-4 | ~70 | ENA PRJEB23709, with processed tables in the supplement |
| Kim 2018 | Gastric, pembrolizumab | ~45 | ENA PRJEB25780, clinical in the supplement |
| IMvigor210 (Mariathasan 2018) | Urothelial, atezolizumab | ~300 | The `IMvigor210CoreBiologies` R package from Genentech has counts and clinical data. Raw data are on EGA (EGAS00001002556). |
| Jung 2019 / Cho 2020 | NSCLC, anti-PD-(L)1 | ~15–30 each | GEO (GSE135222, GSE126044) |
| Zhao 2019 | Glioblastoma, anti-PD-1 | ~20 | SRA (PRJNA482620) |

The NSCLC and glioblastoma sets are too small to validate on alone. They are only useful for pooling.

## Controlled access (you have to apply)

- **dbGaP (phs000452):** This covers Van Allen 2015 (ipilimumab, melanoma) and Liu 2019 (anti-PD-1, melanoma, ~120 with RNA-seq). You need an eRA Commons account and a data access request co-signed by your institution's signing official. Expect weeks to a couple of months.
- **EGA:** Braun 2020 (ccRCC, nivolumab, CheckMate 009/010/025, ~300 with RNA-seq) and IMmotion150 (atezolizumab, RCC) sit behind a Data Access Committee. Check each paper's data availability statement for the current accession.
- Some of the processed expression matrices for these cohorts are in the supplements, so check before you apply.

## Harmonized collections

These save a lot of reprocessing time. Check how each one handles licensing and response definitions.
- **CRI iAtlas** (cri-iatlas.org) has several harmonized ICI cohorts, including Riaz, Hugo, Gide, Van Allen and IMvigor210.
- **TIDE** (tide.dfci.harvard.edu) has curated ICI datasets with response labels.
- **TIGER** and **ICBatlas** are curated ICI transcriptome resources. Verify that they are still maintained.
- **Kaplan-Meier Plotter** has an immunotherapy module, but it is mostly useful for exploration, not training.

## Pitfalls for cross-study validation

1. **Overlapping patients:** Liu 2019 and Van Allen 2015 share patients, and some melanoma cohorts overlap in other ways. Deduplicate, or you'll leak data between your training and validation sets.
2. **Pre-treatment samples only:** Riaz and Gide include on-treatment biopsies. Filter them out.
3. **Mixed treatments and prior therapy:** Riaz splits patients by ipilimumab-naive versus progressed. Gide mixes monotherapy and combination. Treat these as covariates, or stratify.
4. **Response definitions:** Studies use RECIST with different cutoffs, "clinical benefit" with different follow-up windows, or both. Harmonize explicitly (for example, CR/PR versus SD/PD).
5. **Batch effects:** Library prep, platform and normalization differ between cohorts. Reprocess from raw reads where you can. If you can't, rank-normalize within each cohort.
6. **Melanoma dominance:** Most of the data is melanoma. Leave-one-cohort-out validation will mostly test melanoma-to-melanoma transfer, and urothelial, gastric and RCC are your real out-of-tissue tests.
7. **No untreated control arm:** A signature that predicts response here may just be prognostic. If that matters for your claims, check it against TCGA survival in untreated patients.

I can do a live search to verify the current accessions and access status for any of these, or draft the dbGaP and EGA access requests. Tell me which you'd like.

graders.name: 01-recall-mimic-cxr
graders.evidence:
## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** chest X-ray images.
- **R2 (must):** the radiologist's original free-text report for each image or study, not only labels extracted from it.
- Nice-to-have: English first, with one non-English set for a secondary experiment. I assumed non-commercial academic use, and that waiting days for access is acceptable.

I searched DataCite, Hugging Face, OpenAIRE, PhysioNet and Zenodo (about 200 candidates) and did web searches for datasets the registries don't index. "Checked" below says how I know each fact. Checks were done 2026-11-12.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | MIMIC-CXR | Credentialed PhysioNet access, days | PhysioNet Credentialed Health Data License 1.5.0 | 377,110 images, 227,835 studies, 5.1 TB | Strong, English | Today (PhysioNet record and page) |
| 2 | CheXpert Plus | Stanford agreement, days | Stanford Dataset Research Use Agreement | ~223k image-report pairs, 187,711 studies | Strong, English | Web search only |
| 3 | ReXGradient-160K | Hugging Face login plus agreement, minutes | Non-commercial agreement | ~160k studies (from memory) | Strong, English | Access today, contents from memory |
| 4 | IU X-Ray (Open-i) | Open download, minutes | Not confirmed | 3,955 reports, 7,470 images | Strong but small, English | Size from search; terms not readable |
| 5 | PadChest (BIMCV) | Request form, weeks | BIMCV agreement | ~160k images, ~109k reports, ~1 TB | Strong, **Spanish** | Web search only |
| 6 | REFLACX | Free PhysioNet account plus restricted DUA, minutes | PhysioNet Restricted Health Data License | 3,032 cases | Partial, English | Today |
| 7 | Naija-CXR | Open on Zenodo, minutes | CC-BY-4.0 in the record; the description says non-commercial | Not stated | Partial, English | Today (page text) |

## Details
**1. [MIMIC-CXR](https://physionet.org/content/mimic-cxr/2.1.0/)**
- It has DICOM chest radiographs with free-text reports from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. It is the standard report-generation benchmark.
- **Access (confirmed):** "Only credentialed users who sign the DUA can access the files."
- **Steps:**
  1. Make a PhysioNet account.
  2. Complete the CITI human-subjects training.
  3. Apply for credentialing. This is personal and the usual wait is days. That timing is from memory.
  4. Sign the data use agreement on the project page.
- **Terms:** the agreement forbids sharing the data. PhysioNet's [24 Sept 2025 post](https://physionet.org/news/post/llm-responsible-use/) says you may not send credentialed data through APIs or online platforms, so use locally deployed models only.
- **Reports:** the reports contain de-identification placeholders.

**2. [CheXpert Plus](https://stanfordaimi.azurewebsites.net/datasets/5158c524-d3ab-4e02-96e9-6ee9efc110a1)**
- It adds de-identified reports, split into sections, to the CheXpert images. It also has CheXbert labels, RadGraph-XL annotations and demographics.
- **Access:** accept Stanford's research use agreement on the AIMI site. It is research-only, with no commercial use and no redistribution. The full set is about 6.8 TB.
- **Not confirmed:** this comes from search snippets, not the page itself. The pair count is 223,228 unique pairs in the paper's text and 223,462 in its table.

**3. [ReXGradient-160K](https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGradient-160K)**
- **Access (confirmed):** the repo is gated. You accept the "ReXGradient-160K Non-Commercial Data Access and Use Agreement" with a Hugging Face login. It is non-commercial and non-clinical only.
- **From memory, not confirmed:** it is a multi-site set of about 160k studies with reports. Check the dataset card for the report fields.

**4. [IU X-Ray / Open-i](https://openi.nlm.nih.gov/)**
- The NLM FAQ is reported to give 3,955 reports (XML, with indication, findings and impression) and 7,470 images (PNG or DICOM). The usual published counts agree.
- The Open-i page is drawn by JavaScript, so I could not read its terms. Check the NLM terms before redistributing.
- Use the NLM copy rather than the Hugging Face mirrors, which are unofficial.
- It is small, so it works for a quick run but not for pretraining.

**5. [PadChest](http://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest/)**
- This is your non-English set. It has Spanish reports from San Juan Hospital (2009–2017), 67k patients, 54 zip files, about 1 TB.
- **Access (from search results):** request through the BIMCV form and agree not to share the data or re-identify anyone. The URL may have moved, so check it. Allow weeks.
- **Public reports:** they were heavily processed for anonymisation. [PadChest-GR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05085) retrieved the original, anonymised reports and is bilingual.

**6. [REFLACX](https://physionet.org/content/reflacx-xray-localization/1.0.0/)**
- **Contents:** radiologists dictated reports on 3,032 frontal MIMIC-CXR images, with timestamped transcripts and eye tracking.
- **Access (confirmed):** "Only registered users who sign the specified data use agreement can access the files." You need a free account, not credentialing.
- **Limit:** it is small. The images also need MIMIC-CXR access.

**7. [Naija-CXR](https://zenodo.org/records/21781842)**
- The page says frontal CXRs are "paired with expert radiologist annotations and diagnostic reports". It is open, so you can start on it today.
- **Not confirmed:** I don't know the size or whether the reports are raw text.
- **Licence conflict:** the record says CC-BY-4.0, but the text says "non-commercial scientific research and educational purposes only". Treat it as non-commercial.

## Known, not confirmed
- **[FMCEB-CXR](https://zenodo.org/records/20750284)** (Zenodo, CC-BY-4.0) is built from 5,517 reports from a Lagos hospital. The page does not say whether the raw report text is released or only labels extracted from it. Open the files to check before using it.
- **PadChest, CheXpert Plus and IU X-Ray** are listed above and need a first-hand look at their access pages. I did not verify them through a registry.

## Not recommended, and why
- **NIH ChestX-ray14, VinDr-CXR and similar:** labels only, with no report text (from memory).
- **MIMIC-CXR-JPG:** images and labels. The reports are in MIMIC-CXR.
- **BRAX:** its 14 labels came from Brazilian Portuguese reports, but the page doesn't say the report text is released.
- **Derivatives such as RadGraph and CXR-PRO:** annotations built on MIMIC-CXR reports, useful add-ons but not independent report sets.
- **Hugging Face copies of IU X-Ray:** unofficial mirrors, so use the NLM source.

## What I could not find
I found no open, non-English chest X-ray set with full report text confirmed. PadChest is the best non-English option and needs a request. I did not search for Chinese, German or Portuguese hospital sets. I did not run the evidence-of-use paper lookup per dataset.

## Next step
Start with IU X-Ray, REFLACX or ReXGradient while you apply for credentialing for MIMIC-CXR and send the PadChest request. For a first model, the standard route is to train on MIMIC-CXR and test on IU X-Ray.

Interactive page: `/private/tmp/e-zuULR7/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`

**3. [ReXGradient-160K](https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGradient-160K)**
- **Access (confirmed):** the repo is gated. You accept the "ReXGradient-160K Non-Commercial Data Access and Use Agreement" with a Hugging Face login. It is non-commercial and non-clinical only.
- **From memory, not confirmed:** it is a multi-site set of about 160k studies with reports. Check the dataset card for the report fields.

**4. [IU X-Ray / Open-i](https://openi.nlm.nih.gov/)**
- The NLM FAQ is reported to give 3,955 reports (XML, with indication, findings and impression) and 7,470 images (PNG or DICOM). The usual published counts agree.
- The Open-i page is drawn by JavaScript, so I could not read its terms. Check the NLM terms before redistributing.
- Use the NLM copy rather than the Hugging Face mirrors, which are unofficial.
- It is small, so it works for a quick run but not for pretraining.

**5. [PadChest](http://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest/)**
- This is your non-English set. It has Spanish reports from San Juan Hospital (2009–2017), 67k patients, 54 zip files, about 1 TB.
- **Access (from search results):** request through the BIMCV form and agree not to share the data or re-identify anyone. The URL may have moved, so check it. Allow weeks.
- **Public reports:** they were heavily processed for anonymisation. [PadChest-GR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05085) retrieved the original, anonymised reports and is bilingual.

**7. [Naija-CXR](https://zenodo.org/records/21781842)**
- The page says frontal CXRs are "paired with expert radiologist annotations and diagnostic reports". It is open, so you can start on it today.
- **Not confirmed:** I don't know the size or whether the reports are raw text.
- **Licence conflict:** the record says CC-BY-4.0, but the text says "non-commercial scientific research and educational purposes only". Treat it as non-commercial.

## Known, not confirmed
- **[FMCEB-CXR](https://zenodo.org/records/20750284)** (Zenodo, CC-BY-4.0) is built from 5,517 reports from a Lagos hospital. The page does not say whether the raw report text is released or only labels extracted from it. Open the files to check before using it.
- **PadChest, CheXpert Plus and IU X-Ray** are listed above and need a first-hand look at their access pages. I did not verify them through a registry.

## Not recommended, and why
- **NIH ChestX-ray14, VinDr-CXR and similar:** labels only, with no report text (from memory).
- **MIMIC-CXR-JPG:** images and labels. The reports are in MIMIC-CXR.
- **BRAX:** its 14 labels came from Brazilian Portuguese reports, but the page doesn't say the report text is released.
- **Derivatives such as RadGraph and CXR-PRO:** annotations built on MIMIC-CXR reports, useful add-ons but not independent report sets.
- **Hugging Face copies of IU X-Ray:** unofficial mirrors, so use the NLM source.

## What I could not find
I found no open, non-English chest X-ray set with full report text confirmed. PadChest is the best non-English option and needs a request. I did not search for Chinese, German or Portuguese hospital sets. I did not run the evidence-of-use paper lookup per dataset.

## Next step
Start with IU X-Ray, REFLACX or ReXGradient while you apply for credentialing for MIMIC-CXR and send the PadChest request. For a first model, the standard route is to train on MIMIC-CXR and test on IU X-Ray.

- It has the original findings and impression text for each study.

  - Complete CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" training.
  - Apply for credentialing.
  - Sign the DUA for your project.

- If you plan to send reports to a hosted LLM API, check the DUA first. PhysioNet has restricted this before (from memory).

**2. [CheXpert Plus](https://aimi.stanford.edu/datasets/chexpert-plus)**
- The [AIMI page](https://aimi.stanford.edu/datasets/chexpert-plus) says it has "223,462 unique pairs of radiology reports and chest X-rays".
- Each report is split into 11 subsections.

- This is the quickest large English set to get.

**4. [PadChest](https://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest/)**
- This is my pick for the non-English experiment, with reports in Spanish.
- The agreement forbids sharing the data and re-identification.
- From memory, only part of the reports are expert-labelled and the rest are auto-labelled. The report text is all radiologist-written.

**5. [Naija-CXR](https://zenodo.org/records/21781842)**
- Its Zenodo description says images come with "expert radiologist annotations and diagnostic reports".
- I didn't open the files, so check they are free text before relying on it.

## Known, not confirmed

- **IU X-Ray / Open-i (Indiana University).**
  - From web search: 7,470 chest X-rays with 3,955 reports (indication, findings, impression), downloadable from NLM with no application.
  - The verifier couldn't check the site because it's a JavaScript app, so open it in a browser.
  - Search results disagree on the licence (one source says CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), so read the terms on the NLM page.
  - It's small, but it's the standard quick-start set, and the one you could start on today.
  - The Hugging Face and Kaggle copies are unofficial mirrors. Use the NLM source.
- **CheXpert Plus tier and licence.** What I believe is research-use terms. I couldn't confirm it.

## Not recommended, and why

- **NIH ChestX-ray14:** labels were mined from reports, and the reports aren't released.
- **MIMIC-CXR-JPG:** images plus structured labels only. Take reports from MIMIC-CXR.
- **BRAX:** labels only, no free text (from memory).
- **FMCEB-CXR (Nigeria):** 5,517 reports with NLP labels, but the record is a 42 KB file with no images.

## What I could not find

- I didn't survey other non-English sets beyond PadChest. BIMCV-COVID19 (Spanish) and Chinese-language collections are worth a look. I didn't search for them.
- Registries searched were PhysioNet, Zenodo, DataCite, OpenAIRE and Hugging Face, plus literature and web search. Any of the checks above may be out of date, so confirm before applying.
- I checked on 2026-11-11 and 2026-11-12.

## Next step

Start your PhysioNet credentialing now, since it's the slowest step and MIMIC-CXR is the standard benchmark. In parallel, accept the ReXGradient-160K terms on Hugging Face and pull IU X-Ray for a quick pipeline test. Then request PadChest for the Spanish experiment.

The interactive page is at `/private/tmp/e-RVOBlu/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

graders.name: 01-recall-mimic-cxr
graders.evidence:
Several English datasets pair each chest X-ray with the radiologist's original report text, and a few non-English ones do too. I checked what I could today (2026-11-11). Two official pages (Stanford AIMI and Open-i) are JavaScript apps the tool couldn't read, so those entries rest on web search.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** a free-text radiologist report for each study, not just labels extracted from it.
- **R2 (nice to have):** English reports. Other languages are fine for a secondary experiment.
- I assumed research use only. Several licences below are non-commercial.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Language | Access | Licence | Size | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [MIMIC-CXR 2.1.0](https://physionet.org/content/mimic-cxr/2.1.0/) | English | Credentialed PhysioNet account, CITI training, signed DUA; weeks | PhysioNet Credentialed Health Data License 1.5.0 | 227,835 studies, 377,110 images | today |
| 2 | [ReXGradient-160K](https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGradient-160K) | English | Hugging Face login and click-through agreement; minutes | Non-commercial agreement | ~160,000 studies, 3 US health systems | today (registry); size per paper |
| 3 | [CheXpert Plus](https://stanfordaimi.azurewebsites.net/datasets/5158c524-d3ab-4e02-96e9-6ee9efc110a1) | English | Register on Stanford AIMI and accept the Research Use Agreement; days | Stanford Research Use Agreement, non-commercial | 223,228 report-image pairs | web search only |
| 4 | [IU X-ray / Open-i](https://openi.nlm.nih.gov/faq) | English | Direct download from NLM | not confirmed | 3,955 reports, 7,470 images | web search only |
| 5 | [PadChest](https://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest/) | Spanish | Access request to BIMCV, then approval; weeks | PadChest Research Use Agreement | 160k+ images, ~109k reports | page read today |
| 6 | [ViX-Ray](https://huggingface.co/datasets/MilitaryHospital175/VNMedical_bv175) | Vietnamese | Open download, not gated | CC-BY-NC (registry); web search said CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | not checked | today (registry) |
| 7 | [CASIA-CXR](https://www.casia-cxr.net/) | French | ~80 MB sample is open; full set on request | Use agreement on the site | not checked | today |

## Details
1. **MIMIC-CXR.** This is the standard benchmark. The page states "free-text radiology reports", with one `.txt` per study and a combined `mimic-cxr-reports.tar.gz`.
   - **Steps:** make a PhysioNet account, complete the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" course, apply for credentialing, sign the DUA, then download.
   - **Caveats:** the DUA says you won't share the data. If you plan to send reports to an online LLM service, check that clause first. Reports also mention prior exams. [CXR-PRO](https://physionet.org/content/cxr-pro/1.0.0/) is a version with those references removed (same credentialed access).
   - **Paper:** [the MIMIC-CXR dataset paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-019-0322-0).
2. **ReXGradient-160K.** Reports are split into Indication, Comparison, Findings and Impression, and there are 140k/10k/10k train/val/test splits. A further 10k test set is held back for the ReXrank leaderboard. Use is non-commercial and non-clinical only. This is the quickest large set to get.
3. **CheXpert Plus.** Search results describe it as report text, RadGraph annotations and demographics added to CheXpert images. I couldn't machine-check the page, so confirm in a browser where the images are hosted.
4. **IU X-ray / Open-i.** It's small, so it's useful mainly for cross-dataset testing rather than training. Use the NLM source, not the Kaggle or Hugging Face copies, which are unofficial mirrors. Licence terms are unconfirmed.
5. **PadChest.** This is the best large non-English option. The page says to read the Research Use Agreement before downloading. The request steps beyond that come from web search. [PadChest-GR](https://bimcv.cipf.es/bimcv-projects/padchest-gr/) is a smaller bilingual (Spanish/English) subset of 4,555 studies, also on request. I haven't read its page, so that is from web search.
   - **Paper:** [the PadChest paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2020.101797).
6. **ViX-Ray.** It pairs PA chest X-rays with Vietnamese reports by certified radiologists. Quality and size are unchecked.
   - **Paper:** [the dataset paper](https://doi.org/10.63317/3do8tpzockx8).
7. **CASIA-CXR.** Its page says the full records "are not available to download. We may provide them upon request." Timeline unknown.

## Known, not confirmed
- **CN-X2RG / Chinese MRGMI.** A search result describes 40,000+ Chinese X-ray/report pairs as public. I didn't find or verify a download page. Check the [Springer chapter](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-47401-9_8) for the data link.
- **Derived MIMIC-CXR sets** (CXR-PRO, REFLACX, RadGraph, CXRGraph) all need PhysioNet access. [REFLACX](https://physionet.org/content/reflacx-xray-localization/1.0.0/) adds eye-tracking and dictated reports.

## Not recommended, and why
- **BRAX** (Brazilian Portuguese): its page says "Free-text reports are not yet provided in the current version". It has labels only.
- **NIH ChestX-ray14, VinDr-CXR, RSNA Pneumonia, original CheXpert and MIMIC-CXR-JPG:** labels only, with no report text. This is from memory, except MIMIC-CXR-JPG, whose page I read.

## What I could not find
No public German or Portuguese chest X-ray report set turned up. I searched DataCite, Hugging Face, OpenAIRE, PhysioNet and Zenodo, plus the web. Private hospital collections wouldn't show up this way.

## Next step
Start the MIMIC-CXR credentialing now, since the CITI course and approval take the longest. While you wait, ReXGradient-160K and IU X-ray need no approval wait. For the secondary experiment, PadChest (Spanish) is the largest, and ViX-Ray (Vietnamese) is available immediately.

The interactive comparison page is at `/private/tmp/e-ByaFNw/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

Sources: [PadChest search results](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.07441), [CheXpert Plus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19538), [ReXGradient-160K](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00228), [Open-i FAQ](https://openi.nlm.nih.gov/faq).

graders.name: 01-recall-mimic-cxr
graders.evidence:
Only a handful of public chest X-ray datasets ship the radiologist's actual free-text report. Many popular ones (CheXpert, ChestX-ray14, VinDr-CXR, PLCO) release only labels. This is from memory, so check each access page before you plan around it. Terms and sizes change.

## English reports

| Dataset | Size | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **IU X-Ray (Open-I)** | ~7.5k images, ~3.9k studies (frontal and lateral) | Open, no application |
| **MIMIC-CXR** | ~377k images, ~227k studies, ~65k patients | PhysioNet credentialed access |
| **CheXpert Plus** | ~223k image-report pairs, ~187k studies | Stanford AIMI registration and agreement |
| **ReXGradient-160K** | ~160k studies from several US health systems | Gated release (I believe on Hugging Face), with a terms agreement |

**IU X-Ray** is the easiest to get.
- Download the images and XML reports from the NLM Open-I site. Kaggle mirrors also exist.
- Each report has indication, comparison, findings, and impression sections.
- It's small, and some studies have empty findings. Most papers use the R2Gen or Li et al. split so results are comparable.

**MIMIC-CXR** is the standard benchmark for report generation.
1. Create a PhysioNet account.
2. Complete the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" training.
3. Apply for credentialed status, which needs references and takes days to weeks.
4. Sign the data use agreement for MIMIC-CXR (and MIMIC-CXR-JPG if you want JPEGs).
5. Download with `wget` or from the cloud buckets.

- The DICOMs are about 4.7 TB. The JPG version is roughly 550 GB and comes with the official train/val/test split and CheXpert labels.
- The reports are a separate, small download. Use the official `create_section_files.py` to extract findings and impression.
- PhysioNet's policy restricts sending the data to third-party LLM APIs. That matters if you plan LLM-based evaluation or augmentation. Use an approved route, such as a compliant Azure OpenAI setup or a local model.
- There are known issues to handle: `___` de-identification placeholders, and references to prior studies the model can't see. CXR-PRO is a derivative on PhysioNet that removes the prior references.

**CheXpert Plus** adds reports to Stanford's CheXpert images. The original CheXpert has no reports. You register at the AIMI site and agree to a research-use license. The download is large.

**ReXGradient-160K** is newer, so check its dataset card for current terms.

## Non-English reports

- **PadChest (Spanish, Valencia/BIMCV):** ~160k images. Access is by request form and is usually fast. Its public metadata is mostly labels and UMLS-mapped findings, and I'm not sure the full report text is in the main CSV. Verify that before committing. There is also a newer grounded-report extension, PadChest-GR, with Spanish and English sentences. It may fit better.
- **BIMCV-COVID19+ (Spanish):** it has reports but is skewed toward COVID cases, so it's weaker for general report generation.

## What I'd do
1. Prototype on IU X-Ray, since it's open and small.
2. Train and benchmark on MIMIC-CXR. Start the PhysioNet credentialing now, because it's the slowest step.
3. Use CheXpert Plus or ReXGradient as a second English source for generalization.
4. Use PadChest for the non-English experiment, after confirming what text it includes.

I can check the current access pages and dataset cards to confirm sizes, licenses, and the PadChest report question if you want.

graders.evidence:

## English, with free-text reports

| Dataset | Size | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **MIMIC-CXR** (and MIMIC-CXR-JPG) | ~377k images, ~227k studies, ~65k patients (BIDMC) | Credentialed (PhysioNet) |

| **IU X-ray (Open-I)** | ~3.9k reports, ~7.4k images | Open download |
| **ReXGradient-160K** | ~160k studies from several US health systems | Gated on Hugging Face |

**MIMIC-CXR** is the standard benchmark for this task.
- **Access:**
  1. Create a PhysioNet account.
  2. Complete the CITI "Data or Specimens Only Research" course.
  3. Submit the credentialing application, which needs a reference. Approval can take days to weeks.
  4. Sign the data use agreement for the project.
- **Download:** Use `wget` with your PhysioNet login, or pull from the GCP/AWS buckets. The DICOMs are several TB. MIMIC-CXR-JPG is far smaller (~570 GB) and includes the official train/val/test split plus CheXpert/NegBio labels.
- **Reports:** The reports are a small separate zip of plain text. The repo's `create_sections_files.py` splits out the findings and impression sections.
- **LLM policy:** PhysioNet restricts sending credentialed data to third-party LLM APIs. Read that policy first if you plan to use an API model for evaluation or augmentation.
- **Derived resources:** Some build on MIMIC-CXR and need the same access. Examples are Chest ImaGenome (scene graphs) and CXR-PRO (impressions with references to prior studies removed).

**CheXpert Plus** extends the original CheXpert, which had labels only. This release adds the radiology reports. You register with Stanford AIMI and agree to a research-use license. Access is quicker than PhysioNet credentialing.

**IU X-ray (Open-I)** needs no credentialing. You download images and XML reports from NLM Open-i, and mirrors exist on Kaggle and elsewhere.
- It's small, so it's good for debugging and for a second benchmark.
- Reports are findings plus impression, with de-identification placeholders (`XXXX`).
- Some studies have empty sections.
- Papers generally use the split from Li et al. (2018), so use that to stay comparable.

**ReXGradient-160K** is a 2025 release and the one I'm least sure of. Check the Hugging Face page for the current license and gating process.

## Non-English

**PadChest** (Hospital San Juan, Alicante) has ~160k images and ~67k patients, with the reports in **Spanish**.
- **Access:** You fill out a request form with BIMCV, and they approve by email. It's usually free for research.
- **Labels:** Only about a quarter of the labels are manually reviewed. The rest come from an automatic labeler, so don't treat the labels as ground truth.
- **Related:** BIMCV-COVID19 also has Spanish reports, but it's COVID-specific.

## Often suggested, but not usable here
- **NIH ChestX-ray14, VinDr-CXR, original CheXpert, BRAX:** These release labels or boxes, not the radiologists' reports.
- **Chinese or other-language report sets:** Several papers use them, but the ones I know of are private hospital data. I can't point you to a public one with confidence.

## Suggested plan
1. Start the **MIMIC-CXR** credentialing now, since it's the slowest step.
2. Prototype on **IU X-ray** while you wait.
3. Add **CheXpert Plus** as a second large English set for cross-dataset checks.
4. Use **PadChest** for the non-English experiment.

I can also write the download and preprocessing scripts, such as section extraction and split handling, once you have access.

graders.evidence:
These are the datasets I know of that release the radiologist's free-text report. I'm going from memory and haven't checked the live pages. Access terms and sizes change, so confirm them before you plan around them.

## English

| Dataset | Size | Source | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MIMIC-CXR** (plus MIMIC-CXR-JPG) | ~377k images, ~227k studies, ~65k patients | BIDMC, Boston | Credentialed, via PhysioNet |
| **IU X-ray (Open-i)** | ~3.9k reports, ~7.4k images | Indiana University, via NLM | Open, no registration |
| **CheXpert Plus** | ~223k image-report pairs, ~187k studies | Stanford | Registration and a research use agreement |
| **ReXGradient-160K** | ~160k studies | Multiple US health systems | Gated download, which I believe is on Hugging Face |

**MIMIC-CXR** is the standard benchmark for report generation.
- **Steps:** Create a PhysioNet account and complete the CITI training ("Data or Specimens Only Research"). Then apply for credentialed status, which needs a reference, and sign the data use agreement. Approval usually takes days to a couple of weeks.
- **Download:** The DICOM release is several TB. MIMIC-CXR-JPG is about 570 GB, and you can also pull it from the GCP or AWS buckets.
- **Reports only:** The reports are a separate small archive (`mimic-cxr-reports.zip`), so you can start on the text without the images. Use the repo's `create_sections_files.py` to split out Findings and Impression.
- **LLM restriction:** PhysioNet restricts sending MIMIC data to external LLM APIs. It only allows services with no-retention terms, such as certain Azure OpenAI or Vertex configurations. Check this if your pipeline calls a hosted model.
- **Derived resources:** Chest ImaGenome and MS-CXR build on MIMIC-CXR. They add sentence-level anatomical and grounding annotations, with the same credentialed access.

**IU X-ray** is the easiest to get, from the NLM Open-i site or mirrors. It's small and has a fairly high share of normal studies, so use it for quick experiments or as a second benchmark. Most papers use the R2Gen split, so use that to compare results.

**CheXpert Plus** is not the original CheXpert, which has labels only and no reports. The Plus release adds the full report text, section-parsed, along with other metadata. It's useful as an out-of-distribution check against MIMIC.

**ReXGradient-160K** is newer and large. Verify its license and access terms yourself, because I'm least sure of this one.

## Non-English (secondary experiment)

- **PadChest** (Spanish) has ~160k images from ~67k patients at Hospital San Juan, Valencia, and the BIMCV group hosts it.
  - **Access:** You fill out a request form on the BIMCV site and wait for approval, then download about 1 TB of images plus a CSV with the reports. Only about a quarter of the labels are manually curated. The rest come from an automatic labeler, which matters only if you use the labels.
  - **PadChest-GR:** This is a newer grounded-report extension. I believe it includes English as well as Spanish, but verify that.
- **BIMCV-COVID19+** (Spanish) has reports too, but it covers a COVID-skewed population.
- **Chinese:** I recall a large Chinese chest X-ray report corpus (CTRG-Chest-548K) from 2024. I'm not confident of its details or license, so check the paper before relying on it.

## Datasets to skip

NIH ChestX-ray14, the original CheXpert, VinDr-CXR and PLCO ship labels or boxes only, with no reports. They're often listed as report datasets by mistake.

## Practical notes

- Split by patient, not by image or study. MIMIC-CXR has an official split, and you should use it.
- Reports often refer to priors ("unchanged from prior"). Models can't see the prior image unless you give it to them, so many papers filter or handle this explicitly.
- MIMIC reports are de-identified, with `___` placeholders, and style varies a lot between institutions. Expect a drop when you transfer between datasets.

I can draft the PhysioNet application steps, or the download and preprocessing scripts for MIMIC-CXR and IU X-ray, if you'd like.

graders.name: 01-recall-fitzpatrick17k
graders.evidence:
## What I assumed you need
- **R1:** a skin tone label (Fitzpatrick or Monk) on every image or patient.
- **R2:** a diagnosis label.
- **R3:** Fitzpatrick V and VI represented in the hundreds or more.
- **R4:** downloadable for research now.

I assumed non-commercial research use is fine and that biopsy-confirmed diagnoses would be ideal but not required.

**Short answer:** three public datasets meet these requirements, and none is perfect. No public dataset I found has both biopsy-proven diagnoses and thousands of expert-labelled V/VI images.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [DDI, Diverse Dermatology Images (Stanford)](https://ddi-dataset.github.io/) | Free registration and signed Research Use Agreement; minutes | Non-commercial, no redistribution | 656 images, about 207 of them V–VI | Strong | Access terms today; V–VI count from a secondary summary |
| 2 | [SCIN (Google)](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/scin) | Open download from a public cloud bucket; minutes | SCIN Data Use Public License | 10,000+ images, about 5,000 cases | Strong for Monk, partial for V/VI | Today |
| 3 | [Fitzpatrick17k](https://github.com/mattgroh/fitzpatrick17k) | CSV open; images fetched from source atlases; days | CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 | 16,577 images, about 2,170 V–VI | Partial | Licence today; counts from a secondary summary |

## Details
**DDI** is the best fit for a rigorous audit.
- Diagnoses are biopsy-proven, with 78 disease labels plus malignant/benign.
- Every image has a Fitzpatrick type, and it was built to compare I–II against V–VI, matched on diagnostic category, age, sex and photo date.
- About 207 images are V–VI (159 benign, 48 malignant). One study reports no basal cell carcinoma in V–VI.
- To get it, register on the Stanford AIMI portal and accept the agreement. Don't share the download link or redistribute any images.
- Subgroup sizes are small, so expect wide confidence intervals.

**SCIN** is the only one with Monk labels.
- It has Monk tone from graders in the US and India, self-reported Fitzpatrick, and dermatologist-estimated Fitzpatrick.
- Per the [SCIN paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.18545v1), V/VI make up about 16% of cases by self-report, but only 5.3% (V) and 0.6% (VI) by dermatologist estimate. Monk 8–10 is about 1–1.5%.
- Diagnoses are weighted dermatologist differentials, not biopsy, and some cases are "not diagnosable."
- Skin tone isn't always gradable, and many self-reports are blank (`NONE_SELECTED`). For a V/VI audit, use self-reported Fitzpatrick (about 800 cases) and treat dermatologist-estimated V/VI as a small sample.
- The licence forbids re-identifying contributors. I didn't read it fully, so check it for other limits.

**Fitzpatrick17k** is the only large set.
- It has 114 conditions, and its V+VI share is about 13%.
- Skin tone labels came from crowd annotators (Scale AI, Centaur Labs), not dermatologists, so tone labels are noisy. Diagnoses come from the source atlases and aren't biopsy-confirmed.
- It has duplicates and mislabels. Use the cleaned [Fitzpatrick17k-C](https://zenodo.org/records/11101338) (Zenodo, CC BY-NC 4.0) and its [data-quality paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-025-04382-5).

| 2 | [SCIN (Google)](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/scin) | Open download from a public cloud bucket; minutes | SCIN Data Use Public License | 10,000+ images, about 5,000 cases | Strong for Monk, partial for V/VI | Today |
| 3 | [Fitzpatrick17k](https://github.com/mattgroh/fitzpatrick17k) | CSV open; images fetched from source atlases; days | CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 | 16,577 images, about 2,170 V–VI | Partial | Licence today; counts from a secondary summary |

## Details
**DDI** is the best fit for a rigorous audit.
- Diagnoses are biopsy-proven, with 78 disease labels plus malignant/benign.
- Every image has a Fitzpatrick type, and it was built to compare I–II against V–VI, matched on diagnostic category, age, sex and photo date.
- About 207 images are V–VI (159 benign, 48 malignant). One study reports no basal cell carcinoma in V–VI.
- To get it, register on the Stanford AIMI portal and accept the agreement. Don't share the download link or redistribute any images.
- Subgroup sizes are small, so expect wide confidence intervals.

**SCIN** is the only one with Monk labels.
- It has Monk tone from graders in the US and India, self-reported Fitzpatrick, and dermatologist-estimated Fitzpatrick.
- Per the [SCIN paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.18545v1), V/VI make up about 16% of cases by self-report, but only 5.3% (V) and 0.6% (VI) by dermatologist estimate. Monk 8–10 is about 1–1.5%.
- Diagnoses are weighted dermatologist differentials, not biopsy, and some cases are "not diagnosable."
- Skin tone isn't always gradable, and many self-reports are blank (`NONE_SELECTED`). For a V/VI audit, use self-reported Fitzpatrick (about 800 cases) and treat dermatologist-estimated V/VI as a small sample.
- The licence forbids re-identifying contributors. I didn't read it fully, so check it for other limits.

**Fitzpatrick17k** is the only large set.
- It has 114 conditions, and its V+VI share is about 13%.
- Skin tone labels came from crowd annotators (Scale AI, Centaur Labs), not dermatologists, so tone labels are noisy. Diagnoses come from the source atlases and aren't biopsy-confirmed.
- It has duplicates and mislabels. Use the cleaned [Fitzpatrick17k-C](https://zenodo.org/records/11101338) (Zenodo, CC BY-NC 4.0) and its [data-quality paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-025-04382-5).

A suggested design is to run the main audit on DDI, because its labels are the most trustworthy. Then replicate on Fitzpatrick17k-C for statistical power and on SCIN for the Monk scale.

- **DDI-2:** 665 images of self-identified Asian patients from Stanford. I didn't check its skin type labels or V–VI counts.
- **SkinCAP:** 4,000 images drawn from Fitzpatrick17k and DDI, with captions. It adds nothing new for labels.

## Not recommended, and why
- **PAD-UFES-20:** has Fitzpatrick labels, but only 10 type V and 1 type VI images out of 1,494 labelled.
- **MRA-MIDAS (Stanford):** biopsy-proven and Fitzpatrick-labelled, but only 16.8% are III–VI and the authors flag few IV–VI.
- **Pipsqueak:** all V–VI, but only about 16 original images (80 after augmentation), mostly taken from Fitzpatrick17k.
- **Acral lesions in Black patients (Zenodo):** access is restricted and I found no Fitzpatrick label.
- **HAM10000 and the standard ISIC release:** from memory, no skin tone labels and almost no V–VI. I didn't check this today.

## What I could not find
No large, open set pairs expert skin tone labels with pathology diagnoses and has thousands of V/VI cases. A 2025 [atlas of digital dermatology](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2025.12.27.25342585v1.full) reports that V–VI are only about 5.8% of images across datasets. The registry search mostly returned noise. Most of what's above came from the literature and web search.

## Next step
Register for DDI first, since approval is quick. Then pull the SCIN CSVs and Fitzpatrick17k-C and count V/VI per diagnosis class, so you can see which classes are too small to audit.

Checked 12 November 2026. The interactive page is at `/private/tmp/e-2fYWAV/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

graders.evidence:
Three public datasets fit: SCIN, Fitzpatrick17k and DDI. Each covers different gaps, and you could use all three. I checked them on 2026-11-12. Where I rely on memory instead, I say so.

I did not build the interactive shortlist page. This answer is the complete result.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** Images of skin, either clinical photos or dermoscopy.
- **R2 (must):** A skin tone label per image or patient, as Fitzpatrick or Monk.
- **R3 (must):** A diagnosis label per image.
- **R4 (must):** Fitzpatrick V and VI present in numbers large enough to give a stable subgroup metric.
- **R5 (nice):** Biopsy-confirmed diagnoses, many conditions, and a download you can start today.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | SCIN (Google) | Open download, no application | SCIN Data Use License | 10,000+ images | R1–R3 met. Only dataset here with both Fitzpatrick and Monk. V/VI count not checked. | Landing page today. Details from memory. |
| 2 | Fitzpatrick17k | Open, but images come from the original source sites | CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 | ~16.5k images, 114 conditions (from memory) | R1–R4 met. Tone labels are crowd-annotated. | Landing page today. Counts from memory. |
| 3 | DDI, Stanford | Free registration plus a research-use agreement | Non-commercial research only | 656 images (from memory) | R1–R5 met, with the strongest labels. | Terms today. Counts from memory. |

## Details
**SCIN** (https://github.com/google-research-datasets/scin)
- **Contents:** The page says it has "10,000+ images of dermatology conditions, crowdsourced with informed consent from US internet users" and includes "estimated Fitzpatrick skin type and Monk Skin Tone."
- **Diagnosis:** The diagnosis is a dermatologist differential, so it is not biopsy-proven. The paper says 89% of assignable cases were allergic, infectious or inflammatory conditions, so melanoma and other cancers are thin.
- **Skin tone:** The tone labels are estimated by raters (eFST, eMST), not measured. Users also self-reported Fitzpatrick type, which I recall but did not confirm.
- **Access:** The page points to a demo notebook for loading it. From memory, the data sits in a Google Cloud Storage bucket. Read the SCIN Data Use License before use, because I did not read its terms.
- **Paper:** https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.46615

**Fitzpatrick17k** (https://github.com/mattgroh/fitzpatrick17k)
- **Contents:** It is a CSV of Fitzpatrick annotations plus the training script.
- **Access:** The README says you download the images from their original source, given in the `url` column. Links may have rotted since release, so check how many still resolve.
- **Licence:** "Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0."
- **Skin tone:** From memory, the tone labels came from crowd annotators, not clinicians. The published literature questions their reliability, including a Zenodo record titled "Investigating the Quality of DermaMNIST and Fitzpatrick17k Dermatological Image Datasets" (https://zenodo.org/records/12739457). I have not read it.
- **Paper using it for a similar purpose:** https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-023-02728-3

**DDI, Diverse Dermatology Images** (https://ddi-dataset.github.io/)
- **Contents:** Pathology-confirmed images. The page says it was designed to compare "FST I-II and FST V-VI by matching diagnostic category, age within 10 years, gender, and date of photograph within 3 years." That makes it a good fit for a fairness audit.
- **Counts:** From memory, there are 656 images and roughly 200 each in the I–II, III–IV and V–VI groups. I did not confirm this.
- **Access:** Register on the Stanford AIMI portal and accept the Research Use Agreement. The agreement says "personal, non-commercial research purposes only" and forbids redistribution and sharing the download link. Each person in your organization must register individually.
- **Paper:** https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abq6147. It reports that AI models do worse on dark skin tones and uncommon diseases.

## Known, not confirmed
- **"Assessing the Generalizability of Deep Neural Networks-Based Models for Black Skin Lesions"** (https://zenodo.org/records/10570316).
  - **Access:** The record page says "files are restricted" and you must fill in a request form. The licence is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
  - **Contents:** I did not open it, so I don't know its skin tone labels or diagnosis classes. From the title, it is probably dark-skin only, which would make it unsuitable for comparing across tones.

## Not recommended, and why
- **PAD-UFES-20** (https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/zr7vgbcyr2/1) is open under CC BY-4.0 and has smartphone images with Fitzpatrick types. From memory, it is mostly Brazilian patients with Fitzpatrick I–III, so V/VI is too sparse. It could serve as a light-skin baseline.
- **HAM10000 and similar dermoscopy sets** are the usual benchmarks, but from memory they carry no per-image tone labels and have almost no V/VI.
- **The SCGAN skin-tone-balanced HAM10000 extension** (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0331081) is synthetic. It would test the generator, not real-world performance.

## What I could not find
- No dermoscopy dataset with Fitzpatrick or Monk labels and substantial V/VI. All three picks are clinical photos.
- I did not count the V/VI images in SCIN or Fitzpatrick17k from the files. Do that first.
- I searched five registries, the literature and the web. Dataset hosting sites that block automated clients may hide other candidates.

## Next step
1. Download SCIN today, since it needs no application.
2. Tabulate V/VI counts per diagnosis in SCIN and Fitzpatrick17k, and decide which conditions have enough images per tone.
3. Register for DDI. Use it as the cleanest held-out test set, and use Fitzpatrick17k and SCIN for broader coverage.

I don't know of any dataset that pairs the pathology-confirmed labels of DDI with the volume of the other two. For a headline fairness claim, report results per dataset instead of pooling them, because the label quality differs.
