graders.name: 01-recall-fitzpatrick17k
graders.evidence:
The best fit is **DermaCon-IN**, **Fitzpatrick17k**, **SCIN** and **DDI**, and each has a gap you should know about. I checked access and licence for most of them on 2026-11-11. I did not check the per-type image counts, so every count below is from memory unless I say otherwise.

I didn't build the interactive HTML page, so there is no `dataset-shortlist.html`. The registry search covered Hugging Face, Zenodo, DataCite, OpenAIRE and PhysioNet.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** skin images with a diagnosis label.
- **R2 (must):** a Fitzpatrick or Monk label per image or patient.
- **R3 (must):** Fitzpatrick V–VI present in numbers large enough to give stable subgroup metrics.
- **R4 (nice):** patient IDs, so you can split by patient.
- **R5 (nice):** downloadable now.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | DermaCon-IN | Open download (Harvard Dataverse) | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 5,450+ images, ~3,000 patients, 240+ diagnoses | Skin tone scores per image, South Indian patients, so likely V–VI-heavy. The scale and distribution are unchecked. | Record today; skin tone scale not verified |
| 2 | Fitzpatrick17k | Open: GitHub CSV, images fetched from the source atlases | CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 | 16,577 images, 114 conditions | Fitzpatrick label on every image. V–VI is a minority, and I recall roughly a tenth. | Page today; counts from memory |
| 3 | SCIN (Google) | Open download, under the SCIN Data Use License | SCIN Data Use License | 10,000+ images | Dermatologist-estimated Fitzpatrick, layperson Monk and self-reported Fitzpatrick. Diagnoses are dermatologist differentials. V–VI is a minority. | Page today; counts from memory |
| 4 | DDI (Stanford Diverse Dermatology Images) | Free registration and research use agreement | Non-commercial research use | ~656 images, ~570 patients (memory) | Biopsy-proven diagnoses. Built to compare I–II against V–VI. I recall about 200 V–VI images. | Page today; counts from memory |
| 5 | "Black skin lesions" (Zenodo 10570316) | Request form; files restricted | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | Unknown | Acral lesions, assessed against the Fitzpatrick scale. | Access page today; contents not read |
| 6 | MRA-MIDAS (Stanford AIMI) | Registration or data agreement; I couldn't read the terms | Not stated | Not checked | Fitzpatrick type per lesion and biopsy-based labels. I don't know the V–VI share. | Page today; V–VI share unknown |

## Details
- **DermaCon-IN** (https://doi.org/10.7910/dvn/w7ouzm). It is prospective clinical photos with hierarchical diagnoses and body location. The record says "skin tone scores" without naming the scale, so check whether it is Fitzpatrick before you rely on it. Harvard Dataverse blocked my automated check, so open the page in a browser.
- **Fitzpatrick17k** (https://github.com/mattgroh/fitzpatrick17k). The page says it holds "16,577 clinical images sourced from two dermatology atlases" labelled by Scale AI and Centaur Labs. Two caveats:
  - The skin tone labels are crowd-annotated and noisy.
  - There are no patient IDs, and I recall near-duplicates, so a patient-level split isn't possible. The Zenodo record "Investigating the Quality of DermaMNIST and Fitzpatrick17k" (https://zenodo.org/records/12739457) covers its quality problems.
- **SCIN** (https://github.com/google-research-datasets/scin). The page states "estimated Fitzpatrick skin type (eFST) and layperson estimated Monk Skin tone (eMST)". It is the only one here with Monk labels. The images are US crowd-donated, not clinical, and the diagnoses are differentials rather than biopsy-proven. A JAMA Network Open paper describes it (https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.46615).
- **DDI** (https://ddi-dataset.github.io/). The page says it was designed to compare I–II with V–VI, matched on diagnostic category, age, gender and photo date. It also says "personal, non-commercial research purposes only". A Stanford group used it to test LLM accuracy by skin tone (https://doi.org/10.1111/ijd.70452).
- **Black skin lesions** (https://zenodo.org/records/10570316). The page says "The record is publicly accessible, but files are restricted" and asks you to fill in a form. It may be useful for acral lesions. I haven't seen its contents or label scheme.
- **MRA-MIDAS** (https://doi.org/10.71718/15nz-jv40). Pages say Fitzpatrick type was recorded per lesion. Stanford AIMI datasets usually need registration, but I couldn't read the terms. If V–VI is thin, it fails R3.

## Known, not confirmed
- **PASSION** (Digital-Dermatology group): from memory, about 4,900 pediatric images from several Sub-Saharan African countries, mostly Fitzpatrick IV–VI, with a handful of common conditions. This could be the strongest source of V–VI images. The registry search didn't find it. Check its Hugging Face page and the paper, and confirm the licence and access terms.
- **DDI-2** (https://doi.org/10.57761/pgwn-6b62). The record describes 665 images from 550 self-identified Asian patients with biopsy-proven diagnoses and Fitzpatrick type. The access tier is unknown, and the page is rendered by JavaScript so I couldn't read it. I expect mostly types III–IV, so it adds little for V–VI.

## Not recommended, and why
- **HAM10000, ISIC archives:** no skin tone labels, and the population is predominantly light-skinned.
- **PAD-UFES-20** (https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/zr7vgbcyr2/1): open and CC BY 4.0. The metadata includes Fitzpatrick type, but from memory it has many missing values and almost no V–VI.
- **SOS-ALL** (Zenodo 21064520): an amaXhosa dermatitis cohort, but a 123 KB tabular file with no images.
- **FitzDerm-CF** (https://doi.org/10.7910/dvn/ozks1l): synthetic text notes layered on Fitzpatrick17k and DDI images. It is derivative, so use the originals.
- **Other registry hits:** the Hugging Face copies, "DermaMNIST" and the Fitzpatrick-prompting LLM papers' supplements are re-uploads or unrelated.

## What I could not find
- Verified V and VI counts for any dataset. Count them yourself from the metadata files before committing.
- A clinical dataset with Monk labels other than SCIN.
- PASSION in the registries, as noted above.

## Next step
1. Download the Fitzpatrick17k CSV and the SCIN tables (a few minutes each) and tabulate V–VI by diagnosis.
2. Open DermaCon-IN in a browser and confirm the scale.
3. Register for DDI.

Together these should give you a workable V–VI subgroup. Fitzpatrick17k has the largest, noisiest set. DDI has the cleanest, biopsy-proven set. DermaCon-IN and PASSION may give you the deepest V–VI coverage.

graders.name: 07-long-tail
graders.evidence:
The best fit is **DermaCon-IN**, **Fitzpatrick17k**, **SCIN** and **DDI**, and each has a gap you should know about. I checked access and licence for most of them on 2026-11-11. I did not check the per-type image counts, so every count below is from memory unless I say otherwise.

I didn't build the interactive HTML page, so there is no `dataset-shortlist.html`. The registry search covered Hugging Face, Zenodo, DataCite, OpenAIRE and PhysioNet.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** skin images with a diagnosis label.
- **R2 (must):** a Fitzpatrick or Monk label per image or patient.
- **R3 (must):** Fitzpatrick V–VI present in numbers large enough to give stable subgroup metrics.
- **R4 (nice):** patient IDs, so you can split by patient.
- **R5 (nice):** downloadable now.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | DermaCon-IN | Open download (Harvard Dataverse) | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 5,450+ images, ~3,000 patients, 240+ diagnoses | Skin tone scores per image, South Indian patients, so likely V–VI-heavy. The scale and distribution are unchecked. | Record today; skin tone scale not verified |
| 2 | Fitzpatrick17k | Open: GitHub CSV, images fetched from the source atlases | CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 | 16,577 images, 114 conditions | Fitzpatrick label on every image. V–VI is a minority, and I recall roughly a tenth. | Page today; counts from memory |
| 3 | SCIN (Google) | Open download, under the SCIN Data Use License | SCIN Data Use License | 10,000+ images | Dermatologist-estimated Fitzpatrick, layperson Monk and self-reported Fitzpatrick. Diagnoses are dermatologist differentials. V–VI is a minority. | Page today; counts from memory |
| 4 | DDI (Stanford Diverse Dermatology Images) | Free registration and research use agreement | Non-commercial research use | ~656 images, ~570 patients (memory) | Biopsy-proven diagnoses. Built to compare I–II against V–VI. I recall about 200 V–VI images. | Page today; counts from memory |
| 5 | "Black skin lesions" (Zenodo 10570316) | Request form; files restricted | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | Unknown | Acral lesions, assessed against the Fitzpatrick scale. | Access page today; contents not read |
| 6 | MRA-MIDAS (Stanford AIMI) | Registration or data agreement; I couldn't read the terms | Not stated | Not checked | Fitzpatrick type per lesion and biopsy-based labels. I don't know the V–VI share. | Page today; V–VI share unknown |

## Details
- **DermaCon-IN** (https://doi.org/10.7910/dvn/w7ouzm). It is prospective clinical photos with hierarchical diagnoses and body location. The record says "skin tone scores" without naming the scale, so check whether it is Fitzpatrick before you rely on it. Harvard Dataverse blocked my automated check, so open the page in a browser.
- **Fitzpatrick17k** (https://github.com/mattgroh/fitzpatrick17k). The page says it holds "16,577 clinical images sourced from two dermatology atlases" labelled by Scale AI and Centaur Labs. Two caveats:
  - The skin tone labels are crowd-annotated and noisy.

- **PASSION** (Digital-Dermatology group): from memory, about 4,900 pediatric images from several Sub-Saharan African countries, mostly Fitzpatrick IV–VI, with a handful of common conditions. 3. Register for DDI.

graders.name: 01-recall-fitzpatrick17k
graders.evidence:
Three public datasets fit, and I'd use them together. These are from memory, so check the counts and license terms on each dataset's page before you commit.

| Dataset | Size | Skin tone label | Diagnosis label | Types V/VI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DDI (Diverse Dermatology Images, Stanford)** | ~656 images, ~570 patients | Fitzpatrick, grouped as I–II, III–IV, V–VI | Biopsy-confirmed | Roughly a third of the images, about 200 |
| **SCIN (Google)** | ~10k+ images, thousands of contributors | Self-reported Fitzpatrick, dermatologist-estimated Fitzpatrick, and Monk Skin Tone estimates | Dermatologist differential diagnoses, not biopsy | A few hundred to low thousands, depending on which label you use |
| **Fitzpatrick 17k** | ~16.5k images, 114 conditions | Fitzpatrick I–VI per image (crowd-annotated) | Taken from the source atlases (DermaAmin, Atlas Dermatológico) | A couple thousand combined, but V and VI are much rarer than I–III |

**How I'd use them**
- **DDI** is the best ground truth. Its diagnoses are biopsy-confirmed, and the dark-skin subset was built for exactly this kind of audit. It's small, so subgroup confidence intervals will be wide, and the skin tone label is a V–VI group rather than a single type. Access goes through a Stanford AIMI data use agreement.
- **SCIN** is the only one with Monk labels. It's a good large-scale complement. Its diagnoses are probabilistic differentials, so decide up front how to turn them into a single label, such as the top-weighted condition or only cases above a confidence threshold. It's also self-submitted, mostly smartphone-quality, and covers common inflammatory conditions more than cancers.
- **Fitzpatrick 17k** has the most dark-skin volume. Its labels are noisy: skin tone was annotated by non-dermatologists from web images, diagnoses come from the source sites rather than pathology, and there are duplicates and unlabeled entries (coded -1) to filter out. Use it for stress-testing, and don't treat its labels as ground truth.

**Datasets to skip for this audit**
- **PAD-UFES-20** has per-patient Fitzpatrick labels, but almost all patients are type I–III, so V and VI barely appear.
- **HAM10000, BCN20000, and most of the ISIC archive** have no skin tone labels and are heavily skewed toward light skin. Estimating tone with ITA (individual typology angle) is possible but unreliable, and I wouldn't use it as your label.

**Caveats for the audit**
- Use patient-level splits where patient IDs exist (DDI, SCIN). Fitzpatrick 17k has no patient IDs, so check for near-duplicates.
- Condition mix differs across skin tones in all three datasets. A gap by tone can partly reflect which diseases were photographed, so stratify by condition or restrict to conditions present in both light and dark groups.
- Fitzpatrick and Monk labels are estimated from photos, and they disagree with each other. SCIN lets you check how much your result changes depending on which label you use.

I can pull the current download links and exact Fitzpatrick V/VI counts for each dataset if you'd like.

graders.name: 01-recall-fitzpatrick17k
graders.evidence:
Three public datasets fit your criteria, and a fourth is a common trap. The counts below are from memory and I haven't checked them against the current dataset pages, so confirm them before you plan your subgroup sizes.

**Good fits**

| Dataset | Type | Skin tone label | Diagnosis label | Dark-skin coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Fitzpatrick 17k** (Groh et al., 2021) | Clinical photos, about 16.5k images, 114 conditions | Fitzpatrick I–VI per image, plus an "unknown" category | Condition name from the source atlases | The largest pool of V/VI images, roughly a few thousand. |
| **DDI, Diverse Dermatology Images** (Stanford, Daneshjou et al., 2022) | Clinical photos, about 650 images, about 570 patients | Fitzpatrick, grouped as I–II, III–IV, V–VI | Biopsy-confirmed, with a benign/malignant flag and disease name | Roughly a third of the images are V–VI. |
| **SCIN** (Google, 2024) | Clinical photos, 10k+ images from 5k+ volunteers in the US | Fitzpatrick and Monk, both self-reported and dermatologist-estimated | Dermatologist differential diagnoses, with weighted confidence | Broad skin-tone spread, and it's the only one here with Monk labels. |

- **Fitzpatrick 17k:** the labels were crowd-annotated, so they are noisy, often off by about one type. The images are scraped from two online atlases. The repo mostly distributes URLs plus a CSV, so some links may have rotted.
- **DDI:** it's the cleanest ground truth and was built for this kind of audit. It's too small for fine-grained per-disease analysis, and you must request access under a non-commercial research agreement.
- **SCIN:** the diagnoses are dermatologist opinions rather than biopsy results, and the images are patient-taken and varied in quality. It also skews toward common inflammatory conditions.

**Not suitable for V/VI**
- **PAD-UFES-20:** smartphone images with Fitzpatrick recorded, but almost all are types I–III.
- **HAM10000, ISIC 2019, ISIC 2020 and ISIC 2024:** dermoscopy with little or no skin tone metadata, and very few dark-skin images. Some papers have estimated tone with ITA (individual typology angle) to audit these. That's an estimate rather than a clinical label, so I wouldn't treat it as ground truth.

I don't know of a public dermoscopy dataset with both real Fitzpatrick labels and substantial V/VI representation. If you need dermoscopy specifically, expect to rely on ITA-derived labels or give it up.

**Suggested setup**
- Use DDI as your clean test set, since it has biopsy-proven labels and V–VI is well represented.
- Use Fitzpatrick 17k for statistical power, and treat its tone labels as noisy. You could report results with and without the "unknown" images.
- Use SCIN as an external check, and as your Monk-scale source.
- Check that the disease mix is similar across tone groups. In Fitzpatrick 17k especially, condition and tone are confounded, which can look like a fairness gap when it's a case-mix difference.

I can fetch the current dataset pages and pull exact per-type counts and license terms, if you'd like.

graders.name: 01-recall-ptbxl
graders.evidence:
Several large 12-lead ECG sets meet your constraints. You can download all of them today with no application, credentialing or data use agreement. I checked each registry record and landing page on 2026-11-11/12. I did not render the interactive shortlist page or run the "papers that used it" lookups, to keep this short.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** 12-lead, resting, about 10 s recordings.
- **R2 (must):** labels for AF and conduction disorders (LBBB, RBBB, AV block), assigned or confirmed by physicians.
- **R3 (must):** a few thousand recordings or more.
- **R4 (must):** direct download, no application or credentialing.
- **R5 (nice):** a standard label vocabulary and train/test splits.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [PTB-XL](https://physionet.org/content/ptb-xl/1.0.3/) | Direct download, no account | CC-BY-4.0 | ~21.8k records | Strong | Access and licence today; counts from memory |
| 2 | [Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo ("large scale 12-lead ECG database for arrhythmia study")](https://physionet.org/content/ecg-arrhythmia/1.0.0/) | Direct download | CC-BY-4.0 | ~45k records (memory) | Strong | Access and licence today; count from memory |
| 3 | [PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2020 training data](https://physionet.org/content/challenge-2020/1.0.2/) | Direct download | CC-BY-4.0 | >40k (memory) | Strong for pooling, mixed lengths | Access and licence today |
| 4 | [Challenge 2021 training data](https://physionet.org/content/challenge-2021/1.0.3/) | Direct download | CC-BY-4.0 | Larger superset of #3 (memory) | Same as #3 | Access and licence today |
| 5 | [CODE-15%](https://zenodo.org/records/4916206) | Direct download from Zenodo | CC-BY-4.0 | 345,779 exams | Good for scale, label quality needs care | Size, access and licence today |
| 6 | [CODE-test](https://zenodo.org/records/3765780) | Direct download | CC-BY-4.0 | 827 tracings | Too small for training; a good cardiologist-labelled test set | Today |

## Details
**1. PTB-XL** is the safest first choice.
- The page says "The raw waveform data was annotated by up to two cardiologists, who assigned potentially multiple ECG statements to each record."
- It comes with recommended 10-fold splits that respect patient assignment.
- From memory, the statement list includes AFIB, CLBBB, CRBBB, ILBBB, IRBBB and first-, second- and third-degree AV block. Check the `scp_statements.csv` file for the exact codes.
- From memory, records are 10 s at 100 Hz and 500 Hz.

**2. Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo** has a documented labelling process.
- The page says "a licensed physician labeled the rhythm and other cardiac conditions", a second physician validated, and "a senior physician intervened" on disagreements.
- Its settings are consistent with the Challenge 2021 databases.
- A smaller Shaoxing-only copy is also on [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/16789324). I haven't confirmed which subset it holds; from memory it is about 10.6k records.
- It is strong for AF and bundle branch blocks. AV block is rarer.

**3 and 4. The Challenge sets** pool several sources under one SNOMED-CT label scheme.
- The 2020 page lists the sources, including CPSC 2018 (6,877 recordings), CPSC-Extra (3,453) and Georgia (10,344). Georgia is confirmed as 10 s at 500 Hz.
- CPSC recordings run 6–60 s, so you'd need to crop or filter them.
- Label provenance differs by source. Some labels are physician-assigned and others come from machine-read reports plus review. Check each source's description before calling every label cardiologist-confirmed.
- These sets are useful for external validation across hospitals and countries.

**5. CODE-15%** is the largest but the weakest on your "cardiologist-confirmed" criterion.
- From memory, its AF and conduction labels (including 1st-degree AV block, RBBB and LBBB) come partly from automatic or report-derived annotation, not manual review of each tracing.
- I could not confirm that on the page today, so check the paper before relying on it.
- It is better for pre-training.
- Use CODE-test as the matching expert-labelled evaluation set. The page says a third senior specialist resolved disagreements.

## Known, not confirmed
- The exact counts for #2, #3 and #4 and the AV-block counts in each set are from memory. Count them yourself from the header files before you plan a study.
- I did not check whether CODE-15% has a click-through step beyond the Zenodo download. The record is marked open.

graders.name: 01-recall-ptbxl
graders.evidence:
Four open datasets cover your needs, and two of them hold most of the labels: PTB-XL and the Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo database. All of them can be downloaded today with no application, credentialing or data use agreement. I confirmed the access and licence records on 2026-11-11. I did not build the interactive shortlist page, so there is no `dataset-shortlist.html`.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** standard 12-lead resting ECGs of about 10 s.
- **R2 (must):** diagnostic labels for AF, LBBB, RBBB and AV block, ideally from or checked by cardiologists.
- **R3 (must):** at least a few thousand recordings.
- **R4 (must):** direct download with no application or credentialing.
- **R5 (nice):** a standard train/test split and papers to benchmark against.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | PTB-XL | Direct download | CC-BY-4.0 | ~21.8k ECGs, 10 s | Cardiologist-annotated. AF, LBBB, RBBB and AV block codes are in the statement list. | Access and licence confirmed today; code names from memory |
| 2 | Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo ("large scale 12-lead ECG database for arrhythmia study") | Direct download | CC-BY-4.0 | 45,152 ECGs | Physician-labelled, with a second physician validating. It has AF and bundle-branch and AV-block labels. | Access, licence, size and labelling confirmed today; label list from memory |
| 3 | CODE-15% | Direct download from Zenodo | CC-BY-4.0 | 345,779 exams | Has AF, LBBB, RBBB and 1st-degree AV block labels (from memory). Labels are weaker, and recordings may be 7–10 s. | Access and licence confirmed today; label details from memory |
| 4 | CODE-test | Direct download from Zenodo | CC-BY-4.0 | ~800 ECGs (from memory) | Cardiologist-annotated, same label set as CODE-15%. Too small to train on, but good as a gold test set. | Access and licence confirmed today; size from memory |
| 5 | PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2021 (and 2020) | Direct download | CC-BY-4.0 | >88k public ECGs | A pooled collection with one SNOMED-CT label scheme, so it is convenient. | Confirmed today |

## Details
- **PTB-XL:** [physionet.org/content/ptb-xl/1.0.3](https://physionet.org/content/ptb-xl/1.0.3/)
  - **Labels:** The page says "annotated by up to two cardiologists" and "a large fraction of the records was validated by a second cardiologist". It also says some report strings came from the ECG device's automatic interpretation. So the labels are not all purely human.
  - **Splits:** It ships 10-fold splits split by patient, which suits your benchmark need.
  - **Papers:** Strodthoff et al., [10.1109/jbhi.2020.3022989](https://doi.org/10.1109/jbhi.2020.3022989), is a benchmark paper. The dataset paper is [10.1038/s41597-020-0495-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-020-0495-6).
  - **Access:** "Anyone can access the files", under CC-BY-4.0.
- **Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo:** [physionet.org/content/ecg-arrhythmia/1.0.0](https://physionet.org/content/ecg-arrhythmia/1.0.0/)
  - **Labels:** The page says "a licensed physician labeled the rhythm", "another licensed physician performed a secondary validation", and a senior physician settled disagreements. This is your best match for rhythm labels such as AF and for conduction labels.
  - **Format:** From memory, the ECGs are 10 s at 500 Hz. Check the header files.
  - **Access:** Download with `physionet download ecg-arrhythmia --version 1.0.0` or with a terminal command. The page says the IRB allowed public sharing after de-identification.
- **CODE-15%:** [zenodo.org/records/4916206](https://zenodo.org/records/4916206)
  - **Why it's different:** It is the largest set here, with 233,770 patients from Minas Gerais, Brazil, 2010–2016.
  - **Labels (from memory):** They were derived from clinical reports and automatic analysis, then partly checked by cardiologists. That is weaker than PTB-XL or Chapman. Read the label section of the paper before relying on them as ground truth.
  - **CODE-test pairing:** If you need cardiologist-verified evaluation, use CODE-test as your test set.
- **Challenge 2021:** [physionet.org/content/challenge-2021/1.0.3](https://physionet.org/content/challenge-2021/1.0.3/)
  - **Contents:** The page says there are over 88,000 public training ECGs from several sources. They include CPSC 2018 (10,330 ECGs), INCART (74 ECGs), PTB-XL, Georgia (10,344 ECGs) and Chapman-Ningbo (45,152 ECGs). The reading above showed these sources; I did not check the others.
  - **Pooled labels:** It is the quickest route to multi-source data with consistent labels. It also gives you external validation across hospitals and countries.
  - **Overlap:** It contains PTB-XL and Chapman, so do not count them twice or let them leak between your train and test sets.
  - **Recording length:** The CPSC subset has variable recording lengths (from memory), so you may need to crop to 10 s.
  - **Access:** The registration text on that page is for the competition. The data records are open under CC-BY-4.0.

## Known, not confirmed
- **SPH (Shandong Provincial Hospital) database:**
  - **What it is:** It is titled "A large-scale multi-label 12-lead electrocardiogram database with standardized diagnostic statements", with the DOI [10.6084/m9.figshare.c.5779802.v1](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.c.5779802.v1).
  - **What I confirmed:** The DOI exists. The landing page blocked my automated check.
  - **From memory:** It has about 25k ECGs of 10–60 s, with cardiologist-reviewed labels. I believe it is open on figshare, but I don't know the licence.
  - **What to check:** Open the page in a browser to confirm the licence and whether recordings are all 10 s.
- **Georgia (Emory) and CPSC 2018:** I did not open them separately. The Challenge page confirms they are included in the Challenge data.

## Not recommended, and why
- **MIMIC-IV-ECG and MIMIC-IV-Ext-ECG-Glucose:** They need PhysioNet credentialing, which you ruled out. I confirmed the credentialed licence on the Glucose one. The MIMIC-IV-ECG label situation is from memory and I did not look it up.
- **KURIAS-ECG:** It needs a free account plus a restricted-data licence, so it isn't a plain download.
- **Hugging Face copies (for example `tirandazdylan/ptb-xl-ecg`):** Use the official PhysioNet source instead. The copies are unofficial, and some have no stated licence.
- **Small or off-target sets:** The Brugada, Leipzig paediatric and ventricular-arrhythmia sets, the 100-record SPH-Mini, and MIT-BIH-style single-lead sets don't match your labels or scale.

## What I could not find
I did not find a single dataset with large numbers of **cardiologist-verified** AV-block (2nd and 3rd degree) labels. Those classes are rare in all of these sets, so check the per-class counts before you commit. I also haven't confirmed the exact label names in PTB-XL or Chapman. I searched five registries and the literature. I did not search country-specific portals.

## Next step
1. Download PTB-XL and Chapman first. Together they give about 67k labelled 10 s ECGs, enough for AF, LBBB and RBBB.
2. Count the AV-block examples per class in each set.
3. Add CODE-15% if you need more AV-block or LBBB volume. Use CODE-test to check that its label noise is acceptable.
4. Treat Challenge 2021 as a pooled, pre-harmonised source or for external validation. Don't also train on PTB-XL and Chapman separately without deduplicating.
5. Confirm the licence terms for your intended use. CC-BY needs attribution, and these sets are de-identified.

graders.name: 01-recall-ptbxl
graders.evidence:
**Start with PTB-XL.** It's the closest match to what you describe, and you can download it today with no account, application or credentialing.

## Best options (all open download)

| Dataset | Size | Labels | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PTB-XL** (PhysioNet) | ~21.8k records, ~18.9k patients, 10 s, 12-lead, 500 Hz and 100 Hz | Up to two cardiologists annotated each record. Labels are SCP-ECG statements, including AFIB, AFLT, CLBBB, CRBBB, ILBBB, IRBBB, LAFB/LPFB, 1AVB, 2AVB, 3AVB and IVCD. | CC BY 4.0. It ships with patient-stratified 10-fold splits. Folds 9 and 10 were human-validated, so they work well as val/test. Conduction classes are reasonably represented, but AV block II/III is rare. |
| **Chapman-Shaoxing / Ningbo** (PhysioNet) | ~45k records, 10 s, 500 Hz | Rhythm labels (AF, flutter, SVT, sinus rhythms, etc.) plus other condition labels, assigned by physicians | Open access. It's strong for AF, with more variable coverage of conduction classes. Check the label list for the BBB and AV block counts. |
| **CODE-15%** (Zenodo) | ~345k exams, ~233k patients, ~7–10 s, 400 Hz | 1dAVb, RBBB, LBBB, AF, sinus bradycardia and sinus tachycardia | By far the largest. The training labels are mostly derived from clinical reports and automated processing rather than individually confirmed by cardiologists. Use it for pretraining or scale, not as ground truth. |
| **Shandong Provincial Hospital (SPH)** (Figshare) | ~25k records, 10 s, 500 Hz | 44 AHA/ACC/HRS-coded statements, cardiologist-assigned | Open, but check the license on the record page. |
| **PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2021 training set** | ~88k records pooled from several sources | SNOMED-CT labels. Scored classes include AF, I-AVB, LBBB and RBBB. | It pools PTB-XL, Chapman, Ningbo, Georgia, CPSC and others. Recording lengths vary (CPSC runs 6–60 s, and INCART is 30-minute recordings), so filter to 10 s. It's useful for testing generalization across sites. |

## Practical suggestions
- **Core set:** use PTB-XL for training and evaluation. It has ~22k records with cardiologist labels, which is well past "a few thousand".
- **Rhythm labels:** add Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo for more AF.
- **Generalization:** hold out one source (e.g. Chapman-Shaoxing or SPH) as an external test set, since single-site results often overstate performance.
- **Splits:** split by patient, not by record, when you build your own splits. PTB-XL's folds already do this.
- **Label mapping:** the label vocabularies differ (SCP-ECG, SNOMED, AHA codes). Map them to one scheme early.
- **Skip for now:** MIMIC-IV-ECG is large, but it requires PhysioNet credentialing and a training course. It's an option later if the lab sets that up.

## Caveat on ethics
"Open access" removes the application step. It doesn't necessarily remove your institution's requirements. Many ethics offices want a short exemption or "not human subjects research" determination, even for de-identified public data. It's usually a quick form, but confirm before you publish.

I'm working from memory here, and I haven't checked these against the live pages. Record counts and licenses can change between versions, so check each dataset's landing page. I can fetch them and pull the exact per-class counts for AF, LBBB, RBBB and AV block if you'd like.

graders.name: 01-recall-ptbxl
graders.evidence:
Several large, cardiologist-labeled 12-lead datasets are open access, so you can download them now with no application, credentialing or data use agreement. I'm going from memory and haven't checked the live pages, so confirm the counts and licenses on each dataset page before you commit.

## Best options

**1. PTB-XL (PhysioNet, open access, CC BY 4.0)**
- It has about 21,800 recordings from about 18,900 patients. All are 10 s, available at 500 Hz and 100 Hz.
- Cardiologists annotated them with standardized SCP-ECG statements, and a subset has a validation flag. There is also a suggested patient-wise 10-fold split.
- It covers AF, complete and incomplete LBBB and RBBB, left anterior fascicular block, and 1st, 2nd and 3rd degree AV block.
- 2nd and 3rd degree AV block are very rare in it, with only a handful of records each. 1st degree AV block has several hundred.
- It's the best starting point because it's clean, exactly 10 s, and well documented.

**2. CPSC 2018 (China Physiological Signal Challenge)**
- It has about 6,900 12-lead recordings at 500 Hz, labeled as Normal, AF, I-AVB, LBBB, RBBB, PAC, PVC, ST depression or ST elevation.
- That label set closely matches your targets.
- Recordings are 6–60 s, not a fixed 10 s, so you'd need to crop or segment them.
- It's also included in the Challenge collections below.

**3. Chapman-Shaoxing and Ningbo (PhysioNet, open access)**
- It has about 45,000 patients with 10 s, 500 Hz recordings.
- Rhythm labels such as AF were assigned by cardiologists. Conduction coverage is thinner than in PTB-XL.
- You can get it through the PhysioNet 2021 Challenge package or the original release.

**4. PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2020 and 2021 training data (open access)**
- This bundles PTB-XL, CPSC, CPSC-Extra, Georgia, Chapman-Shaoxing, Ningbo, PTB and St Petersburg INCART. The 2021 set is about 88,000 recordings in total.
- Labels are mapped to SNOMED-CT codes that include AF, LBBB, RBBB, 1st degree AV block and others, so it's the easiest way to get a large multi-source set.
- Recording lengths and sampling rates vary, and label quality differs by source.

**5. CODE-15% (Zenodo, open access)**
- It has about 345,000 ECGs from Brazil's Telehealth Network of Minas Gerais, labeled 1dAVb, RBBB, LBBB, sinus bradycardia, AF or sinus tachycardia.
- It's the biggest option by far.

cases.name: ho-h-measured-bp-surveys
cases.promptMarkdown: I'm writing an epidemiology thesis chapter on hypertension awareness, i.e. what share of adults with high blood pressure don't know they have it. For that I need nationally representative survey data where blood pressure was actually measured by a nurse or examiner, alongside a question on whether a doctor ever told them they have high blood pressure. Self-reported hypertension on its own is useless to me. US data would be ideal, but I'd also like one or two comparable national surveys from other countries (samples of middle-aged and older adults are fine). Which surveys should I use, and what do I have to do to get each one?

graders.name: 01-recall-nhanes
graders.evidence:
I'd use NHANES for the US, with ELSA (England) and CHARLS or LASI (China, India) as the comparison surveys. I confirmed the access routes for NHANES and ELSA today. I couldn't confirm the rest, so those access details come from memory and are marked below.

I also didn't build the interactive shortlist page. This answer is the full deliverable.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** Blood pressure measured by a nurse or examiner, not self-reported.
- **R2 (must):** A question on whether a doctor ever told the respondent they have high blood pressure, in the same survey and person.
- **R3 (must):** Nationally representative samples of adults, US first.
- **R4 (nice):** Middle-aged and older samples abroad, with comparable designs.
- **R5 (nice):** Free or fast to get.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES (US, all adults) | Direct download, no account | US government data, public use | Strong | Site confirmed today; variable details from memory |
| 2 | HRS (US, age 50+) | Free registration, then download | HRS terms of use | Strong | From memory (site returned 403 to my tool) |
| 3 | ELSA (England, age 50+) | Free UK Data Service account, then download | UKDS End User Licence | Strong | Access page read today |
| 4 | CHARLS (China, age 45+) | Registration and application on the CHARLS site | CHARLS terms | Strong | Site exists today; access terms from memory |
| 5 | LASI (India, age 45+) | Application or registration, via IIPS | LASI terms | Strong | From memory; the registry record exists, but I couldn't read the access terms |

## Details

**1. NHANES**
- **What it is:** The US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, with a home interview and a mobile exam centre. The exam takes several blood pressure readings from trained examiners.
- **Awareness variable:** The blood pressure questionnaire asks whether a doctor or health professional ever said you had hypertension. I recall the variable as `BPQ020` in the BPQ file, but I haven't confirmed it today.
- **Access:** Download the files from the NHANES site (https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/). The site lists a Data User Agreement and a "Limited Access Data" category, which is not what you need. There are no application steps, so you can start today.
- **Coverage:** Cycles from 1999 onward, with the latest listed as 2021–2023 (confirmed on the site). Use the exam sample weights, because the blood pressure readings come from the exam sample.
- **Precedent:** The search returned a record for "Awareness of having hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia among US adults: The 2011–2018 NHANES data" (OpenAIRE). It is useful as a methods precedent.

**2. HRS (Health and Retirement Study)**
- **What it is:** A US panel of adults aged 50 and over. Interviewers measure blood pressure in the physical measures, and I recall this covering half the sample each wave since 2006. The interview asks whether a doctor has ever said you have high blood pressure.
- **Access:** From memory, register free at hrs.isr.umich.edu, accept the terms, and download. This should take days at most.
- **Caveat:** Blood pressure is only measured for part of the sample at each wave, so check the sample design before pooling waves.

**3. ELSA (English Longitudinal Study of Ageing)**
- **What it is:** Respondents aged 50+. From memory, nurse visits take measured blood pressure in alternating waves, and the main interview records doctor-diagnosed hypertension. Check which waves have nurse visits before you plan.
- **Access (confirmed):** The ELSA page says "Researchers can download ELSA data from waves 1-11 including wave 0 (HSE), from the UK Data Service." It also says "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS," and non-UK users can request a username. Special Licence and Secure Access data have more restrictions, but you shouldn't need them.
- **Record:** https://doi.org/10.5255/ukda-sn-5050-37 (waves 0–11, 1998–2024).
- **Why it fits:** It is designed to be comparable with HRS.

**4. CHARLS (China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study)**
- **What it is:** Chinese residents aged 45 and over (confirmed on the site). From memory, interviewers measure blood pressure and the survey asks about a doctor's diagnosis.
- **Access:** From memory, sign up on the CHARLS site and apply for the data. Approval usually takes days to weeks.
- **Caveat:** The site currently shows the banner "This repository is under review for potential modification in compliance with Administration directives." Check that downloads still work before you build around it.
- **Related paper:** "Socioeconomic gradients of cardiovascular risk factors in China and India" uses CHARLS and LASI (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00038-017-0968-3).

**5. LASI (Longitudinal Ageing Study in India)**
- **What it is:** Adults aged 45 and over. From memory, trained field staff measure blood pressure and the survey asks about a doctor's diagnosis. The cohort profile is at https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyab266.
- **Access, uncertain:** The DataCite record "Longitudinal Aging Study Asia (LASI)" resolves to a Stanford/Redivis page, and I couldn't read the terms. The IIPS page I fetched had no access text. Treat the access route as unconfirmed and check with IIPS or the Gateway to Global Aging Data (g2aging.org).
- **Try first:** Check whether the LASI team's own data request process is still the route for researchers outside India.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Methods template:** "Unmet needs for hypertension care cascade in older adults and socioeconomic disparities: evidence from five national cohorts" (https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-26341-4). The abstract says the cohorts include the US, UK and China, but it was truncated and I couldn't see the other two. It likely uses the same HRS, ELSA, CHARLS and LASI families.
- **Other candidates from memory:** The Health Survey for England (measured blood pressure, via UKDS) and the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. I haven't checked either today.

## Not recommended, and why
- **Self-report-only surveys** such as the US National Health Interview Survey and BRFSS fail your measured blood pressure requirement.
- **Synthetic hypertension datasets** (for example the Hugging Face and Figshare ones from the search) are not real surveys.
- **NHANES paper supplements on Zenodo and Figshare** are derived or reproducibility files. Use the CDC original.

## What I could not find
- I did not confirm variable names or which waves have blood pressure for HRS, CHARLS and LASI. Check each codebook.
- I couldn't read the HRS or LASI access pages, so those steps come from memory.

## Next step
Start with NHANES today, since it needs no account. Register for ELSA at UKDS and for HRS in parallel. Request CHARLS or LASI at the same time, because those approvals take the longest. Choose one definition of awareness up front and apply it in every survey: measured systolic ≥140 or diastolic ≥90, or on blood pressure medication, then the share who report a doctor's diagnosis.

Checked 2026-11-11. Access rules change, so recheck before you commit.

graders.name: 01-recall-nhanes
graders.evidence:
For your chapter I'd use NHANES as the main US source. Add ELSA (England) and either LASI (India) or CHARLS (China) as comparators. Only part of this is confirmed against official pages today (12 Nov 2026), and I've marked which.

I didn't build the interactive shortlist page. The registry search returned almost only paper supplements, and the real sources live on agency sites.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1:** Nationally representative adults.
- **R2:** BP measured by an examiner or interviewer, not self-reported.
- **R3:** A "ever told by a doctor you have high blood pressure" item, plus a BP medication item, so you can classify aware and unaware among the measured-hypertensive.
- **R4:** Middle-aged and older samples are fine abroad.
- **R5:** Free or academic access is fine.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES** (US, CDC/NCHS) | Direct download, no account (from memory) | US government data, public use, with a data user agreement | Meets R1–R3. Examiner-measured BP in the mobile exam centre, plus the BP questionnaire. | Page confirmed today; variables from memory |
| 2 | **ELSA** (England, 50+) | Free UKDS account, download at End User Licence level | UKDS End User Licence | Nurse-visit waves have measured BP, and the interview asks about doctor-diagnosed hypertension. | Access confirmed today; contents from memory |
| 3 | **HRS** (US, 50+) | Free registration for public files. Biomarker and sensitive health files need a supplemental order form. | HRS terms and conditions | Interviewer-measured BP in the physical measures, plus the doctor-told item. | Access from search today; contents from memory |
| 4 | **LASI** (India, 45+, 2017–18) | Request form to IIPS | Confidential-data conditions | Measured BP and doctor-diagnosis items. Published awareness analyses exist. | Access from search today |
| 5 | **CHARLS** (China, 45+) | Free account on the project site (from memory) | Project terms | Measured BP plus a doctor-diagnosis item. | Site showed a login and register page today; the rest is from memory |

## Details

**NHANES** is the home page (https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/), and it lists a Data User Agreement and ethics approval documentation.
- **Steps:** Open the cycle you want and download the examination BP file, the BP and cholesterol questionnaire file and the demographics file. Merge them on the participant ID (SEQN).
- **Variable:** The doctor-told item is, from memory, `BPQ020`, which asks if a doctor or other health professional ever told the person they had hypertension. Check the code in the cycle's codebook.
- **Method point:** The most recent cycles switched from a mercury sphygmomanometer to an oscillometric device. From memory, that affects comparability across years. I couldn't confirm the file names today. My one guessed URL returned a 404, so I'm not giving you a link.
- **Complex survey:** Use the MEC exam weights and the strata and PSU variables.

**ELSA** (https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data)
- The page says: "Researchers can download ELSA data from waves 1-11 including wave 0 (HSE), from the UK Data Service."
- It also says: "Note that End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS."
- UK institutions log in with their institutional account. Everyone else requests a username.
- From memory, only some waves have nurse visits, so check which waves carry BP before you design the analysis.

**HRS** (https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/data-products)
- My fetch of this page was refused (HTTP 403), so I used a web search.
- Public data are free to registered users. Biomarker and sensitive health data need an extra step, via the Sensitive Health Data Order Form (https://hrsdata.isr.umich.edu/data-products/sensitive-health).
- It is unclear whether the measured BP values sit in the public core files or only in the biomarker files. Check the new-user guide (https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/new-user-guide/HRS-New-User-Guide-July-2025.pdf) before planning around it.
- From memory, physical measures were taken on a rotating half-sample from 2006.

**LASI**
- Wave 1 data and documentation are reported to be available through the IIPS site, data.gov.in and the Gateway to Global Aging.
- The request form is at https://iipsindia.ac.in/sites/default/files/LASI_DataRequestForm_0.pdf. A PLOS Medicine paper says data go to researchers who meet the criteria for confidential data. This is second-hand, and my direct fetch of an IIPS page returned a 404.
- Per a secondary paper, three BP readings were taken and the last two averaged. BP is missing for about 9% of participants.
- A close methods precedent is the PLOS Medicine paper on [hypertension awareness, treatment and control in India](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pmed.1003740).

**CHARLS** (https://charls.charlsdata.com/)
- The data page lists the 2011 baseline through the 2021–23 follow-up, plus Harmonized CHARLS.
- The page is drawn by JavaScript, so I couldn't read the terms. From memory, it needs a free account and an application describing your use, and it's usually fast.

## Known, not confirmed
- **KNHANES (Korea):** From memory, a free download after registering with KDCA. I didn't check it.
- **Health Survey for England:** From memory, a nurse-measured BP survey via UKDS, with a self-report item on doctor-diagnosed hypertension.

## Not recommended
- **SHARE:** From memory, it has no routine BP measurement, so you can't classify unaware hypertension.
- **Add Health, L.A.FANS and the Zenodo, figshare and Hugging Face hits:** These are not representative adult surveys or are derivative files. Re-analysis files are not the source.

## What I could not find
- I couldn't confirm the exact NHANES file names for each cycle.
- I couldn't read the CHARLS or HRS terms pages directly.
- I didn't run the paper lookup for each dataset.

## Next step
1. Start with NHANES, since you need no approval.
2. Register for ELSA at UKDS and for HRS the same day.
3. Submit the LASI or CHARLS request early, since those are the slow ones.
4. Define "aware" before merging. The standard definition is among people with measured SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 or on BP medication, the share who report a doctor told them. Check that each survey's measurement protocol matches.

Sources:
- [NHANES](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/)
- [ELSA data access](https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data)
- [HRS data products](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/data-products)
- [HRS sensitive health data](https://hrsdata.isr.umich.edu/data-products/sensitive-health)
- [LASI data request form](https://iipsindia.ac.in/sites/default/files/LASI_DataRequestForm_0.pdf)
- [CHARLS](https://charls.charlsdata.com/)

| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES** (US, CDC/NCHS) | Direct download, no account (from memory) | US government data, public use, with a data user agreement | Meets R1–R3. Examiner-measured BP in the mobile exam centre, plus the BP questionnaire. | Page confirmed today; variables from memory |
| 2 | **ELSA** (England, 50+) | Free UKDS account, download at End User Licence level | UKDS End User Licence | Nurse-visit waves have measured BP, and the interview asks about doctor-diagnosed hypertension. | Access confirmed today; contents from memory |
| 3 | **HRS** (US, 50+) | Free registration for public files. Biomarker and sensitive health files need a supplemental order form. | HRS terms and conditions | Interviewer-measured BP in the physical measures, plus the doctor-told item. | Access from search today; contents from memory |
| 4 | **LASI** (India, 45+, 2017–18) | Request form to IIPS | Confidential-data conditions | Measured BP and doctor-diagnosis items. Published awareness analyses exist. | Access from search today |
| 5 | **CHARLS** (China, 45+) | Free account on the project site (from memory) | Project terms | Measured BP plus a doctor-diagnosis item. | Site showed a login and register page today; the rest is from memory |

**NHANES** is the home page (https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/), and it lists a Data User Agreement and ethics approval documentation.
- **Steps:** Open the cycle you want and download the examination BP file, the BP and cholesterol questionnaire file and the demographics file. Merge them on the participant ID (SEQN).
- **Variable:** The doctor-told item is, from memory, `BPQ020`, which asks if a doctor or other health professional ever told the person they had hypertension. Check the code in the cycle's codebook.
- **Method point:** The most recent cycles switched from a mercury sphygmomanometer to an oscillometric device. From memory, that affects comparability across years. I couldn't confirm the file names today. My one guessed URL returned a 404, so I'm not giving you a link.
- **Complex survey:** Use the MEC exam weights and the strata and PSU variables.

**ELSA** (https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data)
- The page says: "Researchers can download ELSA data from waves 1-11 including wave 0 (HSE), from the UK Data Service."

- UK institutions log in with their institutional account. Everyone else requests a username.
- From memory, only some waves have nurse visits, so check which waves carry BP before you design the analysis.

**HRS** (https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/data-products)
- My fetch of this page was refused (HTTP 403), so I used a web search.
- Public data are free to registered users. Biomarker and sensitive health data need an extra step, via the Sensitive Health Data Order Form (https://hrsdata.isr.umich.edu/data-products/sensitive-health).

- From memory, physical measures were taken on a rotating half-sample from 2006.

- Wave 1 data and documentation are reported to be available through the IIPS site, data.gov.in and the Gateway to Global Aging.
- The request form is at https://iipsindia.ac.in/sites/default/files/LASI_DataRequestForm_0.pdf. A PLOS Medicine paper says data go to researchers who meet the criteria for confidential data. This is second-hand, and my direct fetch of an IIPS page returned a 404.
- Per a secondary paper, three BP readings were taken and the last two averaged. BP is missing for about 9% of participants.

- The data page lists the 2011 baseline through the 2021–23 follow-up, plus Harmonized CHARLS.
- The page is drawn by JavaScript, so I couldn't read the terms. From memory, it needs a free account and an application describing your use, and it's usually fast.

## Known, not confirmed
- **KNHANES (Korea):** From memory, a free download after registering with KDCA. I didn't check it.
- **Health Survey for England:** From memory, a nurse-measured BP survey via UKDS, with a self-report item on doctor-diagnosed hypertension.

- **SHARE:** From memory, it has no routine BP measurement, so you can't classify unaware hypertension.
- **Add Health, L.A.FANS and the Zenodo, figshare and Hugging Face hits:** These are not representative adult surveys or are derivative files. Re-analysis files are not the source.

- I couldn't confirm the exact NHANES file names for each cycle.
- I couldn't read the CHARLS or HRS terms pages directly.
- I didn't run the paper lookup for each dataset.

1. Start with NHANES, since you need no approval.
2. Register for ELSA at UKDS and for HRS the same day.
3. Submit the LASI or CHARLS request early, since those are the slow ones.
4. Define "aware" before merging. The standard definition is among people with measured SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 or on BP medication, the share who report a doctor told them. Check that each survey's measurement protocol matches.

**NHANES** is the home page (https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/), and it lists a Data User Agreement and ethics approval documentation.
- **Steps:** Open the cycle you want and download the examination BP file, the BP and cholesterol questionnaire file and the demographics file. Merge them on the participant ID (SEQN).
- **Variable:** The doctor-told item is, from memory, `BPQ020`, which asks if a doctor or other health professional ever told the person they had hypertension. Check the code in the cycle's codebook.
- **Method point:** The most recent cycles switched from a mercury sphygmomanometer to an oscillometric device. From memory, that affects comparability across years. I couldn't confirm the file names today. My one guessed URL returned a 404, so I'm not giving you a link.
- **Complex survey:** Use the MEC exam weights and the strata and PSU variables.

**ELSA** (https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data)
- The page says: "Researchers can download ELSA data from waves 1-11 including wave 0 (HSE), from the UK Data Service."
- It also says: "Note that End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS."
- UK institutions log in with their institutional account. Everyone else requests a username.
- From memory, only some waves have nurse visits, so check which waves carry BP before you design the analysis.

**HRS** (https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/data-products)
- My fetch of this page was refused (HTTP 403), so I used a web search.
- Public data are free to registered users. Biomarker and sensitive health data need an extra step, via the Sensitive Health Data Order Form (https://hrsdata.isr.umich.edu/data-products/sensitive-health).
- It is unclear whether the measured BP values sit in the public core files or only in the biomarker files. Check the new-user guide (https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/new-user-guide/HRS-New-User-Guide-July-2025.pdf) before planning around it.
- From memory, physical measures were taken on a rotating half-sample from 2006.

**LASI**
- Wave 1 data and documentation are reported to be available through the IIPS site, data.gov.in and the Gateway to Global Aging.
- The request form is at https://iipsindia.ac.in/sites/default/files/LASI_DataRequestForm_0.pdf. A PLOS Medicine paper says data go to researchers who meet the criteria for confidential data. This is second-hand, and my direct fetch of an IIPS page returned a 404.
- Per a secondary paper, three BP readings were taken and the last two averaged. BP is missing for about 9% of participants.
- A close methods precedent is the PLOS Medicine paper on [hypertension awareness, treatment and control in India](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pmed.1003740).

**CHARLS** (https://charls.charlsdata.com/)
- The data page lists the 2011 baseline through the 2021–23 follow-up, plus Harmonized CHARLS.
- The page is drawn by JavaScript, so I couldn't read the terms. From memory, it needs a free account and an application describing your use, and it's usually fast.

## Known, not confirmed
- **KNHANES (Korea):** From memory, a free download after registering with KDCA. I didn't check it.
- **Health Survey for England:** From memory, a nurse-measured BP survey via UKDS, with a self-report item on doctor-diagnosed hypertension.

## Not recommended
- **SHARE:** From memory, it has no routine BP measurement, so you can't classify unaware hypertension.
- **Add Health, L.A.FANS and the Zenodo, figshare and Hugging Face hits:** These are not representative adult surveys or are derivative files. Re-analysis files are not the source.

## What I could not find
- I couldn't confirm the exact NHANES file names for each cycle.
- I couldn't read the CHARLS or HRS terms pages directly.
- I didn't run the paper lookup for each dataset.

## Next step
1. Start with NHANES, since you need no approval.
2. Register for ELSA at UKDS and for HRS the same day.
3. Submit the LASI or CHARLS request early, since those are the slow ones.
4. Define "aware" before merging. The standard definition is among people with measured SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 or on BP medication, the share who report a doctor told them. Check that each survey's measurement protocol matches.

Sources:
- [NHANES](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/)
- [ELSA data access](https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data)
- [HRS data products](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/data-products)
- [HRS sensitive health data](https://hrsdata.isr.umich.edu/data-products/sensitive-health)
- [LASI data request form](https://iipsindia.ac.in/sites/default/files/LASI_DataRequestForm_0.pdf)
- [CHARLS](https://charls.charlsdata.com/)

graders.name: 01-recall-nhanes
graders.evidence:
You can do this with NHANES for the US and ELSA plus one of CHARLS or LASI for other countries. I checked these through search results and one verified CDC page. I did not build the interactive shortlist page. Only one record (the NHANES questionnaire page) passed the verification tool. The UK Data Service, HRS and Michigan biomarker-network pages block automated checks, so I couldn't read their access terms directly. Where I say "from memory", I haven't confirmed it.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** A measured blood pressure (BP) by an examiner or nurse.
- **R2 (must):** A "has a doctor ever told you that you have high BP" question in the same respondents.
- **R3 (must):** A nationally representative sample with survey weights.
- **R4:** US first, plus one or two comparable countries.
- **R5:** Middle-aged and older adults are fine.
- **R6:** Free microdata that you can get without a long wait.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES (US, all ages, 1999 to 2023) | Open download, no registration (from memory) | Strong | Questionnaire item confirmed today; access from memory |
| 2 | HRS (US, age 50+) | Free registration. Possibly an extra "sensitive data" step. | Strong | Search results only |
| 3 | ELSA (England, age 50+) | Free UK Data Service registration, End User Licence | Strong | Search results only |
| 4 | CHARLS (China, age 45+) | Free registration | Strong | Search results, plus the Gateway to Global Aging page |
| 5 | LASI (India, age 45+) | Open download from several hosts | Strong | Search results only |
| 6 | KNHANES (Korea, all ages) | Free registration, Korean-language site | Strong | Search results only |
| 7 | MHAS (Mexico, age 50+) | Free registration, BP only from 2012 | Partial | Search results only |
| 8 | TILDA (Ireland, age 50+) | Application and fees | Strong, but slow | Search results only |

## Details

**1. NHANES (US).**
- **What it has:** Examiners measure BP in the mobile exam centre, and the household interview asks `BPQ020` ("ever told you had high blood pressure"). The interviewer codes pregnancy-only and "borderline" answers as No. `BPQ030` asks whether you were told on two or more visits.
- **Confirmed today:** The CDC [BPQ documentation](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2021/DataFiles/BPQ_L.htm) loaded, and `BPQ020` was described in the questionnaire PDFs.
- **From memory:**
  - The exam files are `BPX*`.
  - Download is open with no registration and no application, so you can start today.
  - The data are US public domain.
- **Method notes:**
  - Use the exam (MEC) weights when you merge exam and questionnaire files.
  - The 2021–2023 cycle dropped several follow-up items, so check the questions you need cycle by cycle.

**2. HRS (US, age 50+).**
- **What it has:** A longitudinal panel with measured BP in the physical-measures component from 2006. I recall that the diagnosis question is "Has a doctor ever told you that you have high blood pressure or hypertension?" (from memory).
- **Access:** Search results say registration is free. The dried-blood-spot and venous-blood biomarkers are "sensitive" data, which need an order form and a use agreement. One paper used BP from the public physical-measures files, so BP may not need the sensitive step. Confirm this on the [HRS sensitive data page](https://hrsdata.isr.umich.edu/data-products/sensitive-health) and in the [New User Guide](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/new-user-guide/HRS-New-User-Guide-July-2025.pdf).
- **Method note:** BP was measured in a rotating half-sample each wave (from memory).

**3. ELSA (England).**
- **Why it's the best comparator for the US:** Nurse visits measure BP at Waves 2, 4, 6 and 8, plus a half-sample at Wave 9. Wave 0 came from the Health Survey for England.
- **Access:** The data are on the UK Data Service as [SN 5050](https://datacatalogue.ukdataservice.ac.uk/studies/study/5050). The catalogue lists them as "safeguarded", so you register and accept the End User Licence. That takes days.
- **Check yourself:** The catalogue page needs a browser, so I couldn't confirm the record. Also check which nurse waves are in the current edition.
- **Docs:** The [nurse visit user guide](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/population-health-sciences/sites/population_health_sciences/files/5050_waves_2-4-6-8_nurse_data_user_guide_v01_0.pdf).
- **Contacts:** ELSAdata@natcen.ac.uk or elsa@ucl.ac.uk.

**4. CHARLS (China).**
- **What it has:** BP was measured three times at Waves 1 to 3 (2011, 2013, 2015), and there is a 2020 wave. The interview has a doctor-diagnosis question (from memory).
- **Access:** Free, with registration on the CHARLS site (charls.pku.edu.cn). The [Gateway to Global Aging page](https://g2aging.org/additional-resources/gateway-blog/05a8df66-b9ab-47de-879e-b0bde672798d) says harmonized files can be downloaded by any registered user.
- **Check yourself:** Which waves include BP and the diagnosis question.

**5. LASI (India).**
- **What it has:** Wave 1 (2017–18) has measured BP, taken three times at five-minute intervals. The sample is age 45+.
- **Access:** Wave 1 microdata and documentation are public via IIPS, data.gov.in, lasi-india.org and the Gateway to Global Aging. The Gateway's harmonized file includes the measured BP.
- **Check yourself:** The licence terms were not read.
- **Prior use:** Two LASI hypertension awareness papers are listed under evidence of use below.

**6. KNHANES (Korea).**
- **What it has:** An examination survey like NHANES. Published papers define awareness as a prior diagnosis by medical personnel.
- **Access:** Download from [knhanes.kdca.go.kr](https://knhanes.kdca.go.kr) after a login. Raw data come out each December for the previous year's survey. Documentation is largely Korean.

**7. MHAS (Mexico).**
- **What it has:** BP was first measured in 2012, in a subsample, and again in 2018. Use the biomarker weight (`factora_12` for 2012).
- **Access:** Free registration at [mhasweb.org](https://www.mhasweb.org/DataProducts/Home.aspx).

**8. TILDA (Ireland).**
- **What it has:** A health-assessment BP measurement at Waves 1 and 3 only.
- **Access:** ICPSR has withdrawn it, so older guides pointing there are out of date. You apply to TILDA directly (tilda@tcd.ie, [tilda.tcd.ie](https://tilda.tcd.ie/)), and fees apply. Plan for weeks.

## Evidence of use
These are the papers the search returned:
- [Cardiovascular Risk Factor Prevalence and Control by Education Strata in Older Adults in 3 Countries](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.25410) (2026). It compares the US, England and South Korea in adults 50+, so it is close to your design. I only read the abstract, so check which surveys it used.
- [LASI awareness, treatment and control, middle-aged and older](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8726460/).
- [Sex-specific LASI hypertension analysis](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10464490/).
- [KNHANES hypertension awareness trends](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6662850/).

## Known, not confirmed
- **Health Survey for England** (nurse-measured BP plus a doctor-diagnosis question, from memory). I didn't search for it, and it is probably the other UK option.
- **SAGE (WHO)** and **Canadian Health Measures Survey** (both from memory). I didn't search for either.
- **SHARE** does not measure BP, as far as I recall. Confirm before ruling it in or out.

## Not recommended
- **Anything self-report only.** The registry hits were mostly paper supplements, small clinic studies and synthetic data. None is nationally representative.

## What I could not find
- **Terms I couldn't read:** Licence terms for ELSA, CHARLS, LASI and KNHANES, and the exact HRS sensitive-data rule for BP.
- **Registries:** The registry tool only searched DataCite, Hugging Face, OpenAIRE, PhysioNet and Zenodo. These surveys sit in their own archives, so I found them by web search.
- **Variables:** I didn't check variable names, so confirm them in each codebook.

## Next step
1. Download the NHANES `BPX` and `BPQ` files today and build your awareness cascade there.
2. Register with UKDS for ELSA.
3. Register with CHARLS or download LASI.
4. Confirm the HRS BP file tier before you plan around it.

Access details were checked on 2026-11-12, and these rules change, so re-check each one before you rely on it.

- **R6:** Free microdata that you can get without a long wait.

| # | Dataset | Access | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES (US, all ages, 1999 to 2023) | Open download, no registration (from memory) | Strong | Questionnaire item confirmed today; access from memory |
| 2 | HRS (US, age 50+) | Free registration. Possibly an extra "sensitive data" step. | Strong | Search results only |
| 3 | ELSA (England, age 50+) | Free UK Data Service registration, End User Licence | Strong | Search results only |
| 4 | CHARLS (China, age 45+) | Free registration | Strong | Search results, plus the Gateway to Global Aging page |
| 5 | LASI (India, age 45+) | Open download from several hosts | Strong | Search results only |
| 6 | KNHANES (Korea, all ages) | Free registration, Korean-language site | Strong | Search results only |

  - The data are US public domain.
- **Method notes:**
  - Use the exam (MEC) weights when you merge exam and questionnaire files.
  - The 2021–2023 cycle dropped several follow-up items, so check the questions you need cycle by cycle.

**2. HRS (US, age 50+).**
- **What it has:** A longitudinal panel with measured BP in the physical-measures component from 2006. I recall that the diagnosis question is "Has a doctor ever told you that you have high blood pressure or hypertension?" (from memory).

3. Register with CHARLS or download LASI.
4. Confirm the HRS BP file tier before you plan around it.

graders.name: 01-recall-nhanes
graders.evidence:
I'd use NHANES as the main US source and HRS as a second US source for older adults. For comparison countries I'd use ELSA (England) and CHARLS (China), with LASI (India) as an optional third. I'm working from memory, so confirm wave and cycle details in each study's documentation before you finalize your design.

## US

**NHANES (CDC/NCHS)**
- **Blood pressure:** Trained examiners take several seated readings in the Mobile Examination Center. Most analysts average the readings after dropping the first.
- **Awareness item:** BPQ020, "Ever told by a doctor or health professional that you had hypertension?"
- **Coverage:** Nationally representative of non-institutionalized US adults of all ages, in two-year cycles from 1999 on.
- **Access:** The public-use files are free. Download them from the NCHS NHANES site with no application or registration. You need the Demographics, Blood Pressure (BPX/BPXO), Blood Pressure Questionnaire (BPQ) and Medication files, merged on SEQN.
- **Restricted data:** Geography and linked mortality or Medicare files go through the NCHS Research Data Center, which means a proposal and a fee. You probably don't need these.
- **Weights:** Use the MEC exam weights, not the interview weights. Divide by the number of cycles when you pool them.

**Health and Retirement Study (HRS, University of Michigan)**
- **Blood pressure:** Interviewers measure it in the physical-measures component. Since 2006 this has covered a rotating half-sample at each wave.
- **Awareness item:** "Has a doctor ever told you that you have high blood pressure or hypertension?" This is asked at every wave.
- **Coverage:** Adults aged 50 and over, with a longitudinal design.
- **Access:** Free registration at hrs.isr.umich.edu, then download. Some sensitive files, such as geographic identifiers, need a separate restricted-data application.
- **Weights:** Use the biomarker or physical-measures weights, not the main respondent weights.

## Other countries

| Survey | Population | BP measured by | Awareness item | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ELSA** (England) | 50+ | Nurse visit, in selected waves only (check which) | Doctor-diagnosed hypertension | Free through the UK Data Service. Register, accept the End User Licence and apply for the nurse-visit dataset. Academic users can log in through their institution. |
| **CHARLS** (China) | 45+ | Interviewer, in 2011 and later waves | Doctor-diagnosed hypertension | Free. Register and apply at charls.pku.edu.cn. |
| **LASI** (India) | 45+ | Interviewer | Diagnosed hypertension | Apply through the IIPS/LASI data portal. Check the current terms. |

The Health Survey for England (all ages, nurse-measured) is an alternative to ELSA if you want younger adults too. Gateway to Global Aging offers harmonized versions of HRS, ELSA, CHARLS and LASI with comparable variable names. That saves a lot of recoding for a cross-country chapter.

## Design points

- **Definition:** Measured hypertension is usually mean SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90, or currently taking antihypertensive medication. Awareness is the share of those people who report a diagnosis. Decide up front whether you use 140/90 or the 2017 ACC/AHA 130/80 threshold, and report both as a sensitivity check.
- **Protocol differences:** Devices, number of readings, rest periods and which readings get averaged differ across surveys. Document this, because it affects comparability.
- **Single-visit bias:** A single-occasion measurement can overstate prevalence, so awareness can look lower than it is.
- **Survey design:** Use survey weights and design variables (strata and PSU) in every analysis.

I can draft the exact variable lists and merge code for NHANES and HRS if that would help.

graders.name: 01-recall-nhanes
graders.evidence:
I'd use NHANES as the core US source, with HRS as a second US option. For comparison countries, I'd use ELSA (England) and CHARLS (China). I'm working from memory here, so confirm wave years and variable names against each survey's current documentation before you commit.

## Awareness definition (all surveys)
- **Hypertension:** mean measured BP at or above your threshold (140/90, or 130/80 under the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline), or currently taking antihypertensive medication.
- **Aware:** among those people, a "yes" to the doctor-told question.
- **Unaware:** the measured-hypertensive people who answer "no".
- **Medication:** keep it in the definition, so treated people with controlled BP count as hypertensive.

## US

**1. NHANES (CDC/NCHS), the best fit**
- **Design:** nationally representative, all ages. You can restrict to adults 40+ or 18+.
- **Blood pressure:** examiners take multiple readings in the Mobile Exam Center. Average readings 2–3 (or all valid ones), and check how each cycle handled the first reading.
- **Awareness question:** BPQ020, "Ever told by a doctor or health professional you had hypertension?" BPQ040A/BPQ050A cover medication.
- **Access:** free and public-use, with no application. Download the Demographics, Blood Pressure (BPX/BPXO), and Blood Pressure & Cholesterol questionnaire (BPQ) files from the NCHS NHANES site and merge on SEQN.
- **Pitfalls:**
  - Use the MEC exam weights, plus the strata and PSU design variables.
  - Pool cycles for precision, and divide weights appropriately.
  - The 2019–2020 cycle was cut short by COVID, so check how NCHS handles it (the pre-pandemic file and the August 2021–August 2023 cycle are separate).
  - Variable names and the BP device changed across cycles (auscultatory to oscillometric), so check the documentation.

**2. HRS (Health and Retirement Study), for adults 50+**
- **Blood pressure:** measured by interviewers during the physical measures. Since 2006 this has covered a rotating half-sample each wave, so you need to pool waves.
- **Awareness question:** the "has a doctor ever told you that you have high blood pressure" item.
- **Access:** free registration at hrs.isr.umich.edu, then download the public files. The RAND HRS longitudinal file is easier to work with than the raw files.
- **Pitfall:** use the biomarker or physical-measures weights, not the main-interview weights.

## International

**3. ELSA (English Longitudinal Study of Ageing), ages 50+**
- **Blood pressure:** a nurse visit measures BP, and it's offered in alternating waves.
- **Awareness question:** doctor-diagnosed hypertension, asked in the main interview.
- **Access:** register with the UK Data Service and accept the End User Licence. It's free for academic use and usually approved quickly. Use the nurse-visit weights.

**4. CHARLS (China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study), ages 45+**
- **Blood pressure:** measured by trained interviewers with an Omron monitor, in the 2011, 2013, 2015 and 2018 waves (check which waves include the physical exam you need).
- **Awareness question:** "Have you been diagnosed with hypertension by a doctor?"
- **Access:** register at charls.pku.edu.cn, agree to the data-use terms, and download. It's free and usually quick.
- **Pitfall:** use the biomarker weights.

## Alternatives
- **LASI (India, 45+):** a good fit with measured BP and a diagnosis question, but access runs through an application to IIPS or the data distributor.
- **Other options:** MHAS (Mexico), TILDA (Ireland), Health Survey for England (all ages, nurse-measured), and KNHANES (Korea). Check each for BP measurement and the diagnosis question.
- **Not suitable:** SHARE doesn't measure BP, so skip it despite the name recognition.

## Cross-country comparability
The Gateway to Global Aging Data (g2aging.org) provides harmonized files for HRS, ELSA, CHARLS and others. It can save recoding time, but check whether the harmonized files include the measured BP variables, because some only carry the self-reported items. Also note that the surveys differ in BP device, number of readings, and age range, so say so in your limitations section.

If you tell me your age range and which hypertension threshold you're using, I can draft the variable list and merge steps for NHANES and HRS.
