graders.name: 01-recall-nhanes
graders.evidence:
# Recommended surveys

I haven't checked the live access pages, so confirm wave numbers and procedures on each site before you plan around them.

## 1. US: NHANES (core dataset)
- **Why:** It is the standard source for US hypertension awareness. Trained examiners take several BP readings in the Mobile Examination Center. The questionnaire asks whether a doctor or other health professional ever told the participant they had hypertension (the BPQ file).
- **Coverage:** The sample is nationally representative of all US adults. Continuous NHANES runs from 1999 in 2-year cycles, with a pre-pandemic 2017–March 2020 file and a later 2021–2023 cycle.
- **Caveat:** The BP measurement method changed in recent cycles, from mercury sphygmomanometer to an oscillometric device. Check the documentation before pooling across years.
- **Access:** It's free and needs no application or registration. Download the XPT files from the CDC/NCHS NHANES website. You need the demographics, blood pressure, BP questionnaire and medication files, merged on `SEQN`. Use the MEC exam weights. Linked mortality files and exact geography are restricted and go through the NCHS Research Data Center, which needs a proposal. You won't need those for awareness.

## 2. US, older adults: Health and Retirement Study (HRS)
- **Why:** It covers adults 50 and over. Interviewers take BP in the physical-measures component, and respondents also report whether a doctor ever told them they had high blood pressure. It is longitudinal, so you can study awareness over time.
- **Caveat:** Physical measures cover only a rotating half-sample each wave, from 2006 onward.
- **Access:** It's free. Register on the HRS website (Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan), accept the terms of use, and download the public files. The RAND HRS longitudinal file is a convenient starting point. Sensitive and geographic data need a separate restricted-data application.

## 3. England: English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA)
- **Why:** It follows adults 50 and over. A nurse visit in alternating waves measures BP, and the main interview asks about doctor-diagnosed hypertension. It is designed to be comparable with HRS.
- **Caveat:** Nurse visits happen only in some waves, so use the nurse-visit datasets and merge them with the main-wave files.
- **Access:** Register with the UK Data Service, accept the End User Licence, and download. This is free for academic users, and you usually get access immediately with institutional login or registration. The Health Survey for England, also on the UK Data Service, is an option if you want all adults rather than just 50 and over.

## 4. China: CHARLS
- **Why:** It is nationally representative of Chinese adults 45 and over. Interviewers measure BP, and respondents are asked whether they have been diagnosed with hypertension. It is a useful contrast with the two high-income settings.
- **Access:** Register on the CHARLS website (Peking University's National School of Development) and agree to the data-use terms. Approval is usually quick for students, and the download is free. Harmonized versions are also available.

## Optional fifth: LASI (India)
It has measured BP and a diagnosis question for adults 45 and over. Access runs through the survey's host institute (IIPS) and its data-request process, which is slower and less certain than the others. Check its current data-access page before committing.

## Harmonization shortcut
The **Gateway to Global Aging Data** (USC) provides harmonized variables across HRS, ELSA, CHARLS, LASI, SHARE and others. It is free with registration. It can save you a lot of recoding, but check which BP variables it includes for each study.

## Analysis points that matter for the thesis
- **Hypertension:** Define it the same way in every survey. The usual definition is mean SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 mmHg, or current use of antihypertensive medication. The stricter 130/80 threshold is also common, so state your choice.
- **Awareness:** Among measured hypertensives, awareness is a "yes" to the doctor-told question. Many studies also count those on treatment as aware. Decide this and report it.
- **Readings:** Specify how you average readings. NHANES discards the first reading in some conventions, and the other surveys take fewer readings.
- **Weights and design:** Use the survey weights, strata and PSUs. Nonresponse to the BP exam is non-trivial, so use the exam weights and not the interview weights.
- **Comparability:** Differences in device, number of readings, age range and wording of the diagnosis question will affect cross-country comparisons. Restrict to ages 50 and over for a like-for-like comparison.

I need data from at least a few thousand adults who wore the device on the wrist for several days to a week or longer, linked to follow-up outcomes such as hospital records, diagnoses or death registrations. Wrist placement matters to me because I want my results to be comparable with other wrist-based studies. I'm at a US university and happy to go through applications. Which datasets should I consider, and what does getting access involve for each?

- **R1 (must):** Wrist-worn accelerometer or tracker worn in daily life for at least several days.
- **R2 (must):** A few thousand adults or more.

- **R4 (must):** Obtainable by a US university through an application.

**What I could and couldn't check (12 Nov 2026).**
- I ran searches on Zenodo, OpenAIRE, PhysioNet and Hugging Face, plus a literature search.
- Registries were mostly noise for this topic, so the useful candidates came from my own recall and the papers.
- The UK Biobank, UCL and China Kadoorie sites blocked automated access. The sleep-research site (sleepdata.org) failed on an SSL error in this sandbox.
- **What I did confirm today:** the NHANES, NCHS, All of Us and PhysioNet pages.
- **Everything else is from memory.** It is labelled that way below, and you should confirm it on the owner's page.

## Shortlist

| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | UK Biobank accelerometer substudy | Application, institutional agreement, fee; about weeks | Data access agreement | about 90–100k | Strong | Papers confirmed today; access from memory |
| 2 | NHANES 2011–14 wrist data + NCHS linked mortality | Public download, minutes | US public data | about 7–8k adults | Strong for death; hospital outcomes need a restricted application | Mortality page confirmed today; wrist details from memory |
| 3 | All of Us (Fitbit) | Institutional agreement, training, registration; about weeks | Program terms | tens of thousands (memory) | Partial: consumer device | Access page confirmed today |
| 4 | NSRR: MrOS Sleep, SOF, MESA Sleep | Free account + data use agreement; about days | Per study | about 2–3k each | Strong, but older adults only | From memory |
| 5 | PhysioNet minute-level NHANES | Open, minutes | CC0-1.0 | not checked | Partial: no outcomes | Registry record confirmed today |
| 6 | Whitehall II | Data-sharing request to UCL; months | Unknown | about 4k (memory) | Partial | From memory |
| 7 | China Kadoorie Biobank | Application; months | Unknown | about 25k wearers (memory) | Unknown | From memory |

## Details

**1. UK Biobank**
- **Contents (from memory):** A dominant-wrist Axivity AX3 worn for 7 days in 2013–15. It is linked to hospital inpatient, death and cancer registries, with raw files available.
- **Why it fits:** It is the cohort most wrist-based papers compare against. A 2026 paper in PLOS Medicine used wrist data from 95,559 participants to study incident disease (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213).
- **Access (from memory):**
  1. Register on the UK Biobank Access Management System.
  2. Submit a project application.
  3. Have your institution sign the Material Transfer Agreement and pay the access fee. Check the current tariff.
  4. Analyse on the cloud Research Analysis Platform, because data isn't downloaded.
- **Caveats:** The cohort is healthy-volunteer, UK-based and mostly white. Follow-up from the wear date is about 8–10 years.

**2. NHANES 2011–14 plus linked mortality**
- **Contents:** From memory, an ActiGraph GT3X+ on the non-dominant wrist, worn 24 hours a day for 7 days.
- **Access:** The NHANES site loaded today, and I believe the files need no account. The NCHS page confirms public-use linked mortality files: "The linked public-use files contain a limited set of mortality (death) data for adults."
- **Restricted option:** "Restricted-use LMFs can be accessed only through the NCHS Research Data Center (RDC) network for approved projects." You'd need that route for anything beyond death.
- **Caveats:** Public mortality data is deaths only, and some fields are altered for privacy. Follow-up is about 5–8 years.
- **Start here today:** This is the one you can begin on before any application clears. A paper using NHANES wrist data and mortality is https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-36062-y.

**3. All of Us**
- **Access page, confirmed today:** The Registered Tier "includes data from electronic health records (EHRs), wearables, surveys, and physical measurements." You need a "data passport" and work in the Researcher Workbench.
- **Institutional agreement and training:** These are from memory.
- **Caveats:** Fitbit output is vendor-derived minute-level steps, heart rate and sleep summaries, not raw acceleration. It won't compare directly with research-grade wrist studies. Death data are patchy, from memory.
- **Literature:** The search returned a 2025 paper titled "Fitbit Physical Activity and Sleep Data in the All of Us Research Program: Data Exploration and Processing Considerations". I didn't capture its DOI.

**4. NSRR (MrOS Sleep, SOF, MESA Sleep)**
- **Contents (all from memory):** Wrist actigraphy for roughly 5–7 nights, in older adults, with mortality and cardiovascular events. Each cohort has a few thousand people.
- **Access (from memory):** A free account on sleepdata.org, then a data use agreement per dataset, with approval in days.
- **To check:** How many outcomes are in the NSRR release versus held by each parent cohort's coordinating centre.
- **Caveats:** Data are epoch-level actigraphy, not raw. The devices differ from the UK Biobank and NHANES ones.
- **Literature:** An MrOS Sleep paper is https://doi.org/10.5665/sleep.3562.

**5. PhysioNet minute-level NHANES**
- It is open under CC0-1.0, confirmed by the registry (https://physionet.org/content/minute-level-step-count-nhanes/1.0.2/).
- It has no outcomes, so you'd merge the NCHS mortality files yourself.
- It's useful for method development.

## Known, not confirmed

- **Whitehall II:** I recall GENEActiv wrist data in about 4,000 people, with hospital and mortality linkage, and access by a data-sharing request. A 2026 JAMA Neurology paper used it as a validation cohort (https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.1232). The UCL page blocked me, so confirm access terms and sample size with the study team.
- **China Kadoorie Biobank:** I recall a wrist-accelerometer subsample of about 25,000 people with death and disease registry linkage. The site returned a 403 error, and I'm not sure the accelerometer data are released. Check ckbiobank.org/data-access.

## Not recommended, and why

- **NHANES 2003–06 accelerometer:** From memory, this was hip-worn, so it fails the wrist requirement.
- **Zenodo and Hugging Face hits:** Small or non-cohort files with no linked disease outcomes. An example is the Vanuatu GENEActiv files.

## What I could not find

- I could not confirm the UK Biobank fee, current process or timeline today.
- I could not confirm the NSRR or Whitehall II outcome coverage.
- I didn't search other possible cohorts such as the Rotterdam Study, Our Future Health or Generation Scotland.

## Next step

1. Download NHANES wrist data and the public mortality files this week to prototype your analysis.
2. Start the UK Biobank application in parallel, since it is the main dataset.
3. Request the NSRR datasets for older-adult validation.
4. Ask your institution early whether a human-subjects exemption determination is needed.
5. If you use a hosted AI service on restricted data, check each agreement first. Many forbid sharing data with third parties.

graders.name: 01-recall-ukbiobank-accelerometer
graders.evidence:
## What I assumed you need

- **R1 (must):** a wrist-worn device worn for several days to a week or more.
- **R2 (must):** at least a few thousand adults.
- **R3 (must):** linked follow-up outcomes (hospital records, diagnoses or death registration).
- **R4 (must):** wrist placement, so results are comparable with other wrist-based studies.
- **Constraint:** you can wait for an application, and you are at a US university.

I checked on 12 November 2026. The registries I could search (Zenodo, DataCite, OpenAIRE, Hugging Face, PhysioNet) only returned paper supplements and code. The real cohorts came from web search and the literature. Several key sites blocked my tools (UK Biobank, China Kadoorie Biobank, the sleep-data site NSRR, MrOS Online), so some access details below are marked as unconfirmed.

## Shortlist

| # | Dataset | Access | Licence / terms | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–14 with NCHS linked mortality | Open download | Public-use; no registration mentioned | Several thousand adults (exact N not confirmed) | Strong on R1, R4. Death only, no hospital records. | Today |
| 2 | All of Us (Fitbit plus health records) | Institutional agreement plus researcher registration, about weeks | All of Us data use agreement; analysis only in their cloud workbench | About 59,000 with Fitbit data; about 22,000 with health records and 6+ months of data | Partial: a consumer tracker, not a research-grade accelerometer | Today |
| 3 | UK Biobank (Axivity AX3 wrist) | Application and fee, **applications reported paused** | Material transfer agreement; analysis on their platform | About 100,000 | Strongest scientific fit, but not available now | Partly (search results only) |
| 4 | MrOS Sleep Study (older US men) and SOF (older US women) | Request via MrOS Online / SOF Online, about weeks | Not confirmed | About 3,000 each | Partial: 3–5 days of wear, older adults, single sex | Partly |
| 5 | MESA Sleep (NSRR) | NSRR account plus data access request, about weeks | NSRR data use agreement | 2,156 | Partial: under "a few thousand", outcome availability unconfirmed | Partly |
| 6 | China Kadoorie Biobank | Registration plus application, about months | Agreement with Oxford; £2,500 per approved request outside China | About 20,000 | Partial: release to overseas researchers not confirmed | Partly |

## Details

**1. NHANES 2011–14 (start here).**
- **Device:** an ActiGraph GT3X+ on the non-dominant wrist for 7 days. Documentation is at [CDC PAXHD_G](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2011/DataFiles/PAXHD_G.htm).
- **Outcomes:** deaths come from the [NCHS public-use linked mortality files](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm). The CDC page confirms a CDC FTP download and no registration.
- **Follow-up end date:** the page says the files were updated through 31 December 2022, but it doesn't give the end date for the public-use version. One paper cites follow-up through 2019, so check this.
- **Limit:** no hospital or diagnosis outcomes. Restricted files, which include more detail, need an application to the NCHS Research Data Center.
- **Steps:** download the accelerometer files and the mortality file, merge them, and apply the survey weights.
- **Used in:** [NHANES 2011–2014: Objective Physical Activity is the Strongest Predictor of All-Cause Mortality](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/). One analysis used 3,032 adults aged 50 or older.

**2. All of Us.**
- **Data:** participants' own Fitbit data linked to health records, so you can study incident diagnoses.
- **Access:** per the [Researcher Workbench page](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/workbench/), your institution must have signed a Data Use and Registration Agreement. You then register, verify your identity, complete Responsible Conduct of Research training and sign a code of conduct. Access to the workbench is free, with a $300 starting credit.
- **Comparability:** consumer-device metrics are not directly comparable with accelerometer outputs, so weigh this against your goal of matching other wrist-based studies. Users are also a self-selected group.
- **Used in:** [step counts and chronic disease](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9671804/).

**3. UK Biobank.**
- **Data:** about 100,000 people wore an Axivity AX3 on the wrist for 7 days, with linked hospital, cancer and death records ([documentation](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/ukb/ukb/docs/PhysicalActivityMonitor.pdf)). Most of the published literature on your question uses it, for example [this PLOS Medicine study](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213).
- **Pause:** search results say UK Biobank paused new applications after an April 2026 incident involving exported data. They give a plan to reopen in late 2026 and say the next data release is expected in the first half of 2027. UK Biobank's own pages returned HTTP 403 to my tools, so I could not confirm this. Check the application page before planning around it.
- **Fees (from search results, unconfirmed):** Tier 1 is £3,000 for 3 years plus VAT, with a £500 student rate. Platform compute costs extra. The historical average was about 15 weeks from application to data.

**4. MrOS Sleep and SOF.**
- **Device:** a SleepWatch-O on the non-dominant wrist for 3–5 days. MrOS has about 3,000 men and SOF about 3,000 women.
- **Outcomes:** mortality is well studied, for example [rest/activity rhythms and mortality](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20370475).
- **Access:** the NSRR copy of MrOS has no actigraphy. Papers point to MrOS Online (mrosonline.ucsf.edu) and SOF Online (sofonline.ucsf.edu), which I could not read. The request process is unconfirmed.

**5. MESA Sleep.**
- **Device:** an Actiwatch Spectrum on the wrist for 7 days, per the [documentation](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/mesa/files/m/browser/documentation/MESA_Sleep_Data_Documentation_Guide.pdf).
- **Outcomes:** I could not confirm whether NSRR hosts the event and mortality data. They may need a proposal to the MESA Coordinating Center.
- **Used in:** [sleep and cardiovascular disease in MESA](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/JAHA.122.025252).

**6. China Kadoorie Biobank.**
- **Data:** the [published description](https://ijbnpa.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8) covers 20,370 participants with 7-day wrist data.
- **Access (from search results):** register on their data access system and apply. Students apply with a supervisor. Outside China the fee is £2,500 per approved request.
- **Release:** the data may go first to collaborators in China and the UK. Follow-up for this resurvey is also short.

## Known, not confirmed

- **Whitehall II** (GENEActiv wrist, 9 days, 2012/13) and the **Rotterdam Study** (GENEActiv wrist, 7 days) both exist. Access is by request to the study teams, who are listed in the papers. I did not confirm their sample sizes or outcome linkage.
- **UK Biobank's pause** is from search results only.

## Not recommended, and why

- **Zenodo and Figshare hits** such as the NHANES sleep–mortality supplements are code and tables from papers, not cohort data.
- **Hip-worn cohorts** (NHANES 2003–06, WHI OPACH, Women's Health Study) fail the wrist requirement. This is from memory.

## What I could not find

- Confirmed access pages for UK Biobank, CKB, NSRR and MrOS Online.
- Whether MESA event and mortality data sit on NSRR.
- A confirmed end date for the public-use NHANES mortality follow-up.

## Next step

Start on NHANES today, since it needs no application. In parallel:
1. Ask your institution whether it already has an All of Us agreement.
2. Check the UK Biobank application page for reopening.
3. Email the MrOS and MESA teams to confirm outcome data.

Your institution may also want to confirm that the work counts as exempt from ethics review.

The interactive shortlist is at `/private/tmp/e-M9qMzZ/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

- **Constraint:** you can wait for an application, and you are at a US university.

I checked on 12 November 2026. The registries I could search (Zenodo, DataCite, OpenAIRE, Hugging Face, PhysioNet) only returned paper supplements and code. The real cohorts came from web search and the literature. Several key sites blocked my tools (UK Biobank, China Kadoorie Biobank, the sleep-data site NSRR, MrOS Online), so some access details below are marked as unconfirmed.

## Shortlist

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–14 with NCHS linked mortality | Open download | Public-use; no registration mentioned | Several thousand adults (exact N not confirmed) | Strong on R1, R4. Death only, no hospital records. | Today |
| 2 | All of Us (Fitbit plus health records) | Institutional agreement plus researcher registration, about weeks | All of Us data use agreement; analysis only in their cloud workbench | About 59,000 with Fitbit data; about 22,000 with health records and 6+ months of data | Partial: a consumer tracker, not a research-grade accelerometer | Today |
| 3 | UK Biobank (Axivity AX3 wrist) | Application and fee, **applications reported paused** | Material transfer agreement; analysis on their platform | About 100,000 | Strongest scientific fit, but not available now | Partly (search results only) |
| 4 | MrOS Sleep Study (older US men) and SOF (older US women) | Request via MrOS Online / SOF Online, about weeks | Not confirmed | About 3,000 each | Partial: 3–5 days of wear, older adults, single sex | Partly |
| 5 | MESA Sleep (NSRR) | NSRR account plus data access request, about weeks | NSRR data use agreement | 2,156 | Partial: under "a few thousand", outcome availability unconfirmed | Partly |
| 6 | China Kadoorie Biobank | Registration plus application, about months | Agreement with Oxford; £2,500 per approved request outside China | About 20,000 | Partial: release to overseas researchers not confirmed | Partly |

- **Outcomes:** deaths come from the [NCHS public-use linked mortality files](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm). The CDC page confirms a CDC FTP download and no registration.
- **Follow-up end date:** the page says the files were updated through 31 December 2022, but it doesn't give the end date for the public-use version. One paper cites follow-up through 2019, so check this.
- **Limit:** no hospital or diagnosis outcomes. Restricted files, which include more detail, need an application to the NCHS Research Data Center.
- **Steps:** download the accelerometer files and the mortality file, merge them, and apply the survey weights.
- **Used in:** [NHANES 2011–2014: Objective Physical Activity is the Strongest Predictor of All-Cause Mortality](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/). One analysis used 3,032 adults aged 50 or older.

- **Access:** the NSRR copy of MrOS has no actigraphy. Papers point to MrOS Online (mrosonline.ucsf.edu) and SOF Online (sofonline.ucsf.edu), which I could not read. The request process is unconfirmed.

**5. MESA Sleep.**
- **Device:** an Actiwatch Spectrum on the wrist for 7 days, per the [documentation](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/mesa/files/m/browser/documentation/MESA_Sleep_Data_Documentation_Guide.pdf).
- **Outcomes:** I could not confirm whether NSRR hosts the event and mortality data. They may need a proposal to the MESA Coordinating Center.
- **Used in:** [sleep and cardiovascular disease in MESA](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/JAHA.122.025252).

**6. China Kadoorie Biobank.**
- **Data:** the [published description](https://ijbnpa.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8) covers 20,370 participants with 7-day wrist data.
- **Access (from search results):** register on their data access system and apply. Students apply with a supervisor. Outside China the fee is £2,500 per approved request.
- **Release:** the data may go first to collaborators in China and the UK. Follow-up for this resurvey is also short.

## Known, not confirmed

- **Whitehall II** (GENEActiv wrist, 9 days, 2012/13) and the **Rotterdam Study** (GENEActiv wrist, 7 days) both exist. Access is by request to the study teams, who are listed in the papers. I did not confirm their sample sizes or outcome linkage.
- **UK Biobank's pause** is from search results only.

## Not recommended, and why

- **Zenodo and Figshare hits** such as the NHANES sleep–mortality supplements are code and tables from papers, not cohort data.
- **Hip-worn cohorts** (NHANES 2003–06, WHI OPACH, Women's Health Study) fail the wrist requirement. This is from memory.

## What I could not find

- Confirmed access pages for UK Biobank, CKB, NSRR and MrOS Online.
- Whether MESA event and mortality data sit on NSRR.
- A confirmed end date for the public-use NHANES mortality follow-up.

1. Ask your institution whether it already has an All of Us agreement.
2. Check the UK Biobank application page for reopening.
3. Email the MrOS and MESA teams to confirm outcome data.

The interactive shortlist is at `/private/tmp/e-M9qMzZ/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

graders.name: 01-recall-ukbiobank-accelerometer
graders.evidence:
Several good wrist-worn datasets with linked outcomes exist. One of them (NHANES 2011–2014) you can start on today. I didn't build the interactive shortlist page. The verification step was partial, because the UK Biobank, China Kadoorie Biobank (CKB) and NSRR pages refused my automated fetch (403 or certificate errors). I used web-search summaries for those instead. All checks were done 2026-11-12.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a wrist-worn device, free-living wear of at least about 5–7 days, at least a few thousand adults, and linked outcomes (death, and ideally hospital or diagnosis records).
- **Access:** application-based is fine, you're at a US university, and I assumed no commercial use.
- **Not required:** a particular device brand. The comparability question is wrist versus hip or thigh, so I note which wrist and which device each study used.

## Shortlist

| # | Dataset | Wrist device | N (accelerometer) | Outcomes | Access | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–2014 | ActiGraph GT3X+, non-dominant wrist, up to 9 days | roughly 12,000 examined, fewer with valid wear | Mortality through the public-use linked files | Open download; restricted-use route via NCHS Research Data Center (RDC) | Today (search summaries of CDC pages) |
| 2 | UK Biobank | Axivity AX3, dominant wrist, 7 days, 100 Hz | about 103,700 | Hospital records, cancer and death registries | Application, fee, cloud platform; about 15 weeks | Today (search summaries) |
| 3 | Whitehall II | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, 9 days | 3,991 (ages 60–83) | Mortality via the UK Office for National Statistics register | Gated data-sharing request to UCL | Today (search summaries) |
| 4 | SOF and MrOS (via NSRR or the cohorts' own sites) | Wrist actigraphy, 1-minute epochs | MrOS about 2,800; SOF about 3,000 | Mortality; SOF also lists incident breast cancer and stroke | Controlled access request | Partly today |
| 5 | All of Us (Fitbit) | Consumer Fitbit, long-term | more than 59,000 | Linked electronic health records | Free; institution signs an agreement first | Today (search summaries) |
| 6 | China Kadoorie Biobank | Axivity AX3, 7 days | about 21,000–22,500 | Death and disease registries | Not confirmed as released yet | Today, status unclear |

## Details

**1. NHANES 2011–2014 (start here).**
- **Contents:**
  - The ActiGraph GT3X+ was worn on the [non-dominant wrist](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/) and recorded at 80 Hz. The CDC publishes minute-level files ([PAXMIN_G, 2011–12](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Nhanes/2011-2012/PAXMIN_G.htm), plus PAXMIN_H for 2013–14) and raw data. [Data-quality flags are here](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/Pam/Default.aspx).
  - A [2024 paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/) used 3,653 adults aged 50–80, with 416 deaths over about 24,000 person-years.
- **Outcome limits:** the [public linked mortality files](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm) give vital status and follow-up time. For certain records, follow-up time and cause of death were replaced with synthetic values. Incident disease and hospital records are not in the public files.
- **Access:**
  1. Download the accelerometer files from the CDC.
  2. Download the mortality files from the CDC FTP site.
  3. Merge on the participant ID (SEQN).
  4. For real cause of death, apply to the NCHS RDC. The restricted and public mortality files can't be combined there.
- **Time:** minutes for the open route.
- **Sample size:** the wear-time and covariate criteria cut the sample hard. Expect a few thousand usable adults at most.

**2. UK Biobank.**
- **Contents:**
  - It's the largest wrist-accelerometer cohort. [About 103,700 participants](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/ukb/docs/acc_plos_0169649.pdf) wore the AX3 for 7 days in 2013–15.
  - Hospital, cancer and death outcomes are, from memory, linked through national registries (the 2026 papers returned by the literature search used incident disease and dementia). I did not confirm the linkage details today.
  - Example uses: [sleep stages and incident disease](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213) and [circadian rhythms and dementia](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13195-026-02088-3).
- **Access:**
  1. Register (free); review is aimed within [10 working days](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/).
  2. Submit an application. UK Biobank is open to bona fide health researchers in the public interest.
  3. After approval you have 90 days to pay the fee and sign the material transfer agreement.
  4. Analyse on the UKB Research Analysis Platform. Access is cloud-only, and data can't be redistributed.
- **Time and cost:** about 15 weeks from submission to release on average. Tier 1 is £3,000 and Tier 3 is £9,000 per three years, excluding VAT; students may pay £500. Platform compute costs are extra, and each account starts with £40 of credit.
- **Caveat:** UK Biobank's own [access page](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/enable-your-research/apply-for-access) refused my fetch. The fee and timing figures come from a search summary, so confirm them there.

**3. Whitehall II.**
- **Contents:** 3,991 civil servants aged 60–83 wore the GENEActiv for nine days in 2012–13. Deaths come from the ONS register ([paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11216065/)).
- **Access:** [gated MRC-style data sharing](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/psychiatry/research/mental-health-older-people/whitehall-ii/data-sharing). Send a proposal through the UCL portal. I didn't read the portal, so I don't know the timeline or whether a US institution needs a formal agreement.
- **Use:** the same [paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-30237-5) compares Whitehall II with UK Biobank, which is useful for replication.

**4. SOF and MrOS.**
- **Contents:** both cohorts have wrist actigraphy with mortality follow-up, per [this paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13698916) (MrOS n = 2,844; SOF n = 2,967). Participants are older adults only, and SOF is women only (MrOS is men only).
- **Access:** NSRR needs an account plus an approved request and a data use agreement for each dataset. The current [NSRR MrOS page](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/mros) reportedly lists no actigraphy, so the actigraphy may sit on MrOS Online and SOF Online instead. I couldn't open either page. Check which site holds the actigraphy before you plan around it.
- **Time:** weeks (my estimate, not confirmed).

**5. All of Us.**
- **Contents:**
  - Fitbit data from more than 59,000 participants are in the [Registered Tier](https://researchallofus.org/frequently-asked-questions/). Participants wear their own consumer devices, so wear length, device model and selection differ from a research accelerometer. They are not directly comparable with ActiGraph or Axivity output.
  - Outcomes come from linked electronic health records, not registries.
- **Access:**
  1. Your institution's signing official signs the Data Use and Registration Agreement.
  2. You register, verify your identity, and complete the Responsible Conduct of Research training and the code of conduct.
  3. Describe your project.
- **Cost and time:** the workbench is free ($300 starting credits). Time to access is days to weeks (my estimate).
- **Restriction:** participant-level data can't be linked to other sources without explicit permission from the program.

## Known, not confirmed
- **China Kadoorie Biobank:** 21,400–22,500 participants wore the Axivity AX3 on the wrist for 7 days ([paper](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8)). CKB said it would release the data through its access system after processing and a period of exclusive use by CKB researchers. I found no confirmation that it's released. [CKB's data access page](https://www.ckbiobank.org/data-access/data-2) refused my fetch. Ask CKB directly.
- **From memory, not checked today:** these may have wrist actigraphy with event follow-up, but I didn't verify them.
  - MESA Sleep Ancillary (about 2,000; Actiwatch Spectrum; on NSRR).
  - Rotterdam Study.
  - Rush Memory and Aging Project.
  - Some ARIC visits (I'm unsure whether ARIC used wrist or hip placement).
  - Women's Health Study (I believe it used hip placement).

## Not recommended
- **NHANES 2003–2006:** it has accelerometer data, but the device was worn on the hip. That conflicts with your comparability requirement.
- **Registry search hits** (HAR benchmarks, Parkinson's and sleep-lab sets, PhysioNet small datasets): they have no disease or death follow-up.
- **PhysioNet's [minute-level NHANES step-count set](https://physionet.org/content/minute-level-step-count-nhanes/1.0.2/):** it's a convenient derived copy. Use the CDC files as your primary source.

## What I could not find
- I couldn't confirm Whitehall II's timeline or US eligibility, UK Biobank's current fees from its own site, or NSRR's actigraphy holdings.
- I didn't search outside the US and UK systematically (for example Nordic or Japanese cohorts). The list may be incomplete.

## Next step
1. Start on NHANES 2011–2014 now to build your pipeline, since it needs no application.
2. Apply to UK Biobank in parallel for statistical power and hospital outcomes. Ask your institution's research office about the fee and agreement.
3. Request Whitehall II and the SOF/MrOS actigraphy for replication.
4. Check with your institutional review board early. These datasets are de-identified, but you should confirm the exemption.

I didn't write `dataset-shortlist.html`. Say so if you want it built.

| 6 | China Kadoorie Biobank | Axivity AX3, 7 days | about 21,000–22,500 | Death and disease registries | Not confirmed as released yet | Today, status unclear |

- **Contents:**

  2. Download the mortality files from the CDC FTP site.
  3. Merge on the participant ID (SEQN).

- **Time:** weeks (my estimate, not confirmed).

**5. All of Us.**
- **Contents:**
  - Fitbit data from more than 59,000 participants are in the [Registered Tier](https://researchallofus.org/frequently-asked-questions/).   1. Your institution's signing official signs the Data Use and Registration Agreement.
  2. You register, verify your identity, and complete the Responsible Conduct of Research training and the code of conduct.
  3. Describe your project.

- **Restriction:** participant-level data can't be linked to other sources without explicit permission from the program.

- **China Kadoorie Biobank:** 21,400–22,500 participants wore the Axivity AX3 on the wrist for 7 days ([paper](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8)). CKB said it would release the data through its access system after processing and a period of exclusive use by CKB researchers. I found no confirmation that it's released. [CKB's data access page](https://www.ckbiobank.org/data-access/data-2) refused my fetch. Ask CKB directly.
- **From memory, not checked today:** these may have wrist actigraphy with event follow-up, but I didn't verify them.
  - MESA Sleep Ancillary (about 2,000; Actiwatch Spectrum; on NSRR).
  - Rotterdam Study.
  - Rush Memory and Aging Project.
  - Some ARIC visits (I'm unsure whether ARIC used wrist or hip placement).
  - Women's Health Study (I believe it used hip placement).

## Not recommended
- **NHANES 2003–2006:** it has accelerometer data, but the device was worn on the hip. That conflicts with your comparability requirement.

## What I could not find
- I couldn't confirm Whitehall II's timeline or US eligibility, UK Biobank's current fees from its own site, or NSRR's actigraphy holdings.

1. Start on NHANES 2011–2014 now to build your pipeline, since it needs no application.
2. Apply to UK Biobank in parallel for statistical power and hospital outcomes. Ask your institution's research office about the fee and agreement.
3. Request Whitehall II and the SOF/MrOS actigraphy for replication.
4. Check with your institutional review board early. These datasets are de-identified, but you should confirm the exemption.

- **From memory, not checked today:** these may have wrist actigraphy with event follow-up, but I didn't verify them.
  - MESA Sleep Ancillary (about 2,000; Actiwatch Spectrum; on NSRR).
  - Rotterdam Study.
  - Rush Memory and Aging Project.
  - Some ARIC visits (I'm unsure whether ARIC used wrist or hip placement).
  - Women's Health Study (I believe it used hip placement).

- **Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF):** About 3,000 older women, with mortality follow-up.
- **MESA Sleep:** About 2,000 adults with a 7-day Actiwatch, plus cardiovascular event and mortality follow-up.

**All of Us Research Program**
- **Device:** Fitbit wrist trackers, with data from tens of thousands of participants who linked their accounts. The data are consumer-grade and not raw acceleration, so they're less comparable with research-grade wrist accelerometers.
- **Outcomes:** EHR-derived diagnoses and encounters. Death data are more limited.
- **Access:** Free. Your institution signs a data use agreement, and you complete researcher registration, identity verification and ethics training. You work in the cloud Researcher Workbench.

## Worth checking

- **China Kadoorie Biobank:** I believe a resurvey subset wore wrist Axivity devices, with health-insurance and death-registry linkage. Access is by application, but confirm the sample size and international access terms.
- **Our Future Health (UK):** It may be adding wearable data. Check its status.

- If wrist comparability is the priority, start with **UK Biobank**. It has the best combination of size, wrist-worn research-grade devices, and hospital and death linkage.

- Account for device differences (Axivity vs. ActiGraph vs. Actiwatch). Metrics such as ENMO, MIMS and activity counts aren't directly interchangeable, so plan harmonization early.

Here are the datasets that fit your criteria, in the order I'd consider them. This is from memory without live checks, so confirm fees, sample sizes and follow-up dates on each program's site before you plan around them.

## Best fits

| Dataset | Wrist device and protocol | Approx. N | Outcomes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UK Biobank** | Axivity AX3, 7 days, 24 h/day, 2013–15 | ~100,000 | Hospital records (HES), death and cancer registries, partial primary care |
| **NHANES 2011–2014** | ActiGraph GT3X+, 7 days, with raw data released | ~7–8k adults with valid wear | Mortality only through the public-use linked file (to end of 2019) |
| **All of Us** | Participants' own Fitbits, often months to years of data | Tens of thousands | EHR diagnoses. Mortality is incomplete. |
| **MESA Sleep, MrOS Sleep, SOF** | Wrist actigraphy (Actiwatch or SleepWatch), 5–7 days | ~2,000, ~2,900 (older men), ~3,000 (older women) | Adjudicated CVD events and mortality, with long follow-up |

Other cohorts with wrist accelerometry include China Kadoorie Biobank, Whitehall II, and the Rotterdam Study. They are usually collaboration-based and harder for outside groups to get into, so I'd treat them as second-tier unless you already have a contact.

## What access involves

**UK Biobank**
- Your institution registers, and you submit an application through the UKB Access Management System. It asks for a scientific rationale and the data fields you need, including the accelerometer fields.
- Approval typically takes weeks. There is a tiered access fee, in the low thousands to about £9k plus VAT. Check the current schedule, since US universities are eligible but lower tiers may not apply to you.
- Data are accessed only inside the UKB Research Analysis Platform (DNAnexus), where you pay for compute and storage. Raw `.cwa` files are very large. Most people use the derived summary fields or the open-source `biobankAccelerometerAnalysis` pipeline.

**NHANES**
- The public-use accelerometer data and the NCHS linked mortality files are free downloads with no application.
- Restricted-use linkages, such as Medicare claims for hospitalizations, require a proposal to the NCHS Research Data Center. It is slower, and you work in a secure environment.
- This is the most directly comparable US population sample, but it only gives you mortality unless you go through the RDC.

**All of Us**
- You register your institution, sign a data use agreement, complete the program's training, and verify your identity. Access is free through the cloud-based Researcher Workbench.
- Fitbit data are in the Registered Tier. Check whether your analysis needs Controlled Tier data.
- Fitbit data are consumer-grade and not comparable to Axivity or ActiGraph counts. Coverage of outcomes depends on EHR linkage, so deaths and events outside the health system can be missed.

**NSRR (MESA, MrOS, SOF sleep data)**
- Create an account on sleepdata.org and sign a data use agreement. Actigraphy and many covariates are available quickly.
- Linked events and mortality sometimes sit outside NSRR. You may also need BioLINCC, or an ancillary-study proposal to the MESA or MrOS coordinating center.
- These cohorts are small by "a few thousand" standards. They are best as replication cohorts or for sleep-specific questions.

## Things that affect comparability
- **Devices differ.** Axivity gives ENMO-type metrics, ActiGraph gives counts or MIMS, and Actiwatch gives its own counts. Plan to harmonize, or to analyze each cohort separately and meta-analyze.
- **UK Biobank is not representative.** It is mostly white, healthier than average, and 40–69 years old at baseline. Pairing it with NHANES gives you a more representative US check.
- **Reverse causation.** Standard practice is to exclude the first 1–2 years of follow-up and adjust for baseline illness.

My suggestion is UK Biobank as the discovery dataset, NHANES for a US mortality replication, and MESA or MrOS for sleep-focused work in older adults. I can draft a UKB application rationale or a field list for any of these if that would help.

| **UK Biobank** | Axivity AX3, 7 days, 24 h/day, 2013–15 | ~100,000 | Hospital records (HES), death and cancer registries, partial primary care |
| **NHANES 2011–2014** | ActiGraph GT3X+, 7 days, with raw data released | ~7–8k adults with valid wear | Mortality only through the public-use linked file (to end of 2019) |
| **All of Us** | Participants' own Fitbits, often months to years of data | Tens of thousands | EHR diagnoses. Mortality is incomplete. |
| **MESA Sleep, MrOS Sleep, SOF** | Wrist actigraphy (Actiwatch or SleepWatch), 5–7 days | ~2,000, ~2,900 (older men), ~3,000 (older women) | Adjudicated CVD events and mortality, with long follow-up |

Other cohorts with wrist accelerometry include China Kadoorie Biobank, Whitehall II, and the Rotterdam Study. They are usually collaboration-based and harder for outside groups to get into, so I'd treat them as second-tier unless you already have a contact.

## What access involves

**UK Biobank**
- Your institution registers, and you submit an application through the UKB Access Management System. It asks for a scientific rationale and the data fields you need, including the accelerometer fields.
- Approval typically takes weeks. There is a tiered access fee, in the low thousands to about £9k plus VAT. Check the current schedule, since US universities are eligible but lower tiers may not apply to you.
- Data are accessed only inside the UKB Research Analysis Platform (DNAnexus), where you pay for compute and storage. Raw `.cwa` files are very large. Most people use the derived summary fields or the open-source `biobankAccelerometerAnalysis` pipeline.

**NHANES**
- The public-use accelerometer data and the NCHS linked mortality files are free downloads with no application.
- Restricted-use linkages, such as Medicare claims for hospitalizations, require a proposal to the NCHS Research Data Center. It is slower, and you work in a secure environment.
- This is the most directly comparable US population sample, but it only gives you mortality unless you go through the RDC.

**All of Us**
- You register your institution, sign a data use agreement, complete the program's training, and verify your identity. Access is free through the cloud-based Researcher Workbench.
- Fitbit data are in the Registered Tier. Check whether your analysis needs Controlled Tier data.
- Fitbit data are consumer-grade and not comparable to Axivity or ActiGraph counts. Coverage of outcomes depends on EHR linkage, so deaths and events outside the health system can be missed.

- **Reverse causation.** Standard practice is to exclude the first 1–2 years of follow-up and adjust for baseline illness.

- NHANES 2003–06 used hip placement, so it doesn't meet your wrist requirement.
- Follow-up is shorter than in UK Biobank, and most deaths are all-cause.

- You submit a proposal to the CKB data access committee. International researchers can apply, and approval takes some weeks to months.

- Access is free through the Researcher Workbench. Your institution needs a Data Use and Registration Agreement, and you need to complete identity verification and the required training to reach controlled-tier data.

graders.name: 01-recall-porto-taxi
graders.evidence:
Five datasets fit, and two of them (Porto and San Francisco) you can download today with no application. I checked these sources on 11–12 Nov 2026. Everything below is confirmed from the named page unless I mark it "from memory." I did not build the interactive shortlist page, so there is no `dataset-shortlist.html`.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** timestamped GPS points along each trip or vehicle track, not just pickup and drop-off.
- **R2 (must):** at least a few hundred vehicles, taxi or ride-hailing, any city.
- **R3 (must):** enough points per trip for trajectory similarity and for travel-time labels. Travel time can come from the first and last timestamp of a trip.
- **R4 (nice):** per-trip segmentation, an occupancy flag and a sampling interval of about 15 s or finer.
- **R5 (nice):** a licence that allows publishing results.

I assumed academic use, so I didn't weigh commercial-use clauses heavily.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Porto taxis (ECML/PKDD 2015) | Direct download, no login | CC BY 4.0 | 442 taxis, 1.71M trips, 1 year | Strong. Trips are already segmented; points every 15 s. | Today (UCI page) |
| 2 | San Francisco cabs (CRAWDAD epfl/mobility) | Free IEEE DataPort login | CC BY 4.0 | ~500 cabs, 30 days, 91 MB | Strong. Points about 10 s apart with an occupied flag, but not split into trips. | Today (IEEE DataPort) |
| 3 | T-Drive (Beijing) | Direct download via OneDrive, no registration | None stated; asks you to cite two papers | 10,357 taxis, 1 week, ~15M points | Good for scale. Sampling is coarse (about 177 s) and tracks aren't split into trips. | Today (Microsoft page) |
| 4 | Grab-Posisi (Singapore, Jakarta) | Email request, research only | No licence named; no commercial use | ~84K trajectories, >80M pings, ~2 GB | Strong. 1 s sampling. Vehicle count isn't stated on the page, so check R2. | Today (Grab page) |
| 5 | Rome taxis (CRAWDAD roma/taxi) | IEEE DataPort subscription | Not confirmed | ~320 taxis, 30 days | Good. Points every 15 s, but not segmented into trips. | Search results only |

## Details
**1. Porto: [UCI page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015)**
- **Contents:** each row is one trip. `POLYLINE` is a list of `[lon, lat]` pairs, one per 15 s. Other fields are `TAXI_ID`, `TIMESTAMP` (trip start) and call type. Per-point times are start time plus 15 s × index.
- **Steps:** click "Download (509.3 MB)" on the UCI page, or run `fetch_ucirepo(id=339)` from the `ucimlrepo` package.
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0, so attribution only.
- **Use:** Brébisson et al. won the challenge's destination-prediction task ([arXiv 1508.00021](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.00021)). I didn't search for similarity or travel-time papers that use it.
- **Caveat:** the timestamps are regular by construction, so they carry no information of their own. Some trips have missing GPS segments; check this before using trip length as a label.

**2. San Francisco: [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-epflmobility)**
- **Contents:** one file per cab, each line `lat, lon, occupied, unix_time`. The occupied flag lets you cut each track into trips. Cab IDs are scrambled.
- **Steps:** create a free IEEE account, log in and download `cabspottingdata.tar.gz`. The page says both "Open Access" and "requires a DataPort subscription." My reading is that the free tier is enough, but I haven't tried the download.
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0.
- **Caveat:** the old CRAWDAD address (crawdad.org/epfl/mobility/20090224/) now returns 404, so use the IEEE DataPort page. A figshare copy ([San Francisco taxi trajectories](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302243.v1)) is listed as CC BY 4.0. I haven't checked what's different in it.

**3. T-Drive: [Microsoft Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/)**
- **Contents:** one file per taxi, each line `taxi_id, datetime, lon, lat`, covering 2–8 Feb 2008. The average gap is about 177 s (~623 m).
- **Steps:** click "Download the Trajectory Data" (OneDrive). Cite Yuan et al. (KDD '11 and GIS '10).
- **Licence:** none stated on the page. Treat it as research use with citation. I couldn't tell whether Microsoft's generic site terms apply.
- **Caveat:** a 3-minute gap is too coarse for precise route similarity unless you map-match. The data suits large-scale similarity benchmarks. Trips aren't segmented, so you would need a stay-point heuristic.

**4. Grab-Posisi: [Grab Engineering](https://engineering.grab.com/grab-posisi)**
- **Contents:** one Parquet file per trajectory with latitude, longitude, UTC timestamp, accuracy, bearing and speed at 1 s. It was collected in April 2019 from ride-hailing drivers' phones, with an Android or iOS label.
- **Steps:** email grab.posisi@grabtaxi.com with your name and contact details, your institution and your intended use. I don't have a typical turnaround; plan for days to weeks.
- **Licence:** research only, and you must cite Huang et al. 2019 ([DOI 10.1145/3356995.3364536](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3356995.3364536)). A published paper counts as research use.
- **Caveat:** the page doesn't say how many distinct drivers contributed. If you need a few hundred vehicles, ask when you email. A companion set, Grab-Posisi-L, has map-matched ground truth for 2,937 trajectories.

**5. Rome: [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi)**
- **Contents:** about 320 taxis, 1 Feb–2 Mar 2014, one point every 15 s. A user reports a 1.6 GB file of 21.8M lines. Details come from a search summary; I did not open the page.
- **Steps:** per the search summary, you need an IEEE DataPort subscription, which is free with an IEEE society membership. I did not confirm whether a plain free account is enough.
- **Licence:** not confirmed. The CRAWDAD version is cited as doi:10.15783/C7QC7M.

## Known, not confirmed
- **DiDi GAIA (Chengdu and Xi'an):** this is the best-known ride-hailing set, with driver tracks at 2–4 s sampling, order IDs, and a 2016 and an alternate 2018 release. The portal ([outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/)) returned HTTP 501 to my checker. From memory and search summaries, access is by registration and an application stating your research plan, with credit to DiDi in publications. A paper citing the portal in January 2026 suggests it was still up, but I found nothing on whether applications are currently open. Open the portal in a browser. If it's closed, use Porto and Grab-Posisi instead.
- **Bangkok taxi trajectories ([Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/17003809)):** open, CC BY 4.0, 4–24 Apr 2019, but only 33.5 MB. The page doesn't give the number of taxis, and sampling is 1–3 minutes. Check the vehicle count before relying on it.
- **Other possible sources:** Shanghai SUVnet and several Shenzhen or Shanghai files on figshare. I haven't verified their access or contents.

## Not recommended
- **[NYC telematics (Zenodo 6647220)](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220):** 16 files, about 25 MB, from a single session, with no vehicle count given. It is not a fleet.
- **GeoLife:** I didn't search for it. From memory it holds individual people's tracks rather than taxis, so it doesn't meet R2.
- **Hugging Face trajectory hits:** the HF hits ("Porto_Taxi_Trajectory", "porto_taxi") are third-party copies. Use UCI for Porto.

## What I could not find
- A trip-segmented, high-frequency (≤5 s) taxi set from several hundred vehicles with no application required. Grab-Posisi is the closest but needs an email request. DiDi would also fit but is unconfirmed.
- I didn't search for papers on how each dataset is used for similarity or travel time, beyond the Porto one above. [T-JEPA (arXiv 2406.12913)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.12913) came up in the T-Drive search, but I didn't open it to see which datasets it uses.

## Next step
Download Porto first. It is the only one that is fully open, already split into trips, and large enough. Use it to build and test your similarity and travel-time code. In parallel, email Grab for Grab-Posisi, since it has 1 s sampling and per-trip files, and register for IEEE DataPort to get San Francisco. Open the DiDi portal in a browser to see whether applications are open. Add T-Drive if you need a very large fleet and can accept the 3-minute sampling.

Sources:
- [UCI Porto](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015)
- [T-Drive](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/)
- [Grab-Posisi](https://engineering.grab.com/grab-posisi)
- [CRAWDAD epfl/mobility](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-epflmobility)
- [CRAWDAD roma/taxi](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi)
- [Zenodo Bangkok](https://zenodo.org/records/17003809)
- [Zenodo NYC telematics](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220)
- [DiDi GAIA portal](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/)

The portal ([outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/)) returned HTTP 501 to my checker. From memory and search summaries, access is by registration and an application stating your research plan, with credit to DiDi in publications. - **Hugging Face trajectory hits:** the HF hits ("Porto_Taxi_Trajectory", "porto_taxi") are third-party copies. Use UCI for Porto.

- **R1 (must):** timestamped GPS point sequences along each trip, not just pickup and drop-off.
- **R2 (must):** at least a few hundred vehicles, in any city.
- **R3 (must):** usable for trajectory similarity and travel-time estimation. That means a fixed trip start and end, or enough points to cut trips yourself.
- **R4 (nice):** downloadable now, with a licence that allows research use.

## Shortlist

| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Porto taxi trajectories (ECML/PKDD 2015) | Direct download, no account stated | CC BY 4.0 | 442 taxis, 1.71M trips, one point every 15 s | Today, UCI page |
| 2 | T-Drive, Beijing | Download from a Microsoft Research page (hosted on OneDrive) | None stated; citation requested | 10,357 taxis, about 15M points, one week in Feb 2008, about 177 s between points | Today |
| 3 | Rome taxi (CRAWDAD roma/taxi) | Free IEEE DataPort account | CC BY 4.0 | About 320 taxis, 30 days, about 374 MB compressed | Today, partly |
| 4 | Didi GAIA, Chengdu and Xi'an | Registration or application to Didi | Didi terms of use | Chengdu has about 1.1M drivers, Nov 2016 | Partly, from search results |

## Details

**1. Porto.** This is the safest start. Each trip is one row with a `POLYLINE` of `[lon, lat]` pairs and a `TIMESTAMP`. The sampling is regular at 15 s, so each point's time is trip start plus 15 s times its index. Trip start and end are explicit.
- **Access:** download `train.csv.zip` (about 509 MB) from the [UCI page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015), or run `pip install ucimlrepo` and call `fetch_ucirepo(id=339)`. The page shows only an optional login link.
- **Mirrors:** there are copies on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Davidham3/Porto_Taxi_Trajectory) (Apache-2.0, ungated) and [figshare](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302165.v1) (CC BY 4.0). The UCI copy is the original, so use that one.
- **Caveats:** `MISSING_DATA` flags gaps in some trips. The data has trip-level timestamps and fixed 15 s spacing rather than per-point times.
- **Use:** it is the standard benchmark for travel-time and destination prediction, and I recall (not checked today) that it is common in trajectory-similarity papers.

**2. T-Drive.**
- **Contents:** one text file per taxi, with lines of `taxi_id, datetime, lon, lat`.
- **Access:** the [Microsoft Research page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/) has a "Download the Trajectory Data" link. The page states no registration and no licence, only a request to cite the KDD '11 and GIS '10 papers. The [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf) may say more, and I didn't read it.
- **Caveats:** there are no trip boundaries, so you have to split trips yourself. The long gaps between points (about 177 s) are poor for fine-grained similarity. That is also why it is a good test of sparse-trajectory methods.
- **Copies to avoid:** some secondary descriptions of this dataset (6 months, 30,000 taxis) don't match Microsoft's own description. The [TIB record](https://doi.org/10.57702/enayhf6y) returned a 404. The [IEEE DataPort "POETIC – Tdrive and nyc"](https://doi.org/10.21227/rgbn-cw81) copy needs a subscription.

**3. Rome.** Lines look like `DRIVER_ID;TIMESTAMP;POINT(lat lon)`, sorted by time. The data was originally on CRAWDAD and is now on [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-romataxi). The page says open access but also that a logged-in account is needed, and one line mentions a "subscription". A free IEEE account is probably enough, but confirm this when you download.
- **Caveats:** there are no trip IDs, so you have to segment trips. The sampling interval is inconsistent between sources (the page says 7 s, another source says 15 s). Check this against the data.

**4. Didi GAIA (Chengdu and Xi'an, Oct/Nov 2016).** This is the largest source and the closest to ride-hailing. Records have driver ID, order ID, timestamp, lon and lat. It is the only one here that is ride-hailing rather than taxi data.
- **Access:** the portal is [outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/). My fetch returned HTTP 501, so I could not read the form.
- **What I found:** a PLOS ONE paper says you can access it after free registration. A 2026 MDPI paper says it is available from Didi for academic research under their terms, and that derived data can only be shared with Didi's permission.
- **Before you plan around it:** confirm today whether the portal is still accepting requests, how long approval takes, and whether the terms restrict redistribution.

## Known, not confirmed
- **San Francisco Cabspotting.** I recall about 500 taxis with timestamped GPS from the original CRAWDAD epfl/mobility trace. There is a [figshare copy](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12302243.v1) with a CC BY 4.0 record, but I couldn't open the landing page. Its terms may differ from the original's, so check them before relying on it.
- **Shenzhen and Shanghai taxi datasets** (for example [Pingshan, Shenzhen](https://doi.org/10.13140/rg.2.2.20676.80007), [Shanghai taxi demand/flow](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31481464.v2)). The DOIs are real but both landing pages blocked me. The Shanghai one may be aggregated flows rather than raw points. The Pingshan one covers a single day. I haven't checked either one's size or fit.
- **Bangkok taxi trajectories on Zenodo** ([tourist trajectories](https://zenodo.org/records/17005200) and [segmented trips](https://zenodo.org/records/17003809)). Both are open under CC BY 4.0 (confirmed). They look like derived subsets, and I didn't check the vehicle count.

## Not recommended
- **IEEE DataPort "Taxi trajectories"** ([10.21227/rxw4-1r28](https://doi.org/10.21227/rxw4-1r28)): it needs a paid subscription, and the file names look like NYC 2015 taxi data, which is pickup and drop-off only.
- **NYC TLC trip records:** pickup and drop-off only.
- **GeoLife:** about 180 users, not taxis.
- **The [NYC telematics Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/6647220):** I verified that it exists but not its contents, so I left it out.

## What I could not find
- **Several searches returned nothing relevant.** The "ride-hailing GPS" query returned nothing useful from DataCite, OpenAIRE and Zenodo.
- **Pages I couldn't open.** Didi's portal gave a server error, and the original CRAWDAD page returned 404. Neither Didi's current terms nor T-Drive's user-guide terms were read.
- **No evidence-of-use check.** I did not run the step that finds papers using each dataset. The literature search returned only generic surveys, so I can't point you to similarity or ETA baselines from this session.
- **No HTML shortlist page.** I skipped it because this reply covers the same content.

## Next step
1. Start with Porto, since it is clean and open and has a known benchmark setup.
2. Add Rome or T-Drive for a second city with a different sampling rate.
3. Apply to Didi now if you want ride-hailing data, because approval may take time.

The registries (Zenodo, DataCite, OpenAIRE, Hugging Face) mostly returned noise, so the datasets below come from web search. I did not build the interactive shortlist page.

I checked these on 2026-11-11. "Confirmed" means I read it today from the source named. "Memory" means I believe it but didn't confirm it.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** timestamped GPS points along each trip, not only pickup and drop-off.
- **R2 (must):** at least a few hundred vehicles, taxi or ride-hailing, any city.
- **R3 (nice):** a sampling interval fine enough for travel-time estimation and similarity measures.
- **R4 (nice):** downloadable today. I assumed you're doing academic, non-commercial work.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Porto taxi (ECML/PKDD 2015) | Direct download | CC BY 4.0 (memory; UCI page's licence text didn't load) | 442 taxis, 1.71M trips, 1 year, point every 15 s | Strong | Today (contents); licence from memory |
| 2 | CRAWDAD epfl/mobility (San Francisco cabs) | Free IEEE DataPort account | Not stated on the page; no-deanonymisation clause | ~500 cabs, 25–30 days, ~11M points | Strong | Today |

| 5 | DiDi GAIA (Chengdu, Xi'an) | Application and approval (memory) | DiDi's terms (memory) | Millions of orders, ~3 s sampling (per papers) | Strong if you get it | Not confirmed: official site returned HTTP 501 |

## Details

**1. Porto.** All trips are in one CSV, one row per completed trip. Each row has a `POLYLINE` of GPS points, taxi ID, start timestamp, and call type.

graders.name: 01-recall-porto-taxi
graders.evidence:
Here are the ones I know that fit your criteria. I'm going from memory and haven't checked the links or terms live, so confirm each before you build on it.

| Dataset | City / scale | Sampling | What you do to get it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Porto taxi (ECML/PKDD 2015)** | Porto, 442 taxis, about 1.7M trips, 1.5 years | 15 s | Easiest. Download it from the UCI ML Repository (search "Taxi Service Trajectory – Prediction Challenge") with no login, under CC BY 4.0. It's also on Kaggle, where you need an account and have to accept the rules. |
| **T-Drive (Microsoft Research)** | Beijing, 10,357 taxis, about 15M points, one week in Feb 2008 | Irregular, about 3 min on average | Download from the Microsoft Research T-Drive page. Registration is minimal or none, but you must cite their papers. |
| **Didi GAIA Open Data** | Chengdu and Xi'an, Nov 2016, thousands of cars | 2–4 s | Apply through the GAIA portal with your institution and research purpose. Approval is manual and aimed at academics. Access has changed over time, so check that it's still open. |
| **Rome taxi (CRAWDAD `roma/taxi`)** | Rome, 320 taxis, 30 days in Feb 2014 | About 7 s | Create a free CRAWDAD account and accept the data-use agreement. |
| **San Francisco Cabspotting (CRAWDAD `epfl/mobility`)** | SF, about 536 taxis, about 1 month in 2008 | About 1 min, with an occupancy flag | Same CRAWDAD account and agreement. |

**Notes**
- **Porto**: Each trip is a `POLYLINE` of lon/lat pairs. There is only a start `TIMESTAMP`, so point *i* is at start + 15·*i* s. Some rows are empty or have missing-data flags, so filter them. The dataset has `ORIGIN_CALL` and `TAXI_ID` fields, and trips are already split. This makes it the cleanest for travel-time estimation, because trip duration is the polyline length times 15 s.
- **T-Drive and Cabspotting**: These are continuous per-vehicle logs, not trips. You'll have to segment them yourself. Cabspotting's occupancy flag makes that easy, but T-Drive has no such flag, so you'd split on time gaps or stops. T-Drive also has duplicate and noisy points, and you'll probably want to map-match it.
- **Didi**: It has the densest sampling and real ride-hailing behavior. If you only need a fast start, it's the least convenient of the five.
- **Excluded**: NYC TLC and Chicago taxi data give only pickup/drop-off, so they don't meet your requirement. GeoLife has dense GPS but its 182 users aren't taxis.
- **Possibly restricted**: Shanghai SUVnet (about 4,000 taxis) and Grab-Posisi (Southeast Asia) have been available on request or via past challenges. I'm not sure they're currently open.

**Suggestion**: Start with Porto for both tasks, since its fixed sampling interval makes similarity metrics like DTW, Fréchet and EDR simple to run. Then use T-Drive or Didi to test robustness on irregular or denser sampling. If you want, I can write a loader and trip-segmentation script for any of these.

graders.name: 01-recall-porto-taxi
graders.evidence:
I'm going from memory rather than live-checking the pages, so confirm the links, license terms and sizes before you commit to one. Hosting for older datasets (CRAWDAD especially) has moved over the years.

## Easiest to get, no approval needed

| Dataset | Scale and sampling | What you have to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Porto taxi (ECML/PKDD 2015)** | 442 taxis, about 1.7M trips, July 2013 to June 2014. One GPS point every 15 s, stored as a `POLYLINE` of lon/lat per trip. | Download it from the UCI ML Repository, which needs no login. The Kaggle copy needs a Kaggle account and acceptance of the competition rules. |
| **T-Drive (Microsoft Research, Beijing)** | 10,357 taxis, one week in Feb 2008, about 15M points. Sampling is sparse, around 3 minutes on average. | Download it from the Microsoft Research page, which is free. They ask you to cite the T-Drive papers. |

## Registration or a request required

| Dataset | Scale and sampling | What you have to do |
|---|---|---|
| **San Francisco "epfl/mobility" (Cabspotting)** | 536 taxis, about 30 days in May 2008. Points arrive roughly every minute, with an **occupancy flag**. | It's hosted via CRAWDAD. Create an account, accept the data-use terms, and download. Check whether it has moved to IEEE DataPort. |
| **Rome taxi (CRAWDAD `roma/taxi`)** | 320 taxis, 30 days in Feb 2014, about 7 s sampling. | Same CRAWDAD process as above. |
| **Didi GAIA Open Data (Chengdu and Xi'an)** | Ride-hailing cars, Oct to Nov 2016. Sampling is about 2 to 4 s, so very dense. | Apply on the GAIA site with your institution and project description. Approval is manual, and you agree not to redistribute. Availability has been inconsistent, so check it's currently accepting applications. |
| **Shanghai taxi (SUVnet)** | Several thousand taxis. | Email the SJTU group that maintains it and state your academic purpose. Response times vary. |

## Which to use

- **Trajectory similarity:** Porto and T-Drive are the standard benchmarks, so your results will be comparable with published work.
- **Travel-time estimation:** Porto is the practical choice. Trip duration is (number of points − 1) × 15 s, and trips are already segmented. Didi is better if you can get it, because its dense sampling supports finer-grained road-level work.

## Caveats

- **Porto:** some trips have `MISSING_DATA=True`, and others have GPS jumps. Filter these first. It has no map-matching, so you'll need OSM plus something like Valhalla or FMM if you want road segments.
- **T-Drive:** it's continuous per-taxi logs with no trip boundaries or occupancy flag. You'd have to segment trips yourself. The sampling is also too sparse for fine-grained similarity.
- **San Francisco:** the occupancy flag lets you split trips cleanly, but the sampling is coarse.

**Skip** NYC TLC, Chicago and Uber Movement. They only have pickup/drop-off or aggregated speeds, not point sequences. GeoLife has real trajectories but comes from 182 people, mostly walking and transit, not taxis.

Porto alone meets your "few hundred vehicles" bar, so I'd start there. Add T-Drive or Didi for cross-city generalization. I can write a loader and cleaning script for Porto if that would help.

cases.promptMarkdown: I'm a second-year PhD student in labor economics. graders.name: 01-recall-german-iab
graders.evidence:
I found no open or free-download dataset that lets you follow workers across firms with firm identifiers. Every usable option needs an application, and the realistic ones take weeks to months. Search results from the data registries were mostly noise, so the access facts below come from the agency pages (checked 2026-11-12) unless I say "from memory".

## What I assumed you need
- **R1:** a panel of at least 10 years.
- **R2:** a worker ID and a firm ID on every job spell.
- **R3:** enough job movers to give a large connected set.
- **R4:** wages or earnings for each job.
- I assumed any country is fine, that you can wait for an application, and that you have no affiliation with a particular country's institutions.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Size / span | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [MCVL (Spain)](https://portaldatos.seg-social.gob.es/mcvl) | Application, free, non-commercial research; weeks | Worker sample, annual waves (from memory: 4% sample, since 2004) | Strong on R1–R3; earnings are capped | Today (page); sample size from memory |
| 2 | [LIAB (Germany)](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/integrated-establishment-and-individual-data/liab/) | Application, on-site or remote desktop with vetted output; weeks to months | Daily biographies 1975–2024 | Strong, but selective sample | Today |
| 3 | [SIAB (Germany)](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/) | The downloadable file needs a use agreement; the version with establishment IDs is on-site or remote only | Biographies from 1975 | Partial | Today |
| 4 | [Veneto Worker Histories (Italy)](https://www.frdb.org/en/dati/dati-inps-carriere-lavorative-in-veneto/) | Signed form emailed to the foundation that distributes it; weeks | 1975–2001 | Good for methods, but ends in 2001 | Today |
| 5 | [Admin3 (Hungary)](https://adatbank.krtk.mta.hu/en/2020/02/) | Data request form; tied to KRTK researchers; months | 2003–2017 | Strong data, hard to access | Today, partly |
| 6 | [LEHD (US)](https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/) | Research data center proposal; 6–12+ months | Quarterly earnings, state-based | Strong, slow | Today |
| 7 | [Statistics Denmark IDA](https://dst.dk/en/TilSalg/Forskningsservice/Dataadgang/Autorisering) | Needs a Danish host institution; months | From memory: from 1980 | Strong, but needs a host | Access today, coverage from memory |

## Details
- **MCVL (Spain), my pick for a second-year student.** Institutions that justify non-commercial research can request it, and the Social Security data portal has an online form. A directorate there must approve it, and one academic source mentions about 11 forms (it may have changed). Employer episodes are identified by the employer's social-security account code. Contributions are capped, which understates the top of the distribution, and that matters for rising inequality. You must cite the directorate and send them your outputs. Research rooms in Madrid, Barcelona and Albacete are an alternative. The weeks-level timing is my estimate, not something I confirmed.
- **LIAB (Germany).** Workers come from firms in the IAB Establishment Panel. Firms with up to 49 employees contribute all workers, and larger firms contribute a 20% sample. You pick one base period per project (1993–2000, 2000–2007, 2007–2017 or 2014–2024). The biographies run 1975–2024. The page says the FDZ will provide AKM effects for 1985–2023 on request, which is a useful check on your own estimates. The page doesn't say whether researchers abroad can use it (the FDZ's international network, IDAN, may be the route), so email the FDZ before you plan around it.
- **SIAB (Germany).** The page says the downloadable file has no establishment identifiers, so you can't run AKM on it. The version that has them is on-site or remote only. The 2% sample size is from memory.
- **Veneto (Italy).** The foundation's page says to "fill and sign the attached form" and email it. It has worker and firm files with firm tax codes. A 2018 INPS paper says access is free. It stops in 2001, so it can't speak to recent inequality trends. It does give you full AKM data to build and test your code.
- **Admin3 (Hungary).** The page describes it as 2003–2017, with a successor database (Admin4) described in a 2026 working paper. The access pages suggest you need a KRTK researcher as co-author or supervisor, and the same pages cover several datasets, so confirm the Admin3 terms.
- **LEHD (US).** You work in a secure research data center after Census approval, and the proposal must show a benefit to Census. A regional center's page quotes 6–12 months or more.
- **Denmark IDA.** The statistics office only authorises Danish institutions, so foreign researchers need a Danish host.

## Known, not confirmed
I only searched the web for these and have no verified record.
- **Finland (FLEED).** Population-wide employer-employee data. Foreign access is possible, but remote access needs a Finnish affiliation and business data are often on-site only (old source).
- **Sweden (MONA).** Online remote platform. I found no current rules for foreign researchers.
- **Norway.** The remote system serves researchers with a Norwegian ID.
- **Canada (CEEDD).** Access through Statistics Canada's research data centers or its Centre for Data Development and Economic Research. Researchers cover the full cost (older source).
- **Portugal (Quadros de Pessoal).** Ask the labor ministry's planning office. I found no formal procedure. The Banco de Portugal route appears restricted to the bank's researchers (2018 guide).
- **France, Netherlands, Austria.** Not searched; from memory, restricted-access data exist for all three.

## Not recommended
- **Brazil public RAIS.** It is open, but de-identified, so you can't follow workers across years. The identified version needs a request to the Ministry of Labour and a cooperation agreement.
- **SIAB Campus File.** Free, but teaching only, with no publications allowed.
- **LEHD public aggregates (QWI, LODES, J2J).** No worker histories.
- **Replication packages for the Taiwan and Brazil AKM papers.** Useful as code, but the microdata are restricted. The pages blocked my automated checks.

## What I could not find
- An open worker-by-firm panel with identified firms.
- Current foreign-researcher rules for Sweden, Norway and Finland.

## Next step
**What you can start on today:**
1. Write and test your AKM pipeline on simulated worker–firm data: connected-set pruning, high-dimensional fixed effects, and variance decomposition with a bias correction for limited mobility (e.g. Kline–Saggio–Sølvsten). These tools exist from memory; I did not check them here.
2. Read the replication code from the Taiwan and Brazil papers.

**Applications:**
- Start the MCVL application now.
- In parallel, email the German research data center about LIAB access from abroad.
- Ask your advisor whether anyone has a Danish, Hungarian or US research data center link.

The interactive comparison page is at `/private/tmp/e-G1qLVr/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

Search results from the data registries were mostly noise, so the access facts below come from the agency pages (checked 2026-11-12) unless I say "from memory".

## What I assumed you need

- **R2:** a worker ID and a firm ID on every job spell.
- **R3:** enough job movers to give a large connected set.
- **R4:** wages or earnings for each job.

| 1 | [MCVL (Spain)](https://portaldatos.seg-social.gob.es/mcvl) | Application, free, non-commercial research; weeks | Worker sample, annual waves (from memory: 4% sample, since 2004) | Strong on R1–R3; earnings are capped | Today (page); sample size from memory |

| 6 | [LEHD (US)](https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/) | Research data center proposal; 6–12+ months | Quarterly earnings, state-based | Strong, slow | Today |
